## 0.4 Identifier conventions

  DEF-nnn   A defect in existing material. Has: location, class, severity,
            failure mode, corrected artifact.
  CTL-nnn   A control in the canonical stack. Has: invariant served, artifact,
            failure mode if absent, verification test.
  EP-n      One of the Red Team's seven easiest entry points.
  TEST-nnn  An automated test. Lives in the repo. Runs in CI. Fails the build.
  RISK-nnn  A residual risk that is accepted, not mitigated.

Severity scale for DEF:
  S1  Enables key theft, fund loss, or full account takeover.
  S2  Enables data exfiltration, privilege escalation, or persistent access.
  S3  Enables denial of service, control bypass, or detection evasion.
  S4  Code does not run, silently no-ops, or is operationally self-defeating.
  S5  False premise, contradiction, or dishonest claim. Corrupts later decisions.



## 0.5 The contract with the implementing agent

You, the implementing agent, must satisfy these conditions. They are not
suggestions.

  C-1  Do not implement any superseded artifact from 0.3. If you find yourself
       copying a snippet from ADDENDUM L or the war game, stop and check 0.3.

  C-2  Do not mark a control complete until its TEST-nnn exists, runs in CI, and
       has been observed to FAIL when the control is deliberately removed. A
       test that has never failed is not a test.

  C-3  When a control cannot be implemented as specified (a dependency does not
       exist on arm64, a free tier changed, an API moved), do not silently
       substitute a weaker control. Record it as a new DEF, propose the
       substitute, and flag it for human decision. Silent downgrade is the
       failure mode that killed the original spec.

  C-4  Every claim of the form "free" must be verified against the provider's
       current pricing page at implementation time and recorded in the cost
       table. See PART 9 for the corrected baseline.

  C-5  Phase 0 does not ship until PART 6 Gate 1 passes in full. There is no
       partial launch of a custody system.

  C-6  Where this document says "reject", it means return an error and do not
       proceed. It does not mean log a warning and continue.

================================================================================
PART 1 — THE ARGUMENT: THIS STACK VERSUS ITSELF
================================================================================

Fourteen arguments. Each is stated as a position, attacked as hard as I can
attack it, defended, and ruled. The ruling is what gets built. Where a ruling
overturns the existing spec, the ruling is authoritative and the reasoning is
recorded so that nobody re-litigates it in six months and quietly reverts it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 1 — Is envelope encryption worth anything when the KEK lives on the
             same host as the ciphertext?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (the existing spec):
"Envelope encryption with KEK/DEK separation is industry standard and correct.
ADDENDUM L implements it. The Red Team's own assessment lists 'Envelope
encryption with HSM-backed KEK' as the number one hardest target: 'we can't
decrypt keys.'"

ATTACK:
Read what actually ships. ADDENDUM L offers three KEK providers: AWS KMS, GCP
KMS, HashiCorp Vault. ADDENDUM D and the docker-compose then configure
`secrets: master_kek: file: /opt/osiris/secrets/master_kek.txt`. The security
env-var block says `# MASTER_KEK=only_for_local_dev`. The Vault option, if
self-hosted, runs on the same Oracle box.

So the deployed reality is one of:
  (a) The KEK is a file on the Oracle host, mounted into the app container.
  (b) The KEK is in AWS KMS, which costs money and requires an AWS account —
      contradicting the entire zero-budget premise the war game was written
      under.

In case (a), the attack chain is: RCE on the app container -> read
/run/secrets/master_kek -> read Postgres (the app already has credentials) ->
unwrap every DEK -> decrypt every private key -> drain every wallet. The DEK
layer added exactly one file read to the attacker's work. It is not a security
boundary. It is a filing system.

Worse, the Red Team's assessment is *built on this being real*. Their conclusion
"we need to break 5+ layers to get keys, that's expensive, we'll move on" is
false if the KEK is on the box. In that world they need to break exactly one
layer: the app process. Everything downstream is one `cat` away. The single most
reassuring line in the entire Red Team assessment is load-bearing on an
assumption the architecture does not satisfy.

DEFENCE ATTEMPT:
"Docker secrets are tmpfs-mounted and not on disk. The container is read-only.
There is no shell in the container."
This is not a defence. A Node process with RCE reads /run/secrets with
`fs.readFileSync`. No shell required. Read-only rootfs does not make files
unreadable. The tmpfs detail protects against disk forensics, which is not the
threat here.

"Then use AWS KMS."
That is a real improvement and I will keep it as an option. But it fails a
different test: it introduces an AWS account as a new crown-jewel credential,
it costs money (breaking the stated constraint, which matters because the
constraint is what makes the plan actually get executed), and — the decisive
point — KMS still returns the plaintext DEK to the app host. The app then
decrypts the private key into Node's heap. So even with KMS, RCE on the app host
during any signing window yields key material, and RCE at rest yields the
ability to request unwrapping of every DEK at will. KMS raises the cost of the
offline attack (stolen DB backup alone is useless) but does almost nothing
against the online attack (compromised app host), which is the attack the Red
Team actually ranked as easiest.

RULING:
Envelope encryption is retained as a component and rejected as the boundary.
The boundary moves. Key material must never be delivered to the application
host at all — not wrapped, not unwrapped, not for 50ms. The application host
sends an *unsigned transaction* to a separate signing service and receives a
*signature* back. It never possesses anything it could steal.

This is CTL-100, the Remote Signer, specified in full in PART 4.1. It is the
single largest change this document makes and everything else in PART 4 assumes
it.

CONSEQUENCE:
  - INV-1 becomes achievable rather than aspirational.
  - "Zero-memory signing" on the app host becomes moot, which conveniently
    resolves ARGUMENT 4.
  - The panic button becomes real (ARGUMENT 6).
  - Some availability is traded away deliberately (ARGUMENT 3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 2 — Doesn't a remote signer just move the single point of failure?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION:
"You have replaced 'compromise the Oracle host' with 'compromise the Cloudflare
account.' The Cloudflare account is one password reset away. You have not
improved anything, you have added a dependency and a new blast radius."

ATTACK ON MY OWN POSITION — steelmanned:
This is the strongest objection to CTL-100 and it is partly right. If the signer
Worker holds the KEK and an attacker takes the Cloudflare account, they can read
the Worker's secret, edit the Worker to log unwrapped keys, or simply replace
the policy engine with `return sign(everything)`. Cloudflare account takeover is
also a *quieter* path than host RCE: no AIDE alert, no auditd event, no unusual
process, nothing on the Oracle box changes at all.

Additionally: Workers free tier has no SLA, a 100k request/day cap, and a 10ms
CPU limit per invocation. Cloudflare can change free-tier terms. A trading
system whose signing path depends on someone's free tier is fragile.

DEFENCE:
The objection assumes the Cloudflare account alone is sufficient. It is not, and
the design must make sure it is not. Three separations do the work:

  1. SPLIT OF MATERIAL. The Worker holds the KEK. It does NOT hold the wrapped
     DEKs or the ciphertext private keys — those live in Postgres on Oracle. The
     Worker is stateless with respect to wallets: it receives the encrypted blob
     in the request. So Cloudflare-account-only gives an attacker a decryption
     oracle with no ciphertext to feed it. They must ALSO reach the database.

  2. SPLIT OF AUTHORITY. Every signing request must carry an Ed25519 signature
     from the application's request-signing key, which is a Docker secret on
     Oracle. The Worker rejects unsigned requests. So Cloudflare-account-only
     also lacks the ability to produce a valid request. They must ALSO reach the
     Oracle host.

  3. SPLIT OF ACCOUNT. The signer Worker lives in a *different Cloudflare
     account* from the one serving DNS and the site, with a different email,
     different hardware key, and no shared API tokens. Compromising the "site"
     Cloudflare account — the one that is used daily, has more tokens, and is
     more likely to be phished — does not touch the signer.

Result: an attacker needs (signer Cloudflare account) AND (Oracle host OR
database), or they need (Oracle host) AND (database) AND to defeat the policy
engine and rate limits, which as shown in ARGUMENT 5 caps the damage rather than
permitting a drain. That is a genuine 2-of-3, and it is the first point in this
architecture where the Red Team's "break 5+ layers" claim becomes true rather
than flattering.

On availability: yes, the signer is a hard dependency and if it is down, nobody
can trade. That is the correct failure direction for a custody system. "Trading
is unavailable" is an inconvenience. "Funds are gone" is terminal. I am
deliberately choosing the inconvenience. See ARGUMENT 3.

On free-tier limits: 100k requests/day against a system whose realistic Phase 0
volume is hundreds of signatures/day is 3 orders of magnitude of headroom. The
10ms CPU limit is the real constraint and it dictates an implementation
decision: the Worker must NOT import @solana/web3.js. It parses the transaction
message with a purpose-written ~150-line parser. This is specified in
CTL-101.

RULING:
Remote signer is adopted, with mandatory account separation, mandatory request
signing, and the wrapped DEKs deliberately kept out of the signer. If the
implementing agent cannot achieve a second, separate Cloudflare account, it must
stop and flag it — running the signer in the same account as the site erases
separation 3 and materially weakens the design.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 3 — Should we just use AWS KMS and stop being clever?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION:
"A Cloudflare Worker with a secret in it is not an HSM. AWS KMS is a real
FIPS-validated HSM boundary with audit logging, IAM, key policies, grants, and
automatic rotation. You are hand-rolling a security-critical service to save one
dollar a month. That is the classic mistake."

DEFENCE:
Two responses, and the second is the important one.

First, on cost: AWS KMS is roughly $1 per key per month plus per-request charges
(verify current pricing at implementation time; see PART 9). That is not the
objection. The objection is that adding an AWS account adds a root credential,
a billing relationship, an IAM surface, and a recovery path — four new things to
secure, each with its own account-takeover story — to a project whose stated
operating premise is minimal surface and no vendor sprawl. The AWS account root
becomes a crown jewel equal to the Cloudflare account. You have not reduced the
number of accounts that can end you; you have increased it.

Second, and decisively: KMS solves the wrong half of the problem. KMS gives you
a strong wrap/unwrap boundary. It does not give you a *policy* boundary. With
KMS, the app host calls Decrypt, receives the DEK, decrypts the private key in
its own heap, and signs whatever it likes. A compromised app host with KMS
access can sign a transaction that sends every lamport to the attacker. The KMS
audit log will faithfully record that the decryption was authorized.

What actually stops a compromised app host from draining a wallet is a signer
that *reads the transaction and refuses*. That is CTL-102, the policy engine,
and it is only possible because signing happens somewhere the app host does not
control. KMS cannot do it — KMS does not know what a Solana transaction is. AWS
Nitro Enclaves or CloudHSM with custom firmware could, at real cost and real
complexity.

RULING:
Cloudflare Worker signer with policy engine is primary. AWS KMS is retained as a
documented alternate KEK provider behind the existing `KEKProvider` interface,
for the case where the operator prefers a commercial custody boundary and
accepts the cost. If AWS KMS is chosen, the policy engine must still exist —
implemented in the signer service, which then runs somewhere else (a second
minimal host), because the policy engine is the control that actually matters.

The order of value is, and the implementing agent should internalize this:
  policy engine  >  where the KEK lives  >  which cipher wraps the DEK.
The existing spec spends most of its security budget on the third item.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 4 — Is "zero-memory signing" real?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (the existing spec):
"Zero-memory signing: keys exist for < 50ms. Listed by the Red Team as hardest
target number 2."

ATTACK:
It is not real in Node.js as written, and the code that implements it has a
separate live bug.

Why it is not real:
  - `Keypair.fromSecretKey(privateKeyBytes)` copies the bytes. tweetnacl copies
    them again internally. `privateKeyBytes.fill(0)` zeroes your buffer and none
    of the copies.
  - V8's generational GC copies live objects between semispaces during scavenge.
    A 64-byte Uint8Array can be duplicated to a new address at any moment. The
    old copy is not zeroed, it is abandoned. `global.gc()` does not scrub freed
    memory; it makes it available for reuse.
  - Node has no `mlock`. The pages can be swapped. Oracle's Ubuntu image has
    swap enabled by default.
  - A core dump, an OOM heap snapshot, `process.report.writeReport()`, an
    inspector session, or any of a dozen diagnostics will happily serialize the
    heap including whatever key bytes are still resident.
  - The 50ms figure describes the intended lifetime of *your* reference, not the
    lifetime of the bytes in RAM, which is unbounded.

The live bug (DEF-050): the reference implementation returns
`transaction.signature?.toString("base64")`. For a `VersionedTransaction`,
`signature` is not a Buffer and for the versioned path the field accessed is
wrong; `Uint8Array.prototype.toString()` ignores its argument and returns a
comma-joined decimal list. The function as written returns strings like
"12,45,200,7,..." and, separately, Solana signatures are conventionally base58,
not base64. Any code downstream that treats this as a transaction signature —
confirmation polling, the webhookEvents UNIQUE constraint, the explorer link —
is broken. This has nothing to do with security and everything to do with the
fact that the snippet was never run.

DEFENCE ATTEMPT:
"Best effort is better than nothing."
Partially true, and best effort is retained. But it must not be *counted on*,
and the Red Team must not be allowed to list it as a hard target, because a
plan that assumes a soft control is hard is worse than a plan with a known gap.

RULING:
Zero-memory signing is deleted as a security boundary and retained as hygiene in
the one place it still applies. Under CTL-100 the application host never
receives key material, so there is nothing to scrub there. Inside the signer
Worker, key material lives in an isolate that is destroyed after the request,
with no swap, no core dumps, no debugger, and no persistence — which is the
first environment in this architecture where the claim is close to true, and
even there it is stated as "short-lived isolate," not "zeroed memory."

The Red Team's "hardest targets" list is corrected in PART 8.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 5 — If the app host is compromised, is anything actually saved?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION:
"Fine, the attacker with RCE can't read keys. But they can call the signer all
day. They will just sign a swap that dumps every wallet into a token they
control. Same outcome, more steps."

This is the correct objection and it deserves a precise answer rather than
reassurance.

ANALYSIS:
What can a compromised app host make the signer do?

The signer's policy engine (CTL-102) enforces, per request:
  P1  Fee payer equals the wallet the request is for, and equals the public key
      derived from the decrypted secret key. Signing for a different wallet than
      the blob provided is impossible.
  P2  Every top-level program ID is on an allowlist. Solana requires invoked
      program IDs to appear in the transaction's *static* account keys, not in
      an address lookup table, so this check is complete without resolving ALTs
      and without an RPC call.
  P3  The only permitted `SystemProgram::Transfer` destinations are the known
      Helius/Jito tip accounts, capped at `tipCapLamports`, plus rent-exempt
      minimums for ATA creation, capped at `rentCapLamports`.
  P4  No top-level SPL Token or Token-2022 `Transfer`, `TransferChecked`,
      `Approve`, `Revoke`, `SetAuthority`, `Burn`, or `MintTo`. A legitimate
      Jupiter swap does not need any of these at the top level; the AMM performs
      transfers by CPI from within the allowlisted program. `SyncNative` is
      permitted. `CloseAccount` is permitted only when the closed account and
      the lamport destination are both the signer, and both are resolvable from
      static keys.
  P5  No `SystemProgram::Assign`, `Allocate`, `CreateAccountWithSeed` to a
      non-derived address, and no nonce instructions.
  P6  Per-wallet, per-user, and global signing rate limits, enforced in the
      Worker's own storage, which the app host cannot write to.
  P7  Revocation and global HALT flags, held in the Worker's own storage,
      checked first, settable from a phone without touching Oracle.

So the attacker cannot: move SOL out, move tokens out, delegate authority,
change mint or freeze authority, close accounts to themselves, or sign for a
wallet whose blob they cannot fetch.

What the attacker CAN still do — stated plainly, because pretending otherwise is
how people get hurt:
  - Force swaps through an allowlisted DEX into a worthless token they created,
    subject to the rate limit. This destroys value. It does not transfer value
    to an address the attacker controls directly, but a rug on the far side of
    the swap is economically equivalent to theft.
  - Read the database: user identities, balances, trade history, Telegram IDs.
  - Serve malicious frontend JavaScript to users, which is a separate and severe
    problem addressed by CTL-303 and CTL-604.
  - Deny service.

How bad is the forced-swap path? Bounded by three things: the per-wallet signing
rate limit (default 6/hour), the per-user notional cap, and detection. Ten
minutes of forced swaps at 6/hour/wallet across N wallets is loud: it trips the
unwrap-rate alarm (CTL-705), the canary wallet (CTL-707) if the attacker
enumerates wallets, and the loss circuit breaker from ADDENDUM C. The correct
comparison is not "safe versus unsafe," it is "attacker gets everything in one
request with no alarm" versus "attacker gets a rate-limited, alarmed, bounded
degradation that a human can halt from a phone in under a second."

That is a real improvement and it is worth the complexity. It is not immunity,
and PART 8 records it as RISK-002 rather than pretending it away.

RULING:
Adopted. Additionally, because the forced-swap path is the residual, two
supporting controls become mandatory rather than optional:
  - CTL-604 output-mint sanity: the signer independently checks that the
    transaction's declared output mint is one the *user's session policy*
    permits, where session policy is written to the Worker at session start via
    a user-authenticated path, not by the app host at signing time.
  - CTL-706 velocity alarm with automatic HALT at 3x baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 6 — Harden SSH, or remove SSH from the internet entirely?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (the existing spec):
"Disable password auth, move to port 2222, fail2ban, ed25519 keys, ufw limit."

ATTACK:
Every item on that list is good and the list is still the wrong shape. It
answers "how do I survive an exposed SSH port" when the available answer is
"do not have an exposed SSH port."

Specific problems with the list as written:
  - Moving to port 2222 while UFW is configured with `ufw allow 22/tcp`
    (ADDENDUM L's harden script does exactly this) locks the operator out. The
    two documents disagree and both are in the corpus.
  - `ufw limit 443/tcp` (war game 1.3) rate-limits by source IP. Behind
    Cloudflare, every request arrives from a handful of Cloudflare egress IPs.
    This does not slow attackers; it takes the site down. See DEF-009.
  - The custom `ssh-monitor.sh` bash loop duplicates fail2ban, greps an
    unbounded log per line (quadratic on a burst), and interpolates a value
    parsed out of an attacker-controlled log line into a `ufw` command — in a
    document whose own section 1.6 says "never parse logs as shell." See
    DEF-014.
  - fail2ban is configured with `backend = systemd` and an explicit
    `logpath = /var/log/auth.log`, plus an `[nginx-http-auth]` jail whose log
    path will not exist because the same document disables nginx. fail2ban
    refuses to start on a jail with a missing logpath. The net effect is that
    the primary SSH defence is not running. See DEF-012.
  - Port 22 open to the internet is, per the Red Team, entry point number one,
    and the mitigation list leaves it open.

DEFENCE ATTEMPT:
"Cloudflare Tunnel adds a dependency and a daemon."
It adds one outbound-only daemon and removes an inbound attack surface entirely.
Cloudflare Zero Trust's free plan covers up to 50 users with full ZTNA, which is
49 more than this project needs. The tunnel is outbound; there is no listening
port to scan, brute force, or exploit. Access policies can require a WebAuthn
hardware key. `cloudflared access ssh` gives a normal ssh client experience.

"What if Cloudflare is down and I need to get in?"
This is the real objection and it needs a real answer, not a shrug. The answer
is the break-glass path in CTL-201: Oracle Cloud's serial console, which is
out-of-band, requires Oracle tenancy authentication, and does not depend on
Cloudflare, the network stack, or sshd. It is slower and unpleasant, which is
correct for an emergency path.

RULING:
Port 22 is closed to the internet at both the Oracle security list and UFW.
SSH is reachable only through Cloudflare Tunnel with an Access policy requiring
a hardware security key. Break-glass is the Oracle serial console. fail2ban is
retained for the application-layer jails only and its SSH jail is corrected but
becomes near-irrelevant, which is the point. This is EP-1's structural fix.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 7 — Application-layer authorization, or database row-level security?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (the existing spec):
"Every tRPC procedure MUST have auth middleware. Resource ownership verification
on EVERY mutation."

ATTACK:
"MUST" and "EVERY" are the two words that appear in every postmortem. The Red
Team's entry point number three is precisely "missing auth check on ONE tRPC
endpoint = total compromise," and the Blue Team's answer is to be careful. The
answer to "you will eventually forget" cannot be "do not forget."

There are two structural answers and the spec uses neither:
  1. Make the unauthenticated procedure unconstructible. If the only exported
     procedure builders already carry the middleware, and the raw `t.procedure`
     is not exported, a developer cannot accidentally create an unprotected
     endpoint. Making it *possible* requires an explicit, reviewable act.
  2. Make the database refuse. PostgreSQL row-level security, enabled and
     FORCEd on every user-scoped table, with policies keyed to a per-transaction
     setting, means a forgotten ownership check returns zero rows instead of
     someone else's wallet. This is free, it is native, and it is a completely
     different mechanism written in a completely different language from the
     application check — which is exactly what INV-2 asks for.

COUNTER-ATTACK ON RLS:
"RLS with a connection pool is a footgun. If you use `SET` instead of
`SET LOCAL`, the setting leaks to the next request that borrows that connection,
and now user A is reading user B's rows with the database's blessing. That is
worse than no RLS."
Correct, and it is the single most important implementation detail. The rule is
absolute: the user context is set with `SET LOCAL` inside an explicit
transaction, never with `SET`, and every user-scoped query runs inside that
transaction. With PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode this is still correct
because `SET LOCAL` is scoped to the transaction that PgBouncer holds the
connection for. A plain `SET` under transaction pooling is catastrophic. The
implementation must expose exactly one way to run a user query — a `withUser()`
wrapper — and lint-ban raw `db.select(...)` outside it. TEST-402 asserts leakage
does not occur across pooled connections under concurrency.

"RLS costs performance."
It costs an index-friendly predicate on user_id, which every one of these
queries already has. Measurable, small, and worth it.

RULING:
Both. CTL-501 makes unprotected procedures unconstructible plus adds a runtime
router assertion test. CTL-401 adds RLS with FORCE on every user-scoped table
plus a `withUser()` transaction wrapper as the only sanctioned query path. A
missing application check is then a bug, not a breach. This is EP-3's structural
fix.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 8 — Fail open or fail closed when Redis is unavailable?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION:
"Rate limiting is a Redis sliding window. If Redis is down, allow the request —
otherwise a Redis blip takes the whole product down."

ATTACK:
That is a free bypass with a trivial trigger. An attacker who can degrade Redis
— and Redis is on the same 4-OCPU box, subject to the same resource exhaustion
the war game's own attack 1.3 describes — turns off rate limiting everywhere,
including on the auth endpoint and the signing path. "Knock over Redis, then
brute force" is a two-step attack and step one is the easy one.

DEFENCE:
Uniform fail-open is wrong and uniform fail-closed is also wrong. Fail-closed on
a price-quote endpoint means a Redis hiccup shows users a blank chart, which is
a bad trade for no security gain. The decision must be per-endpoint-class:

  FAIL CLOSED (reject on limiter error):
    auth, password reset, session create, trade submit, signer request,
    withdrawal-allowlist change, any admin route
  FAIL OPEN (allow on limiter error, log loudly, page after 60s):
    read-only queries, price/chart data, static metadata

And critically, the signer's own rate limits (CTL-102 P6) live in Cloudflare
storage, not Redis. So even total Redis loss on Oracle does not remove the limit
that protects funds. The layers do not share a failure mode. That is the actual
answer to the objection.

RULING:
Per-class policy as above, encoded in the limiter's type signature so that
choosing a policy is mandatory at the call site and the default is
fail-closed. TEST-701 injects a Redis outage and asserts auth rejects while
price reads succeed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 9 — Is Telegram an authenticator?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (the existing spec):
ADDENDUM M Scenario 3 is titled "NO SMS 2FA. Ever." The system authenticates
users via Telegram and issues trading commands over Telegram.

ATTACK:
These two positions are incompatible and the corpus never notices. Telegram
account recovery is, for most users, an SMS code. A SIM swap takes the Telegram
account. The document that bans SMS 2FA has built its primary user channel on
top of SMS-recoverable identity. Additionally, Telegram bot messages are not
end-to-end encrypted — ADDENDUM L says so itself — meaning trade commands and
any secret rendered in a bot message transit Telegram's infrastructure in a form
Telegram can read.

The encryptBotMessage/decryptBotMessage helpers in ADDENDUM L do not fix this:
both endpoints of that channel are the server and the user's Telegram client
cannot decrypt anything, so encrypting a message the user is supposed to read
is either a no-op or renders unreadable text. That code has no coherent use.

DEFENCE:
Telegram is genuinely valuable as a UX surface and as a notification channel. It
should not be deleted. It should be demoted.

RULING — the Telegram trust tier, normative:
  TIER 0 (Telegram alone is sufficient):
    read balances, read positions, read PNL, receive alerts,
    PANIC / revoke-all (deliberately: the destructive-safe direction should be
    as easy as possible, and an attacker using it only stops trading)
  TIER 1 (Telegram plus an active web session bound to a passkey):
    place a trade within existing session limits, pause/resume a session
  TIER 2 (passkey re-authentication required, Telegram cannot authorize):
    raise session limits, add or change a copy-trading target,
    change notification destinations, disable any security control
  TIER 3 (passkey re-auth AND a 24-hour delay AND out-of-band confirmation):
    add a withdrawal destination, raise the withdrawal cap, change the
    recovery email, disable MFA, rotate the Telegram link

Telegram is never sufficient to move value to a new destination. WebAuthn
passkeys become the primary factor (CTL-502); TOTP is the backup; SMS appears
nowhere, including in recovery, for any account in the system.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 10 — Is the anomaly detector a detector?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (the existing spec):
ADDENDUM L Layer 5 detects: unusual trade size (3x average), rapid trading (10+
per minute), off-hours trading (2am-5am local), and new-token trades.

ATTACK:
Consider what this product is. It snipes new tokens on Solana, it copy-trades,
and its users are awake at 3am because that is when memecoins launch.

  - OFF_HOURS_TRADING fires on the core use case.
  - NEW_TOKEN_TRADE fires on approximately every trade, since trading tokens the
    user has never held before is the entire product.
  - RAPID_TRADING at 10/minute fires on any copy-trading session following an
    active target.
  - UNUSUAL_TRADE_SIZE at 3x average fires constantly on a distribution with
    this much variance and a small sample.

Every one of these is logged at severity medium or high, and high-severity
events page. The Red Team's attack 12.2 is literally "generate thousands of
low-severity alerts until the blue team stops reading them." The spec
implements that attack on itself, for free, on day one. Meanwhile
`isSessionSuspicious` decides a session is compromised if the last five trades
all lost money, which describes a bad week, not an intrusion, and will never
fire on an attacker who is making money.

DEFENCE:
"Some signal is better than none."
No. Noise is worse than none, because it trains the operator to dismiss the
channel that will one day carry the real alert. An alerting system has a budget
and the budget is human attention.

RULING:
The four rules above are deleted. Detection is rebuilt around an explicit alert
budget: at most five pages per week in steady state, and every page must have a
documented action. High-signal detectors replace them (CTL-705 through CTL-709),
selected on the criterion that a benign explanation should be rare rather than
typical. The behavioral signals that were deleted are not lost — they are
retained as *risk scores attached to the trade record* for post-incident
forensics and for the user's own dashboard, where they cost nothing and page
nobody.

The single highest-signal detector in this entire architecture is the canary
wallet (CTL-707): a wallet row that no legitimate code path ever signs for. Its
false-positive rate is exactly zero by construction. One such detector is worth
more than four heuristics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 11 — Two origins (osiris.trade + api.osiris.trade, frontend on
             Cloudflare Pages) or one?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (the existing spec):
"Cloudflare Pages static export for the frontend, API on Oracle at
api.osiris.trade, tRPC client points at the API host."

ATTACK:
This split creates four problems the corpus does not resolve:

  1. CSP. Next.js App Router emits inline hydration scripts. A static export on
     Pages cannot use a per-request nonce, so the corpus falls back to
     `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` in ADDENDUM L — which directly
     contradicts the war game's own `script-src 'self'` and disarms the primary
     defence against entry point number six. This is DEF-018.
  2. Cookies. The session cookie is specified `SameSite=Strict`. That works only
     while the frontend is served from the registrable domain osiris.trade. Any
     deploy that serves users from a *.pages.dev preview URL — which Pages does
     by default for every branch — is cross-site, the cookie is not sent, and
     the natural "fix" a developer will reach for is `SameSite=None`, which
     re-opens CSRF.
  3. CORS. Two origins means preflights, credentialed CORS, and an allowlist to
     get wrong. One origin means the CORS problem does not exist.
  4. Secrets in the browser. The war game's CSP includes
     `connect-src ... wss://mainnet.helius-rpc.com`, which means the browser
     talks to Helius directly, which means the Helius API key — it is in the URL
     — ships to every user. That is a credential disclosure with a rate-limit
     and billing impact, and it is written into the security document as a
     security control. This is DEF-021.

DEFENCE OF THE SPLIT:
"Pages gives global CDN and stays up when Oracle is down."
The CDN benefit is real for static assets and is fully obtainable by putting
Cloudflare's proxy in front of the Oracle origin, which the architecture already
does. The availability benefit is largely illusory: if the API is down the
frontend is a shell that cannot show a balance or place a trade. For the genuine
case — origin unreachable — Cloudflare's custom error pages and Always Online
serve a static status page, which is the actual desired behaviour.

RULING:
ONE ORIGIN. `https://osiris.trade` serves both the application and the API,
from Caddy on Oracle, proxied by Cloudflare. Consequences, all of them
improvements:
  - Nonce-based strict CSP becomes possible because Next.js runs as a server.
    `script-src 'self' 'nonce-...' 'strict-dynamic'`. No `unsafe-inline`.
  - CORS is eliminated. `Origin`-header checking becomes a simple same-origin
    assertion rather than an allowlist.
  - `SameSite=Strict` is coherent and preview deployments cannot break it,
    because there are no Pages preview deployments.
  - `connect-src 'self'` only. The browser never talks to Helius, Jupiter,
    PumpPortal, or any third party. All upstream data is proxied by the backend,
    which keeps every API key server-side and removes an entire class of
    third-party-compromise exposure from the user's browser.
  - Alternative for teams that insist on static export: extract the inline
    script hashes at build time and emit them into Pages `_headers`. This works
    and is documented in CTL-303-ALT, but it is more moving parts for less
    benefit and is not the recommendation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 12 — Should the security dashboard be public?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (ADDENDUM N):
"Security transparency sells. Publish a live security score and a real-time
dashboard of which controls are active."

ATTACK:
A live dashboard of which controls are active is a live dashboard of which
controls are *inactive*. It is a reconnaissance feed, published by the defender,
updated in real time, free of charge, with no rate limit. The moment a control
flaps — Redis restarts and the rate limiter degrades, the AIDE job fails, the
signer is mid-deploy — the page announces the window. Marketing has handed the
Red Team a status endpoint for the Blue Team.

DEFENCE:
Transparency genuinely is a differentiator in this market, and it genuinely does
build trust, and users of a custodial-ish trading bot are right to demand it.

RULING:
Publish attestations, not telemetry. Specifically:
  PUBLISH:  the architecture (this document, redacted of identifiers), the
            open-source signer policy engine so anyone can read what it refuses
            to sign, the on-chain-verifiable fact that the treasury is a Squads
            multisig, the daily audit-log root hash anchored publicly (CTL-703),
            incident history with dates and honest postmortems, and the
            per-user security page showing that user's own sessions, devices,
            and recent security events.
  DO NOT PUBLISH: real-time control health, version numbers, dependency
            versions, infrastructure topology, which detectors exist and their
            thresholds, or an aggregate "security score" that moves.
A user-scoped security page is strictly better marketing than a global one: it
is personally relevant, it is actionable, and it leaks nothing about the fleet.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 13 — Is this over-engineered for Phase 0?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION:
"This is a pre-launch product with no users. A remote signer with a policy
engine, RLS on every table, hardware keys, canary wallets, and hash-chained
audit logs is six weeks of work before the first trade. Ship, then harden."

ATTACK ON MY OWN DESIGN — taken seriously:
This is the objection I am most sympathetic to, and it is right about most
products. It is wrong about this one, for one reason: the thing being built
holds other people's private keys. There is no "ship then harden" for key
custody, because the failure is irreversible on a chain with no chargebacks, and
because the migration from "keys were briefly protected badly" to "keys are
protected well" requires rotating every user wallet, which means every user must
move funds, which most will not do. The insecure decision is not a temporary
state; it is permanent for every wallet created during it.

But the objection does force a real prioritization, and I accept the following
cuts to Phase 0:

  BUILD BEFORE ANY MAINNET KEY EXISTS (non-negotiable, Gate 1 in PART 6):
    remote signer + policy engine, RLS + withUser, unconstructible-unprotected
    procedures, Telegram secret-token verification done correctly, SSH removed
    from the internet, Docker port binding fixed, correct client-IP resolution,
    strict CSP + token-label normalization, fail-closed rate limits on auth and
    trade, encrypted off-box backups with a tested restore, canary wallet,
    global HALT switch.
  DEFER TO PHASE 1 (weeks, not before launch):
    hash-chained audit log with public anchoring, auditd rule tuning, AIDE with
    off-box comparison, SBOM and image digest pinning, honeytoken expansion,
    withdrawal allowlist with 24h delay (only needed once withdrawals exist),
    formal incident-response automation.
  DEFER INDEFINITELY OR DELETE (PART 7):
    behavioral biometrics, anti-screen-recording, virtual keyboard, device
    fingerprint session binding, third-party pentest, bug bounty, insurance.

That reduces the pre-launch security work to roughly a week of focused
implementation, most of which is configuration rather than novel code, and the
one genuinely new component — the signer Worker — is about 400 lines.

RULING:
The Gate 1 list above is mandatory before a mainnet private key is generated.
Everything else is scheduled. The deleted list is deleted, permanently, with
reasons, so nobody re-adds it in month three because it sounds impressive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARGUMENT 14 — Is the "$0 budget, 2-3 days" claim honest?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

POSITION (Blue Team final assessment):
"BUDGET: $0. TOOLS: 100% free and open source. TIME TO IMPLEMENT: 2-3 days for
Phase 0 controls. ONGOING COST: $0."

ATTACK:
Every clause is false, and the falseness matters because it drives decisions.

  - The domain is not free.
  - The FIDO2 hardware keys that make the operator-security fix real are not
    free, and the Red Team's single biggest worry ("if the developer's laptop is
    compromised, everything is compromised") is not actually fixed without them.
  - Helius Sender requires a tip on every transaction — 0.001 SOL minimum for
    the priority path, 0.000005 SOL for the SWQOS-only path. "MEV protect, free
    tier" is not accurate; MEV protection has a per-trade cost.
  - Ubuntu Pro livepatch on arm64 only became available on Ubuntu 26.04; the
    spec's Ubuntu 22.04 arm64 host cannot use it, so "kernel live patching" is
    not available on the specified stack.
  - Caddy's `rate_limit` directive is a third-party module requiring a custom
    xcaddy build, not a built-in feature.
  - Cloudflare's free plan includes exactly one rate limiting rule, IP-only,
    with a fixed 10-second window — not general-purpose WAF rate limiting.
  - Oracle Always Free instances are subject to idle reclamation: an instance
    whose 95th-percentile CPU, network, and memory utilization are all under
    20% over a 7-day window may be reclaimed. A quiet trading bot meets that
    definition. There is also no SLA.
  - "2-3 days" describes typing the configs, not implementing, testing, and
    verifying them.

Why the lie is expensive: a plan that claims $0 will, when it meets a $50 cost,
either stall or quietly drop the control. That is exactly how the hardware key
gets dropped and the Red Team's number one worry stays unfixed.

RULING:
PART 9 replaces the cost claim with an itemized, honest table separating
genuinely free, one-time cost, per-transaction cost, and recurring cost, and
flags every place a free tier has a limit that this architecture will hit. The
corrected figure is roughly $60-140 in year one plus per-trade tips — which is
still an extraordinarily cheap security posture and does not need to be
exaggerated to be impressive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 1  KEK on the app host is not a boundary       -> remote signer (CTL-100)
 2  Remote signer needs 2-of-3 separation       -> separate CF account + request

 4  Zero-memory signing is not a hard control   -> deleted as a boundary

                                                   by policy + rate + HALT

    generator
