PART 2 — DEFECT REGISTER
================================================================================

Fifty-seven defects in the existing material. Each entry gives the location, the
class, the severity (S1-S5 per PART 0.4), the concrete failure, why it matters,
and the corrected artifact. The implementing agent must treat a DEF entry as a
work item: the defect is not closed until the corrected artifact is in the repo
and its test passes.

Ordered by layer, not by severity. The severity is on each entry.

################################################################################
GROUP A — CODE THAT DOES NOT WORK
These are not security opinions. These snippets crash, no-op, or return garbage.
They are in the corpus as if they were tested. They were not.
################################################################################

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-001  [S1]  Telegram webhook verification is wrong in two different ways,
               and both wrong versions are in the corpus
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 5.5 item 1; ADDENDUM L Layer 2 `verifyTelegramWebhook`.
CLASS     Broken authentication / protocol misunderstanding.

WHAT IS WRONG
Telegram's `secret_token` mechanism is not a signature scheme. Per the Bot API:
you pass `secret_token` to `setWebhook`, and Telegram then sends that exact
string back, verbatim, in the `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` header on every
webhook request. 1-256 characters, `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -` only. There is no HMAC,
no body hashing, and no per-request derivation.

The war game computes `createHmac('sha256', sha256(BOT_TOKEN)).update(rawBody)`
and compares it to that header. The header will never equal that value, so the
check rejects every legitimate Telegram update — or, if a developer "fixes" it
by removing the check, accepts everything.

ADDENDUM L computes `sha256(sha256(BOT_TOKEN) || rawBody)` and compares it to a
header called `signature` that Telegram does not send. Same outcome.

Separately, the corpus conflates three distinct Telegram verification
mechanisms that use three different algorithms:
  1. Webhook authenticity        -> compare the secret_token header. No crypto.
  2. Login Widget `hash`         -> HMAC-SHA256, key = SHA256(bot_token),
                                    over the sorted `key=value\n` data-check
                                    string.
  3. Mini App `initData` hash    -> HMAC-SHA256, key =
                                    HMAC_SHA256("WebAppData", bot_token),
                                    over the same style of data-check string.
Using the Login Widget key derivation on Mini App data (or vice versa) fails
open or fails closed depending on which side a developer patches.

WHY IT MATTERS
This is Red Team entry point number four. An unverified webhook endpoint accepts
forged updates, which means arbitrary bot control: impersonate any Telegram
user, trigger any bot command as them, and — depending on the Telegram trust
tier — move value. The corpus's stated mitigation does not work.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT — src/bot/webhook-auth.ts
```typescript
import { createHmac, createHash, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

/**
 * Constant-time string comparison that is safe for attacker-controlled input of
 * arbitrary length. Node's timingSafeEqual throws RangeError when the two
 * buffers differ in length (see DEF-007), which turns a malformed header into
 * an unauthenticated 500. Hashing both sides to a fixed 32 bytes first removes
 * the length dependency entirely and leaks nothing.
 */
function safeEqual(a: string, b: string): boolean {
  const ha = createHash("sha256").update(a, "utf8").digest();
  const hb = createHash("sha256").update(b, "utf8").digest();
  return timingSafeEqual(ha, hb);
}

/**
 * MECHANISM 1 — Webhook authenticity.
 * Telegram echoes the secret you configured via setWebhook. Compare it.
 * TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET must be >= 32 chars from [A-Za-z0-9_-].
 */
export function verifyTelegramWebhook(headerValue: string | null): boolean {
  const expected = process.env.TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET;
  if (!expected || expected.length < 32) {
    // Fail closed and loudly. A missing secret is a deployment error, not a
    // reason to accept traffic.
    throw new Error("TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET missing or too short");
  }
  if (!headerValue) return false;
  return safeEqual(headerValue, expected);
}

/**
 * MECHANISM 3 — Mini App initData verification.
 * key = HMAC_SHA256(botToken, "WebAppData")   <-- note the argument order:
 * "WebAppData" is the KEY and the bot token is the MESSAGE.
 */
export function verifyMiniAppInitData(
  initData: string,
  botToken: string,
  maxAgeSeconds = 300
): { ok: boolean; userId?: string; reason?: string } {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(initData);
  const hash = params.get("hash");
  if (!hash) return { ok: false, reason: "no_hash" };
  params.delete("hash");
  // signature is present on newer third-party-verifiable payloads; exclude it
  params.delete("signature");

  const dataCheckString = [...params.entries()]
    .map(([k, v]) => `${k}=${v}`)
    .sort()
    .join("\n");

  const secretKey = createHmac("sha256", "WebAppData").update(botToken).digest();
  const computed = createHmac("sha256", secretKey)
    .update(dataCheckString)
    .digest("hex");

  if (!safeEqual(computed, hash)) return { ok: false, reason: "bad_hash" };

  const authDate = Number(params.get("auth_date"));
  if (!Number.isFinite(authDate)) return { ok: false, reason: "no_auth_date" };
  const age = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - authDate;
  if (age > maxAgeSeconds || age < -60) return { ok: false, reason: "stale" };

  let userId: string | undefined;
  try {
    userId = String(JSON.parse(params.get("user") ?? "{}").id ?? "") || undefined;
  } catch {
    return { ok: false, reason: "bad_user_json" };
  }
  if (!userId) return { ok: false, reason: "no_user" };

  return { ok: true, userId };
}

/**
 * MECHANISM 2 — Login Widget verification.
 * key = SHA256(botToken). Different from Mini App. Do not merge these.
 */
export function verifyLoginWidget(
  data: Record<string, string>,
  botToken: string,
  maxAgeSeconds = 300
): boolean {
  const { hash, ...rest } = data;
  if (!hash) return false;
  const dataCheckString = Object.keys(rest)
    .sort()
    .map((k) => `${k}=${rest[k]}`)
    .join("\n");
  const secretKey = createHash("sha256").update(botToken).digest();
  const computed = createHmac("sha256", secretKey)
    .update(dataCheckString)
    .digest("hex");
  if (!safeEqual(computed, hash)) return false;
  const age = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - Number(rest.auth_date);
  return age <= maxAgeSeconds && age >= -60;
}
```

ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS
  - The webhook route must read the RAW body before any JSON parsing, reject on
    failed verification with 401 and no body, and must not log the header value.
  - Update deduplication on `update_id` in Redis with a 24h TTL (replay).
  - `setWebhook` must be called with `secret_token`, `allowed_updates` narrowed
    to only the update types the bot handles, and `drop_pending_updates: true`
    on rotation.
TEST      TEST-101, TEST-102 (PART 5).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-002  [S3]  `sanitizeLog` does nothing for the case it was written for
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 1.6 item 1.
CLASS     No-op / log injection remains open.

WHAT IS WRONG
```javascript
.replace(/\n/g, '\n')     // replaces a newline with a newline
.replace(/\r/g, '\r')     // replaces a carriage return with a carriage return
```
Both are identity operations. The author intended `'\\n'` and `'\\r'` (escape
the character), and wrote the unescaped form. CRLF injection into log fields —
the exact attack in war game 1.6 — is therefore not prevented by this function.

The preceding `.replace(/[\x00-\x1f\x7f]/g, '')` does happen to strip CR and LF
as a side effect, which masks the bug during casual review and means the two
following lines are dead code that a future maintainer may "fix" by removing the
control-character strip.

WHY IT MATTERS
Forged log entries defeat post-incident reconstruction, which is the thing you
need most on the worst day.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Do not sanitize strings into a text log. Emit structured JSON and let the
serializer handle escaping. The only sanitization needed is bounding.
```typescript
const MAX_FIELD = 512;

/** For values that go into a JSON log field. JSON.stringify escapes control
 *  characters correctly; our job is only to bound size and strip nulls that
 *  break downstream C-based tooling. */
export function logField(value: unknown): string {
  const s = typeof value === "string" ? value : JSON.stringify(value) ?? "";
  return s.replace(/\u0000/g, "").slice(0, MAX_FIELD);
}
```
And the hard rule (CTL-701): log lines are produced only by the structured
logger. No `console.log` with template interpolation of request data. No shell
consumes a log file. Enforced by TEST-702 (lint rule + CI grep).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-003  [S4]  `ROLE_PERMISSIONS` references itself in its own initializer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 2, `src/lib/rbac.ts`.
CLASS     ReferenceError at module load.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
const ROLE_PERMISSIONS: Record<Role, Permission[]> = {
  [Role.USER]: [...],
  [Role.ADMIN]: [
    ...ROLE_PERMISSIONS[Role.USER],   // TDZ: not initialized yet
    ...
  ],
};
```
`ROLE_PERMISSIONS` is in the temporal dead zone while its own initializer runs.
This throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'ROLE_PERMISSIONS' before
initialization` at import time, which means the module never loads, which means
the app does not boot. Whoever wrote it never imported it.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```typescript
const USER_PERMS = [
  Permission.TRADE_CREATE,
  Permission.TRADE_EXECUTE,
  Permission.SESSION_REVOKE,
  Permission.WALLET_VIEW,
  Permission.WALLET_CREATE,
] as const;

const SUPPORT_PERMS = [
  Permission.USER_VIEW,
  Permission.AUDIT_READ,
] as const;

export const ROLE_PERMISSIONS: Readonly<Record<Role, readonly Permission[]>> =
  Object.freeze({
    [Role.USER]: USER_PERMS,
    [Role.SUPPORT]: SUPPORT_PERMS,
    [Role.ADMIN]: [
      ...USER_PERMS,
      ...SUPPORT_PERMS,
      Permission.USER_MANAGE,
      Permission.SYSTEM_CONFIG,
    ],
    [Role.SYSTEM]: [Permission.TRADE_EXECUTE, Permission.AUDIT_READ],
  });
```
NOTE: giving `Role.ADMIN` the union of user permissions including
`TRADE_EXECUTE` and `WALLET_VIEW` is itself a design error — see DEF-036 and
CTL-902. Admin must not be able to trade with user wallets. Fix the shape first,
then fix the grants.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-004  [S4]  Better Auth password hashing config is invented
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 2.
CLASS     Non-existent API. Silently falls back to the default hash.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
emailAndPassword: {
  password: {
    hash: { algorithm: "argon2id", memoryCost: 65536, timeCost: 3, parallelism: 4 }
  }
}
```
Better Auth's `emailAndPassword.password` takes two *functions*, `hash` and
`verify`. There is no `algorithm` enum and no cost-parameter object. Passing an
object where a function is expected either type-errors at build or is ignored at
runtime, in which case passwords are hashed with the library default, not
Argon2id with the stated parameters. The security checklist item "Argon2id
password hashing (not bcrypt)" would be ticked while being false.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT — src/lib/password.ts
```typescript
import { hash as argonHash, verify as argonVerify, Algorithm } from "@node-rs/argon2";

// OWASP-aligned Argon2id parameters. Tune memoryCost down only if the ARM box
// cannot sustain concurrent logins; never below 19456 (19 MiB).
const OPTS = {
  algorithm: Algorithm.Argon2id,
  memoryCost: 65536,  // 64 MiB
  timeCost: 3,
  parallelism: 4,
  outputLen: 32,
} as const;

export async function hashPassword(password: string): Promise<string> {
  return argonHash(password, OPTS);
}

export async function verifyPassword(data: {
  password: string;
  hash: string;
}): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    return await argonVerify(data.hash, data.password, OPTS);
  } catch {
    return false; // malformed stored hash -> deny, do not throw into auth path
  }
}
```
```typescript
// src/lib/auth.ts
emailAndPassword: {
  enabled: true,
  minPasswordLength: 12,     // see DEF-004b
  maxPasswordLength: 256,
  requireEmailVerification: true,
  password: { hash: hashPassword, verify: verifyPassword },
},
```
DEF-004b [S5] — the spec's `minPasswordLength: 16` combined with composition
requirements pushes users toward reuse. NIST SP 800-63B guidance: long minimum,
no composition rules, no forced rotation, allow paste, and screen against
breached-password corpora. Use 12 as the floor, allow up to 256, run the HIBP
k-anonymity range check (the corpus already has this and it is correct), and
require a passkey for anything in Telegram Trust Tier 2 or 3 (ARGUMENT 9), which
is where the actual security lives.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-005  [S4]  `postgres:16-alpine` does not run as UID 999
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 docker-compose.yml.
CLASS     Wrong UID. Container fails to start or corrupts data directory
          ownership.

WHAT IS WRONG
The compose file sets `user: "999:999"` on the Alpine postgres image. The Debian
variant of the official postgres image uses UID/GID 999. The Alpine variant does
not: its Dockerfile creates the postgres user with
`addgroup -g 70 -S postgres; adduser -u 70 -S -D -G postgres ...`, i.e. UID 70,
GID 70, following Alpine's package convention.

Running the Alpine image as 999 means the process cannot read or write
`/var/lib/postgresql/data` created by 70, and initdb refuses to run as an
unknown user. The result is a container that either crashloops or, if a
developer "fixes" it with `chown -R 999`, a data directory whose ownership no
longer matches the image — which breaks again on the next image update.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```yaml
postgres:
  # Pin by digest, not tag. See DEF-052.
  image: postgres:16-alpine@sha256:<PIN_AT_BUILD_TIME>
  user: "70:70"        # Alpine postgres UID/GID. Verify with:
                       #   docker run --rm postgres:16-alpine id postgres
```
GENERAL RULE (CTL-203): never hardcode a UID from memory. The compose file must
be accompanied by `scripts/verify-container-uids.sh`, run in CI, which executes
`docker run --rm <image> id <user>` for every service and asserts the compose
`user:` matches. TEST-203.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-006  [S3]  `sanitizeInput()` corrupts data, prevents nothing, and contains
               a character-class bug
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 4 `src/lib/validation.ts`.
CLASS     Security theater plus a live data-corruption bug.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
.replace(/[<>]/g, "")        // Remove HTML tags
.replace(/['";]/g, "")       // Remove SQL injection chars
.replace(/[ -]/g, "")        // "Remove control characters"
```
Three problems, escalating:

  1. Stripping `< >` does not prevent XSS. React escapes by default; the actual
     XSS vectors are `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `href="javascript:"`, unsanitized
     `style`, and DOM sinks — none of which this touches. Meanwhile it silently
     mangles legitimate input.
  2. Stripping `' " ;` does not prevent SQL injection. Parameterization does.
     Stripping quotes gives false confidence and breaks names like O'Brien.
     Worse, it encourages the belief that "sanitized" input is safe to
     concatenate, which is how second-order injection happens.
  3. `/[ -]/g` is the real bug. The author intended a control-character range
     and wrote a literal class containing a space, a hyphen-as-range-delimiter
     artifact, and whatever characters survived the copy/paste. As written it
     removes every space and hyphen from user input. A wallet label
     "Main - trading" becomes "Maintrading". A note becomes unreadable. Nobody
     noticed because nobody ran it.

WHY IT MATTERS
Beyond corruption: an input sanitizer at the edge is an invitation to skip the
real control at the sink. This function makes the system less safe by existing.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Delete `sanitizeInput`. Replace with (a) validation, (b) contextual encoding at
the sink, (c) a purpose-built label normalizer for the one genuinely hostile
input class — on-chain token metadata (see CTL-603).
```typescript
// Validate. Do not "sanitize".
export const UserLabelSchema = z
  .string()
  .min(1)
  .max(64)
  .transform((s) => s.normalize("NFKC").trim())
  .refine((s) => s.length > 0, "empty after normalization")
  // Reject rather than strip: the user should know their input was rejected.
  .refine((s) => !/[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\p{Co}\p{Cn}]/u.test(s), "control characters not allowed");
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-007  [S3]  `timingSafeEqual` on attacker-controlled input crashes
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 5.5 item 1; ADDENDUM L Layer 2; anywhere the pattern was
          copied.
CLASS     Unauthenticated denial of service / error-path information leak.

WHAT IS WRONG
`crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b)` throws `RangeError: Input buffers must have the
same byte length` when lengths differ. Both corpus call sites pass a buffer
built from an attacker-supplied header directly into it. Sending a
one-character `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` throws inside the request
handler. Depending on framing that is a 500, an unhandled rejection, or — under
`--unhandled-rejections=strict` — a process exit. A remote unauthenticated
attacker can therefore crash or noisily error the webhook path at will, and the
thrown/not-thrown distinction leaks the expected length.

Additionally `Buffer.from(signature, "hex")` on a non-hex string silently
produces a shorter buffer rather than throwing, compounding the length mismatch.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Use the `safeEqual` helper from DEF-001: hash both sides to a fixed 32 bytes
before comparison. This removes the length dependency, removes the throw, and
leaks nothing. Apply the same pattern to every secret comparison in the codebase
(CSRF token, signer request signature, webhook secrets, admin tokens).
Lint rule: ban direct `timingSafeEqual` usage outside `src/lib/crypto/compare.ts`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-050  [S2/S4]  Signature encoding is wrong, and "zero-memory signing" is
                  claimed as a hard control it cannot be
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 1 `SecureSigner.signTransaction`.
CLASS     Wrong return value (breaks confirmation, dedup, explorer links) plus
          an overstated control (see ARGUMENT 4).

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
const signature = transaction.signature?.toString("base64") || "";
```
  - For a `VersionedTransaction` the signatures live in `transaction.signatures`
    (a `Uint8Array[]`); `.signature` is the legacy-`Transaction` accessor.
  - `Uint8Array.prototype.toString()` ignores its argument. It returns a
    comma-joined decimal string: `"12,45,200,7,..."`. It is not base64.
  - Solana transaction signatures are conventionally base58, not base64. Every
    downstream consumer — `getSignatureStatuses`, the `webhookEvents.signature`
    UNIQUE constraint that provides replay protection, the Solscan link shown to
    the user — expects base58.

So the function returns a string that is wrong in encoding, wrong in source
field, and silently accepted by TypeScript. Replay protection keyed on this
value does not deduplicate anything real.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Under CTL-100 the app host does not sign at all; it receives a base58 signature
string from the signer. For completeness, the correct extraction is:
```typescript
import bs58 from "bs58";
// VersionedTransaction: fee payer's signature is index 0
const sigBytes = tx.signatures[0];
if (!sigBytes || sigBytes.every((b) => b === 0)) throw new Error("unsigned");
const signature = bs58.encode(sigBytes);   // 88-char base58, matches explorers
```
And add a Zod schema used everywhere a signature crosses a boundary:
```typescript
export const TxSignatureSchema = z
  .string()
  .regex(/^[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{86,88}$/, "not a base58 Solana signature");
```
On the "zero-memory" claim: retained as hygiene in the signer isolate only,
removed from the "hardest targets" list. See ARGUMENT 4 and PART 8.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-026  [S4]  `Object.freeze(Object.prototype)` breaks the runtime
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 3.7 item 2.
CLASS     Application-breaking mitigation.

WHAT IS WRONG
Freezing `Object.prototype` and `Array.prototype` process-wide will break
libraries that legitimately define properties on them, break some polyfills,
and produce `TypeError: Cannot add property x, object is not extensible` from
deep inside dependencies with no useful stack. In a Node app with 800 transitive
dependencies this is a coin flip on boot, and a coin flip on every dependency
update thereafter.

WHY IT MATTERS
Prototype pollution is a real risk and deserves a real mitigation. This one gets
reverted the first time it breaks a deploy, and then there is no mitigation.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Three layers, none of which break dependencies:
```jsonc
// 1. Node flag — makes __proto__ in JSON.parse output a plain own property
//    that cannot alter the prototype chain. Put it in the Dockerfile CMD.
//    node --disable-proto=delete server.js
```
```typescript
// 2. Reject rather than strip, at the parse boundary. Rejecting is better than
//    stripping because a payload containing __proto__ is hostile by definition
//    and you want to know.
export function parseUntrustedJson<T>(raw: string): T {
  return JSON.parse(raw, function (key, value) {
    if (key === "__proto__" || key === "constructor" || key === "prototype") {
      throw new Error("prototype_pollution_attempt");
    }
    return value;
  }) as T;
}
```
```typescript
// 3. Zod .strict() on every schema at a trust boundary. Unknown keys are
//    rejected, so a polluting key never reaches application logic even if it
//    survived the parser.
const WebhookSchema = z.object({ ... }).strict();
```
Plus: internal maps that hold user-controlled keys use `new Map()` or
`Object.create(null)`, never object literals. Lint rule bans
`obj[userControlledKey] = ...` on plain objects in `src/server/**`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-024  [S5]  Frame-busting JavaScript does not work and is not needed
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 4.3 item 3.
CLASS     Obsolete mitigation; creates false confidence.

WHAT IS WRONG
`window.top.location = window.self.location` throws a cross-origin
`SecurityError` in every modern browser when the framing page is on another
origin — which is the only case that matters. Sandboxed iframes
(`sandbox="allow-scripts"` without `allow-top-navigation`) block it outright.
It is defeated by the same attacker it is aimed at.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
`Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` (authoritative, respected by
all current browsers) plus `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (legacy belt). Delete the
JavaScript. Covered by CTL-303.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-055  [S5]  `encryptBotMessage` / `decryptBotMessage` have no coherent use
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 2.
CLASS     Dead code that implies a protection that does not exist.

WHAT IS WRONG
The stated purpose is "Since Telegram doesn't support E2EE for bots, we encrypt
sensitive data in the bot messages themselves." But the recipient is a human
reading a Telegram client, which has no key and cannot decrypt. If the recipient
is the server, the server is both encryptor and decryptor and the ciphertext
still traverses Telegram — the plaintext was never needed there in the first
place.

The correct conclusion from "Telegram bot messages are not E2EE" is not
"encrypt them," it is "never put a secret in a Telegram message." The corpus
reaches the right premise and the wrong conclusion.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Delete both functions. Adopt the rule (CTL-802): no secret, key, seed, token,
full address, recovery code, or one-time code is ever sent through Telegram.
Telegram messages may contain: a status, an amount, a truncated address with a
matching identicon, and a deep link to the authenticated web app where the
sensitive action actually happens.

################################################################################
GROUP B — CONTROLS THAT DO NOT CONTROL
The code runs. It just does not stop the attack it is filed under.
################################################################################

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-010  [S1]  UFW rules open PostgreSQL and Redis to the internet, and Docker
               bypasses UFW anyway
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 harden script; war game 2.3 item 1.
CLASS     Firewall misconfiguration + a Docker/iptables interaction the corpus
          never mentions. This is Red Team attack 2.3 succeeding against its own
          countermeasure.

WHAT IS WRONG — TWO SEPARATE FAILURES

Failure 1: the rules say the opposite of the comment.
```bash
ufw allow 5432/tcp    # PostgreSQL (only from localhost)
ufw allow 6379/tcp    # Redis (only from localhost)
```
`ufw allow 5432/tcp` with no source allows 5432 from anywhere. The comment says
"only from localhost." The rule says "from the entire internet." The war game's
version at 2.3 gets the syntax right (`ufw allow from 127.0.0.1 to any port
5432`) but that rule is pointless, because loopback traffic is already permitted
and never traverses these chains.

Failure 2 — the one that actually matters: Docker inserts its own rules into the
`DOCKER` chain of the `nat` and `filter` tables, ahead of the chain UFW
populates. A container started with `ports: ["5432:5432"]` is reachable from the
internet regardless of what UFW says. `ufw status` will show "deny incoming" and
the port will be open. This is the single most common way a self-hosted database
ends up on Shodan, and neither document mentions it.

WHY IT MATTERS
Direct, unauthenticated network reach to Postgres means the entire wallet table
including every encrypted key blob is one credential-guess or one Postgres CVE
away. Under the pre-CTL-100 architecture where the KEK is also on the host, that
is total compromise.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Four changes, all required:

1. Do not publish internal ports at all. Postgres and Redis are on the
   `internal: true` network and are reached by service name from the app
   container. Remove every `ports:` entry from them.
```yaml
postgres:
  # NO ports: block. Reachable only as postgres:5432 on the backend network.
  networks: [backend]
redis:
  # NO ports: block.
  networks: [backend]
```
2. If a port must be published for local operations, bind it to loopback
   explicitly. `"5432:5432"` publishes on 0.0.0.0; `"127.0.0.1:5432:5432"` does
   not.
3. Add a DOCKER-USER rule so that even a mistaken publish is not reachable from
   outside. DOCKER-USER is evaluated before Docker's own rules and is not
   flushed by Docker.
```bash
# /etc/ufw/after.rules  (append, before the final COMMIT of *filter)
# Drop anything arriving on the public interface destined for container subnets
# unless it is an established/related flow.
-A DOCKER-USER -i ens3 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j RETURN
-A DOCKER-USER -i ens3 -j DROP
-A DOCKER-USER -j RETURN
```
   Replace `ens3` with the actual public interface (`ip -o -4 route show to default`).
4. Correct base UFW policy. Note port 22 is absent — see EP-1.
```bash
ufw --force reset
ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing
ufw default deny routed
# 80/443 accepted ONLY from Cloudflare (see CTL-302). No blanket allow.
ufw --force enable
```
TEST      TEST-201 runs `nmap -Pn -p- <public-ip>` from an external host and
          asserts that only the expected ports respond, and TEST-202 asserts
          `psql "postgres://...@<public-ip>:5432"` times out.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-013  [S2]  UFW is not the only firewall on Oracle Cloud
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Absent from both documents.
CLASS     Missing control / guaranteed operational confusion.

WHAT IS WRONG
An Oracle Cloud instance has three independent packet filters:
  1. The VCN Security List / Network Security Group (Oracle-side, outside the
     VM). Ingress is default-deny except 22.
  2. The instance's own iptables. Oracle's Ubuntu images ship with
     `iptables-persistent` and a pre-populated ruleset that ends with a REJECT,
     independent of UFW.
  3. UFW, if enabled.
Opening a port in UFW while the Security List blocks it produces silence.
Opening it in the Security List while the Oracle-shipped iptables REJECT rule
sits above the UFW chain also produces silence. Agents lose hours here and the
common "fix" found on forums is `iptables -F`, which flushes the DOCKER-USER
protections from DEF-010 as collateral damage.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Order of operations, exactly:
```bash
# 1. Oracle Console: VCN -> Security List. Remove the default 0.0.0.0/0:22 rule.
#    Add ingress 443/tcp and 80/tcp from Cloudflare ranges only, or — preferred —
#    add NOTHING and reach the host solely via Cloudflare Tunnel (EP-1), in which
#    case the Security List can be fully closed for ingress.

# 2. On the host: neutralise the shipped ruleset BEFORE enabling UFW.
sudo iptables-save > /root/iptables.oracle.$(date +%F).bak    # keep a copy
sudo apt-get purge -y iptables-persistent netfilter-persistent
sudo iptables -F INPUT && sudo iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT        # transient
# 3. Now configure UFW per DEF-010, then:
sudo ufw --force enable
# 4. Re-apply the DOCKER-USER rules from DEF-010 (they live in
#    /etc/ufw/after.rules so they survive ufw reload).
sudo ufw reload
# 5. Verify from OUTSIDE the VM, not from inside it.
```
Record in the runbook that step 2 is destructive and step 5 is the only proof.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-009  [S3]  `ufw limit 443/tcp` behind Cloudflare is a self-inflicted outage
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 1.3 item 1.
CLASS     Rate limit applied at the wrong layer with an inverted effect.

WHAT IS WRONG
`ufw limit` blocks a source IP that opens more than 6 connections in 30 seconds.
With Cloudflare proxying, every connection originates from a small set of
Cloudflare edge IPs. Normal traffic from a handful of users exceeds 6
connections per 30 seconds per edge IP within moments. UFW then blocks a
Cloudflare edge node, and a fraction of all users — not attackers, users — get
connection timeouts that are invisible in application logs because the packets
never arrive.

Meanwhile it does nothing to an attacker, whose traffic also arrives from
Cloudflare and is indistinguishable at layer 3.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Remove `ufw limit` from 80 and 443 entirely. Rate limiting at the origin must be
keyed on the true client IP (see DEF-025) and must happen in Caddy or the
application, not in the packet filter. The packet filter's job here is exactly
one thing: accept 80/443 only from Cloudflare (CTL-302).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-025  [S1]  Every per-IP control in the system keys on Cloudflare's IP
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Implied throughout; never addressed in either document.
CLASS     Systemic. Turns every rate limit, ban, and audit trail into either a
          no-op or a global outage.

WHAT IS WRONG
Once Cloudflare proxies the origin, `req.socket.remoteAddress` is a Cloudflare
edge IP for every request. Consequences, all of them present in the corpus's
design:
  - The Redis sliding-window limiter keyed on "IP" now counts ALL users
    together. Either the limit is high enough to be useless, or the first busy
    minute rate-limits the entire user base. Red Team entry point seven survives
    a limiter that exists.
  - fail2ban's `[osiris-api]` jail bans Cloudflare edge IPs, taking the site
    offline for everyone routed through that edge.
  - `securityLogger` records Cloudflare IPs, so the audit trail cannot attribute
    anything to an actor.
  - "Impossible travel" detection (war game 5.1 item 5) sees one IP forever.
  - The Telegram webhook IP allowlist (war game 8.1 item 2) compares Telegram's
    published ranges against Cloudflare's IP and rejects every legitimate
    webhook.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
1. Caddy resolves the real client IP, trusting ONLY Cloudflare ranges:
```caddyfile
{
  servers {
    # Only these sources may set the client-IP header. Everything else is
    # treated as the true peer, so header spoofing from a non-CF source fails.
    trusted_proxies static 173.245.48.0/20 103.21.244.0/22 103.22.200.0/22 \
      103.31.4.0/22 141.101.64.0/18 108.162.192.0/18 190.93.240.0/20 \
      188.114.96.0/20 197.234.240.0/22 198.41.128.0/17 162.158.0.0/15 \
      104.16.0.0/13 104.24.0.0/14 172.64.0.0/13 131.0.72.0/22 \
      2400:cb00::/32 2606:4700::/32 2803:f800::/32 2405:b500::/32 \
      2405:8100::/32 2a06:98c0::/29 2c0f:f248::/32
    client_ip_headers CF-Connecting-IP X-Forwarded-For
  }
}
```
   The list must be refreshed from https://www.cloudflare.com/ips-v4 and
   /ips-v6 by a weekly cron that regenerates this snippet and reloads Caddy.
2. Caddy forwards the resolved value to the app on a header the app trusts only
   from Caddy over loopback:
```caddyfile
reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000 {
  header_up X-Real-Client-IP {client_ip}
  header_up Host {host}
  # Strip any inbound value of our internal header so a client cannot forge it.
  header_up -X-Osiris-Trusted-IP
}
```
3. The application reads the client IP from exactly one place:
```typescript
// src/server/client-ip.ts — the ONLY sanctioned source of a client IP.
export function clientIp(headers: Headers): string {
  const v = headers.get("x-real-client-ip");
  if (!v || !isIp(v)) {
    // Caddy always sets this. Absence means the request did not come through
    // Caddy, which means something is wrong. Fail closed.
    throw new UntrustedRequestError("missing x-real-client-ip");
  }
  return v;
}
```
   Lint-ban `req.ip`, `request.socket.remoteAddress`, and direct reads of
   `x-forwarded-for` outside this module.
4. fail2ban's HTTP jails read Caddy's access log and must be configured to
   extract `{client_ip}`, not the peer address. Alternatively — and preferred —
   drop the HTTP fail2ban jails and do this banning in Cloudflare where the
   attacker actually is.
TEST      TEST-301 asserts two requests carrying different `CF-Connecting-IP`
          values from a non-Cloudflare source are attributed to the peer IP, not
          the header; TEST-302 asserts requests through the real path are
          attributed to the header.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-008  [S4]  Caddy's `rate_limit` directive is not built in
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 1.3 item 2 and Final Round ("Caddy rate limiting (free,
          built-in)"); ADDENDUM L Layer 3 Caddyfile.
CLASS     Non-existent feature. Caddy refuses to start.

WHAT IS WRONG
Stock Caddy has no `rate_limit` directive. The Caddyfile in ADDENDUM L will fail
to parse with `Error during parsing: rate_limit is not a registered directive`,
and Caddy will not start — taking the site down at the exact moment the operator
believes they have just added rate limiting. Rate limiting in Caddy requires the
third-party `caddy-ratelimit` module compiled in with `xcaddy`.

It is free and open source. It is not built in. The distinction is the
difference between a config change and a build pipeline.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.caddy — build once, pin the digest, reuse.
FROM caddy:2-builder-alpine AS builder
RUN xcaddy build \
      --with github.com/mholt/caddy-ratelimit \
      --with github.com/caddy-dns/cloudflare

FROM caddy:2-alpine
COPY --from=builder /usr/bin/caddy /usr/bin/caddy
```
Then the `rate_limit` block parses. Verify at build time:
```bash
docker run --rm osiris-caddy caddy list-modules | grep -E 'rate_limit|dns.providers.cloudflare'
```
If the operator does not want a custom Caddy build, the fallback is: Cloudflare's
single free rate-limiting rule on the auth path plus application-layer limiting.
State the choice explicitly in the runbook; do not leave a Caddyfile in the repo
that the running binary cannot parse. TEST-703.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-011  [S4]  `userns-remap` enabled after volumes exist breaks every container
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 `/etc/docker/daemon.json`.
CLASS     Ordering hazard; also interacts badly with the explicit `user:` keys.

WHAT IS WRONG
`"userns-remap": "default"` shifts every container UID by a large offset
(typically 100000). Consequences the corpus does not account for:
  - Existing named volumes are owned by the pre-remap UIDs. After enabling
    remap, the postgres container (now running as host UID 100070) cannot read
    a data directory owned by host UID 70. Postgres refuses to start and the
    error mentions permissions, not user namespaces, so the diagnosis is slow.
  - Docker maintains a *separate* image and container store per remap namespace,
    so all images appear to vanish and must be re-pulled.
  - It is incompatible with `--privileged`, with host networking, and with some
    bind-mount patterns.
It is a genuinely good control. It must be enabled before any volume exists.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Decision, and it must be recorded: for Phase 0, do NOT enable `userns-remap`.
The combination of a non-root `user:` per service, `no-new-privileges`,
`cap_drop: ALL`, and `read_only` provides most of the benefit with none of the
ordering hazard, and rootless containers on a single-tenant box are a smaller
win than the corpus implies.

If it is enabled later, it is a rebuild, not a config change: stop everything,
back up and export volumes, enable remap, recreate volumes, restore, restart.
Corrected daemon.json for Phase 0:
```json
{
  "live-restore": true,
  "no-new-privileges": true,
  "icc": false,
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" },
  "default-ulimits": { "nofile": { "Name": "nofile", "Hard": 8192, "Soft": 8192 } }
}
```
Note `"seccomp-profile"` is omitted: pointing it at a file that does not exist
prevents dockerd from starting, and Docker's built-in default seccomp profile is
already applied when the key is absent. Only set it if you have actually
authored a profile.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-012  [S3]  fail2ban as configured will not start
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 `jail.local`.
CLASS     The primary SSH defence is not running.

WHAT IS WRONG
```ini
[DEFAULT]
backend = systemd
[sshd]
logpath = /var/log/auth.log
[nginx-http-auth]
enabled = true
logpath = /var/log/nginx/error.log
```
  - `backend = systemd` reads the journal; specifying `logpath` alongside it is
    contradictory and, on Ubuntu 22.04 where `/var/log/auth.log` may not be
    populated depending on rsyslog configuration, yields an empty filter.
  - `[nginx-http-auth]` is enabled while the same corpus explicitly disables
    nginx (`systemctl disable --now nginx  # Use Caddy only`). fail2ban fails a
    jail whose logpath does not exist, and depending on version aborts startup.
    The net result is that no jail, including sshd, is active.
  - `[osiris-api]` references `filter = osiris-api`, a filter file the corpus
    never provides.

WHY IT MATTERS
Every mention of fail2ban in the war game as a countermeasure to brute force is
counting on a service that does not run.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Under EP-1, SSH is not internet-reachable, so the sshd jail becomes a
defence-in-depth measure rather than the front line. Keep it correct anyway.
```ini
# /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
[DEFAULT]
bantime  = 3600
findtime = 600
maxretry = 5
backend  = systemd
banaction = ufw
# Never ban Cloudflare or loopback. Banning a CF edge = self-DoS (DEF-009).
ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 ::1 173.245.48.0/20 103.21.244.0/22 103.22.200.0/22 \
           103.31.4.0/22 141.101.64.0/18 108.162.192.0/18 190.93.240.0/20 \
           188.114.96.0/20 197.234.240.0/22 198.41.128.0/17 162.158.0.0/15 \
           104.16.0.0/13 104.24.0.0/14 172.64.0.0/13 131.0.72.0/22

[sshd]
enabled  = true
maxretry = 3
# no logpath; systemd backend reads the journal

# nginx jails deliberately absent: nginx is not installed.
```
Then verify, every time, because a fail2ban that silently died is worse than
none:
```bash
fail2ban-client status            # must list the jails
fail2ban-client status sshd       # must show a filter and 0 or more bans
systemctl is-active fail2ban      # must be "active"
```
TEST-204 asserts `fail2ban-client status` exits 0 and lists exactly the expected
jails; the deployment fails if it does not.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-014  [S2]  The custom `ssh-monitor.sh` violates the document's own rule and
               is a shell-injection sink
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 1.1 item 6.
CLASS     Self-contradiction; injection; quadratic CPU.

WHAT IS WRONG
```bash
IP=$(echo "$line" | grep -oP 'from \K[0-9.]+')
COUNT=$(grep "$IP" /var/log/auth.log | grep "Failed" | wc -l)
ufw deny from "$IP"
```
  - Section 1.6 of the same document says "Never: `echo "$LOG" | grep
    something`" and "never parse logs as shell." This script does exactly that.
  - `$IP` is derived from an attacker-influenced log line. `grep "$IP" file`
    with `$IP` unquoted-in-effect as a *pattern* means an attacker who can get
    regex metacharacters into the parsed field causes pathological matching, and
    a `ufw deny from "$IP"` with a crafted value is an argument-injection
    primitive against a root-run command.
  - `grep "$IP" /var/log/auth.log | wc -l` runs a full-file scan for every
    matching line. Under a brute-force burst that is O(n²) on the log size, at
    root, competing with sshd for CPU on a shared 4-OCPU box. The monitor
    amplifies the DoS it is watching for.
  - It duplicates fail2ban, so bans come from two sources with different state
    and no coordination.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Delete the script. fail2ban with `banaction = ufw` (DEF-012) does this job with
a state machine, unban timers, and no shell interpolation. If an additional
signal is wanted, read the journal with a typed reader:
```bash
# /usr/local/bin/ssh-anomaly.sh — reports only, never acts, never shells out
journalctl -u ssh --since "10 min ago" -o json \
  | jq -r 'select(.MESSAGE | test("Failed password")) | .MESSAGE' \
  | wc -l
```
and feed the count into the alerting pipeline (CTL-704) as a metric.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-015  [S3]  `chattr +a` on live log files breaks log rotation and fills the
               disk
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 1.6 item 3 and 12.1 item 2.
CLASS     Availability failure disguised as an integrity control.

WHAT IS WRONG
`chattr +a` makes a file append-only. logrotate works by renaming the file and
creating a new one (or by copytruncate). Renaming an append-only file fails with
EPERM; truncating it fails with EPERM. So rotation stops. The log grows without
bound on a 200 GB boot volume shared with the Postgres data directory. When the
disk fills, Postgres stops accepting writes and the service dies — an outage
caused by a control intended to preserve evidence of outages.

It also does not achieve the stated goal: root can `chattr -a` and then edit. An
attacker who has root — which is the threat model for "attacker deletes logs" —
is not stopped by a flag root can clear.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Immutability must live somewhere the attacker's root does not reach.
```
1. Local logs: normal files, normal logrotate, size-capped.
   Docker: log-driver json-file, max-size 10m, max-file 3 (DEF-011).
2. Ship every security-relevant event OFF the host within seconds:
   - to the audit_logs table (which is itself hash-chained, CTL-703), and
   - to an append-only external sink the host cannot delete from.
   Free options: a Cloudflare Worker that writes to R2 with a write-only-scoped
   token, or a Backblaze B2 bucket with Object Lock enabled and an application
   key restricted to writeFiles. Object Lock is the important part: it makes
   deletion impossible for the duration of the retention period even with the
   credential.
3. Archived (already-rotated) files may be chattr +a in a separate directory
   that logrotate does not manage. That is safe and pointless-but-harmless.
4. Publish a daily root hash of the audit chain to a location outside the blast
   radius (CTL-703) so tampering is externally detectable even if every copy on
   the host is rewritten.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-042  [S2]  The hash-chained audit log is rewritable by anyone who can write
               to the database
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 7 `appendAuditLog`.
CLASS     Integrity control with no external anchor.

WHAT IS WRONG
The chain is `hash_n = SHA256(event_n || hash_{n-1})`, stored in the same table
as the events. An attacker who can write to `audit_logs` — which is exactly the
attacker the control exists for, since app-host RCE grants database write —
deletes the rows they dislike and recomputes every subsequent hash. The chain is
internally consistent and completely false. Hash chaining without an external
anchor detects accidental corruption, not adversarial rewriting.

Additionally `appendAuditLog` does `findFirst(orderBy: desc(id))` then inserts,
with no locking. Two concurrent appends read the same `previousHash` and both
insert, forking the chain. Under any concurrency the chain is not a chain.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT — CTL-703
```sql
-- Serialize appends and make the previous hash unforgeable within a transaction.
-- A dedicated advisory lock is cheaper than serializable isolation here.
```
```typescript
export async function appendAuditLog(event: AuditEventInput): Promise<void> {
  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    // 1. Serialize: only one appender at a time. Fixes the fork.
    await tx.execute(sql`SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('osiris_audit'))`);
    const prev = await tx
      .select({ hash: auditLogs.hash })
      .from(auditLogs)
      .orderBy(desc(auditLogs.id))
      .limit(1);
    const previousHash = prev[0]?.hash ?? "GENESIS";
    // 2. Canonical serialization. JSON.stringify key order is insertion order,
    //    which is not stable across code changes; sort explicitly.
    const canonical = canonicalJson({ ...event, previousHash });
    const hash = createHash("sha256").update(canonical).digest("hex");
    await tx.insert(auditLogs).values({ ...event, previousHash, hash });
  });
}
```
```
EXTERNAL ANCHOR (this is the part that makes it real):
  Daily at 00:05 UTC a job computes the current head hash and publishes it to at
  least two places outside the host's control:
    - a message to a read-only Telegram channel (immutable to the host),
    - an object in the write-only-scoped R2/B2 bucket from DEF-015,
    - optionally, a Solana memo transaction from a low-value publishing wallet,
      which makes the anchor publicly and permanently verifiable and costs
      fractions of a cent.
  Verification job: recompute the chain from the last anchored point forward and
  assert the head matches. A mismatch is a CRITICAL page (CTL-708).
  Consequence: an attacker can still rewrite history, but cannot rewrite the
  anchors, so the rewrite is detectable and the window is bounded to 24 hours.
```
Also: revoke `DELETE` and `UPDATE` on `audit_logs` from the application role
entirely (CTL-402). The app can INSERT and SELECT. Nothing else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-043  [S3]  AIDE's database lives where the attacker does
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 13.1 item 1; ADDENDUM L Layer 3 step 5.
CLASS     Integrity monitor that the monitored party can rewrite.

WHAT IS WRONG
`aideinit` writes `/var/lib/aide/aide.db` on the host. An attacker with root
installs their rootkit and then runs `aide --update && mv aide.db.new aide.db`.
The next scheduled check is clean. The corpus's APT scenario (13.1) describes an
attacker who waits six months — plenty of time to notice a daily cron and
neutralize it.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```bash
# 1. Build the AIDE database, then move it out of reach.
aideinit
# 2. Hash it and publish the hash off-box immediately.
sha256sum /var/lib/aide/aide.db > /tmp/aide.db.sha256
# 3. Upload BOTH the db and its hash to the write-only external sink.
#    The host can write new objects; it cannot overwrite or delete prior ones
#    (Object Lock). The comparison happens off-box.
# 4. Make the local copy read-only to the app and owned by root.
chmod 400 /var/lib/aide/aide.db
# 5. Daily check writes its REPORT off-box, and a separate external job asserts
#    that today's db hash equals the anchored one. If aide.db changed and no
#    human approved an update, that is the alert — not the file diff.
```
The detection that matters is "the baseline changed," not "a file changed."
Anyone can change a file; only an attacker changes the baseline silently.
Alert on baseline mutation at CRITICAL. TEST-705.

DEF-049  [S3]  `auditd` is installed with no rules

WHAT IS WRONG
`apt install -y auditd && systemctl enable auditd` installs a daemon with the

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-027  [S1]  Envelope encryption has no associated data, so ciphertext blobs
               can be swapped between rows
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 1 `EnvelopeEncryptionService`.
CLASS     Missing cryptographic binding. Enables a confused-deputy attack with
          database write access.

WHAT IS WRONG
Two issues, the second is severe.

  1. `randomBytes(16)` as the AES-GCM IV. GCM's standard nonce is 96 bits. Node
     accepts 128-bit IVs but they are processed through GHASH-based derivation
     rather than used directly, which is a non-standard mode with weaker
     analysis behind it and no benefit. Use 12 bytes.

  2. No AAD. The ciphertext is not bound to *which wallet it is*. The GCM tag
     authenticates the ciphertext, not the context. So an attacker with UPDATE
     on the `wallets` table can copy the `encrypted_private_key`, `iv`, `tag`,
     and `kek_id` from a victim's row into a row they control, then ask the
     system to sign with "their" wallet. Decryption succeeds — the tag is valid,
     it is the same ciphertext — and the system signs with the victim's key
     while believing it is acting for the attacker's account. Every
     application-layer ownership check passes, because the ownership check
     validates the row, and the row is the attacker's.

     This defeats the entire ownership model with a single UPDATE statement and
     no cryptographic break.

WHY IT MATTERS
This is the clean bypass of the tRPC ownership checks that Red Team entry point
three is about, reached from a different direction. It is also the reason
CTL-102's P1 check (derived public key must equal the expected signer) exists as
a second line.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```typescript
/** Context that MUST be identical at encrypt and decrypt time. Any mismatch
 *  fails the GCM tag check, so a blob moved to another row will not decrypt. */
export interface CryptoContext {
  walletId: string;    // the wallet's public key
  userId: string;      // the owning user
  purpose: "wallet_secret_key";
  kekVersion: string;
}

function aad(ctx: CryptoContext): Buffer {
  // Canonical, unambiguous, length-prefixed. Never a naive concatenation:
  // ("ab","c") and ("a","bc") must not produce the same AAD.
  const parts = [ctx.purpose, ctx.userId, ctx.walletId, ctx.kekVersion];
  const buf = parts.map((p) => {
    const b = Buffer.from(p, "utf8");
    const len = Buffer.alloc(4);
    len.writeUInt32BE(b.length);
    return Buffer.concat([len, b]);
  });
  return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from("OSIRIS-AAD-v1"), ...buf]);
}

async encrypt(plaintext: Buffer, ctx: CryptoContext): Promise<EncryptedData> {
  const dek = randomBytes(32);
  const iv = randomBytes(12);                      // 96-bit GCM nonce
  const cipher = createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", dek, iv);
  cipher.setAAD(aad(ctx));                          // <-- the fix
  const ciphertext = Buffer.concat([cipher.update(plaintext), cipher.final()]);
  const tag = cipher.getAuthTag();
  const wrappedDek = await this.kek.wrap(dek, ctx); // KEK wrap also binds ctx
  dek.fill(0);
  return { ciphertext: b64(ciphertext), iv: b64(iv), tag: b64(tag),
           encryptedDek: b64(wrappedDek), kekVersion: ctx.kekVersion };
}

async decrypt(d: EncryptedData, ctx: CryptoContext): Promise<Buffer> {
  if (d.kekVersion !== ctx.kekVersion) throw new Error("kek_version_mismatch");
  const dek = await this.kek.unwrap(Buffer.from(d.encryptedDek, "base64"), ctx);
  try {
    const decipher = createDecipheriv("aes-256-gcm", dek, Buffer.from(d.iv, "base64"));
    decipher.setAAD(aad(ctx));                      // <-- must match exactly
    decipher.setAuthTag(Buffer.from(d.tag, "base64"));
    return Buffer.concat([
      decipher.update(Buffer.from(d.ciphertext, "base64")),
      decipher.final(),                             // throws on any mismatch
    ]);
  } finally {
    dek.fill(0);
  }
}
```
UNDER CTL-100 this runs inside the signer Worker, and the Worker receives the
context from the signed request. The request signature covers the context, so
the app host cannot lie about which wallet a blob belongs to without invalidating
its own signature. Two independent mechanisms now block the swap.
TEST-104 encrypts under context A and asserts decryption under context B throws.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-020  [S5]  Browser certificate pinning is not implementable
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 2.1 item 2, 6.3 item 1.
CLASS     Impossible control listed as a mitigation.

WHAT IS WRONG
"Pin Cloudflare origin certificate hash / Reject unknown certificates" in a web
frontend. HTTP Public Key Pinning was removed from browsers years ago precisely
because it was a footgun that bricked sites. A web page cannot inspect or reject
the TLS certificate of its own connection. There is no API. The mitigation
cannot be written, so it will be quietly skipped, and the MITM row in the threat
matrix will stay ticked.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Split by direction, because pinning IS implementable server-to-server:

BROWSER -> ORIGIN (pinning impossible; use these instead)
  - HSTS with `includeSubDomains; preload`, submitted to hstspreload.org
    (subject to DEF-016).
  - CAA records restricting issuance to the CAs you actually use:
    `osiris.trade. CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"` and
    `osiris.trade. CAA 0 issuewild ";"` plus
    `osiris.trade. CAA 0 iodef "mailto:security@osiris.trade"`.
  - Certificate Transparency monitoring: a daily job querying crt.sh for
    `osiris.trade` and alerting on any certificate not issued by your pipeline.
    This is the real replacement for Expect-CT (DEF-019) and it is free.
  - DNSSEC on the zone plus registry lock at the registrar.

SERVER -> UPSTREAM (pinning is implementable; do it)
  Node's https.Agent can pin the SPKI of Jupiter, Helius, and any upstream whose
  compromise would cost money:
```typescript
import { Agent } from "node:https";
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const PINS: Record<string, string[]> = {
  // sha256(SubjectPublicKeyInfo), base64. Pin the intermediate, not the leaf,
  // and always pin at least two so rotation does not cause an outage.
  "quote-api.jup.ag": ["<pin1>", "<backup-pin>"],
  "mainnet.helius-rpc.com": ["<pin1>", "<backup-pin>"],
};

export const pinnedAgent = new Agent({
  keepAlive: true,
  checkServerIdentity(host, cert) {
    // Run the default hostname/SAN validation first.
    const err = require("node:tls").checkServerIdentity(host, cert);
    if (err) return err;
    const expected = PINS[host];
    if (!expected) return undefined;      // not pinned; default checks apply
    let chain: any = cert;
    const seen = new Set<string>();
    while (chain && !seen.has(chain.fingerprint256)) {
      seen.add(chain.fingerprint256);
      const spki = createHash("sha256").update(chain.pubkey).digest("base64");
      if (expected.includes(spki)) return undefined;   // pin matched
      chain = chain.issuerCertificate === chain ? null : chain.issuerCertificate;
    }
    return new Error(`SPKI pin mismatch for ${host}`);
  },
});
```
  Operational requirement: a weekly job that fetches each pinned host's current
  chain and alerts 30 days before any pinned certificate expires. A pin without
  expiry monitoring is a scheduled outage.
