DEF-019  [S5]  `Expect-CT` is obsolete
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 2.1 item 3.
CLASS     Dead header.
FIX       Remove it. Chrome deprecated and removed Expect-CT; CT enforcement is
          now unconditional for publicly trusted certificates. Replace with the
          crt.sh CT-monitoring job from DEF-020. Sending the header is harmless
          but it occupies a checklist line that should hold a working control.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-017  [S3]  `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block` is harmful
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 Caddyfile.
CLASS     Obsolete header that historically introduced vulnerabilities.

WHAT IS WRONG
The legacy XSS auditor it enables was removed from Chrome and Edge because it
was itself exploitable — the filter could be induced to break otherwise-safe
pages and to disclose cross-origin information. Where the header is still
honored, `1; mode=block` re-enables that behaviour.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```
X-XSS-Protection: 0
```
Explicitly disable it, and rely on CSP. Set to `0` rather than omitting it, so
that a scanner or a future maintainer sees a deliberate decision rather than an
oversight.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-018  [S1]  Two contradictory CSPs, and the one that ships disarms XSS
               protection
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 Caddyfile vs war game 4.1 item 2.
CLASS     Contradiction resolved in favour of the weaker policy.

WHAT IS WRONG
War game:     `script-src 'self'`
ADDENDUM L:   `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`
The Caddyfile is what ships, so `'unsafe-inline'` is what ships. With
`'unsafe-inline'`, injected `<script>alert(1)</script>` executes and every
inline event handler executes. CSP contributes nothing to XSS defence. Red Team
entry point six ("XSS in token name display = session theft") is filed as
mitigated by a policy that does not mitigate it.

The reason `'unsafe-inline'` crept in is structural: Next.js App Router emits
inline hydration scripts, and a static export cannot use per-request nonces.
That is why ARGUMENT 11 rules for a single server-rendered origin — it is what
makes a nonce possible.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT — the single canonical CSP for this system
```
Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
  object-src 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  form-action 'self';
  script-src 'self' 'nonce-{NONCE}' 'strict-dynamic';
  style-src 'self' 'nonce-{NONCE}';
  img-src 'self' data:;
  font-src 'self';
  connect-src 'self';
  manifest-src 'self';
  worker-src 'self';
  media-src 'none';
  require-trusted-types-for 'script';
  trusted-types default dompurify;
  upgrade-insecure-requests;
  report-uri /api/csp-report
```
Notes that matter:
  - `'strict-dynamic'` means the nonce propagates to scripts that nonce'd
    scripts load, which is how Next.js chunk loading survives without a
    host allowlist. Once `'strict-dynamic'` is present, host-source
    expressions in `script-src` are ignored by supporting browsers — this is
    intentional and is why no CDN appears there.
  - `connect-src 'self'` only, because ARGUMENT 11 moves all upstream calls
    server-side. This is what removes the Helius key from the browser (DEF-021).
  - `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` eliminates DOM-XSS sinks structurally
    in Chromium; `innerHTML =` with a string throws instead of executing. This
    is the strongest available answer to entry point six and it is free.
  - `report-uri` must be rate-limited and must never be trusted input.
  - Deploy in `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` for 48 hours first, fix the
    reports, then enforce. Enforcing on day one without a report phase is how
    people end up adding `'unsafe-inline'` at 2am.
  - The nonce is generated per request in Next.js middleware, 16 random bytes
    base64, and passed to the app; it must never be reused or derived from
    anything predictable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-021  [S1]  The CSP ships the Helius API key to every user's browser
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 2.1 item 5:
          `connect-src 'self' https://api.osiris.trade wss://mainnet.helius-rpc.com`
CLASS     Credential disclosure written into a security control.

WHAT IS WRONG
Allowing the browser to open a WebSocket to Helius means the browser must know
the Helius endpoint URL, and Helius authenticates by API key *in the URL*
(`wss://mainnet.helius-rpc.com/?api-key=...`). Therefore the key is in client
JavaScript, in the network tab, and in every user's browser history. Anyone can
extract it in ten seconds.

Consequences: the key is used up by third parties (it is metered), the account
can be rate-limited or suspended, request patterns are attributable, and if the
key has elevated permissions on the Helius account the exposure is worse than
quota theft. The same reasoning applies to PumpPortal and any other keyed
upstream.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Per ARGUMENT 11: `connect-src 'self'` only. The browser opens exactly one
WebSocket, to `wss://osiris.trade/api/stream`, authenticated with the session
cookie. The backend holds a single upstream connection to Helius, fans out to
subscribers, applies per-user authorization to every message, and never
forwards raw upstream frames (which may contain data the requesting user is not
entitled to). Same pattern for Jupiter quotes, DexScreener, RugCheck, and token
metadata.

Additional benefit that justifies the work on its own: one upstream connection
serving N users is dramatically cheaper on a free RPC tier than N connections,
and it gives you one place to cache, one place to rate limit, and one place to
fail over to a backup RPC (DEF-045).
TEST-303 greps the built client bundle for `helius`, `api-key`, `api_key`, and
the literal key values from the environment, and fails the build on any hit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-022  [S3]  Missing isolation and caching headers
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 Caddyfile header block.
CLASS     Incomplete header set.

WHAT IS MISSING
  - `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` — severs the window.opener
    relationship, which is the structural fix for tabnabbing (war game 4.7)
    and a prerequisite for cross-origin isolation.
  - `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin` — prevents other sites from
    embedding your resources.
  - `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` — optional; only if SharedArrayBuffer
    is needed. Do not enable it blindly; it breaks third-party embeds.
  - `Cache-Control: no-store` on every authenticated response. Without it,
    account data is written to the browser's disk cache and to any intermediary
    that ignores the absence of a directive. On a shared machine that is a
    disclosure. This is separate from `Clear-Site-Data` on logout.
  - `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` — the corpus uses
    `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, which still leaks your origin to
    third parties. For a trading app, send nothing.
  - `Permissions-Policy` should be comprehensive, not three entries.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT — canonical header block (see also CTL-303)
```caddyfile
header {
    Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload"
    X-Content-Type-Options    "nosniff"
    X-Frame-Options           "DENY"
    X-XSS-Protection          "0"
    Referrer-Policy           "no-referrer"
    Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy   "same-origin"
    Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy "same-origin"
    Permissions-Policy "accelerometer=(), ambient-light-sensor=(), autoplay=(), battery=(), camera=(), display-capture=(), document-domain=(), encrypted-media=(), fullscreen=(self), geolocation=(), gyroscope=(), magnetometer=(), microphone=(), midi=(), payment=(), picture-in-picture=(), publickey-credentials-get=(self), screen-wake-lock=(), serial=(), usb=(), xr-spatial-tracking=()"
    -Server
    -X-Powered-By
}

@authed path /api/* /dashboard/* /settings/*
header @authed Cache-Control "no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate"
header @authed Pragma "no-cache"
```
Note `publickey-credentials-get=(self)` is required for WebAuthn (CTL-502) —
a blanket `Permissions-Policy` that omits it will silently break passkeys.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-016  [S3]  HSTS preload with includeSubDomains is a one-way door
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 2.1 item 1.
CLASS     Irreversible configuration shipped without a warning.

WHAT IS WRONG
Submitting to hstspreload.org bakes the domain into browser binaries. Removal
takes months and does not reach users who do not update. With
`includeSubDomains`, every current and future subdomain must be HTTPS forever —
including internal tooling, a status page on a third-party host that only speaks
HTTP, a mail-provider verification subdomain, or a partner integration.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Staged rollout, recorded in the runbook as an irreversible gate:
```
Week 1: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=300
Week 2: max-age=86400; includeSubDomains         (audit every subdomain first)
Week 3: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
Week 4: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload  -> submit
```
Precondition for week 2: enumerate every DNS record in the zone and confirm each
host serves valid HTTPS. Precondition for week 4: sign-off that no future
subdomain will need plain HTTP, ever.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-023  [S3]  Origin validation as written accepts requests with no Origin
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 4.2 item 5.
CLASS     Incomplete CSRF check.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
const allowedOrigins = ['https://osiris.trade', 'https://app.osiris.trade'];
if (!allowedOrigins.includes(req.headers.origin)) return 403;
```
  - `req.headers.origin` is `undefined` for same-origin GETs and for some
    non-browser clients. `includes(undefined)` is false, so this rejects
    legitimate same-origin navigation — or a developer adds `|| !origin` to
    "fix" it, which then accepts every request that simply omits the header,
    including some curl/CSRF-adjacent cases.
  - `Origin: null` is sent by sandboxed iframes and by some redirect chains and
    must be explicitly rejected, not accidentally accepted.
  - Under ARGUMENT 11 there is exactly one origin, which simplifies this
    considerably.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```typescript
const SELF_ORIGIN = "https://osiris.trade";

export function assertSameOrigin(req: Request): void {
  const method = req.method.toUpperCase();
  if (method === "GET" || method === "HEAD" || method === "OPTIONS") return;

  const origin = req.headers.get("origin");
  const referer = req.headers.get("referer");

  if (origin !== null && origin !== "null") {
    if (origin !== SELF_ORIGIN) throw new ForbiddenError("bad_origin");
    return;
  }
  // No Origin header on a state-changing request. Fall back to Referer, and if
  // that is also absent, reject. A browser always sends one of the two on a
  // cross-site POST; a request with neither is not a browser doing something
  // legitimate.
  if (!referer) throw new ForbiddenError("no_origin_no_referer");
  const refOrigin = new URL(referer).origin;
  if (refOrigin !== SELF_ORIGIN) throw new ForbiddenError("bad_referer");
}
```
Layered with `SameSite=Strict` cookies, a double-submit CSRF token compared with
the `safeEqual` helper from DEF-007, and — because tRPC always sends
`content-type: application/json`, which is not a simple request type — the
browser's own preflight requirement. Four layers; any one of them holding is
enough.

################################################################################
GROUP C — CONCURRENCY, STATE, AND CORRECTNESS
################################################################################

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-028  [S1]  The race-condition fix does not cover the race
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 3.6 item 1.
CLASS     Check-then-act across a lock boundary.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  const session = await tx.select()...for('update');
  if (session.status !== 'active') throw ...;
  await tx.update(tradingSessions).set({ status: 'signing' })...;
});
// transaction commits, row lock released
// ... later, in a different job, the actual signing happens
```
The `FOR UPDATE` lock lives only for the transaction. It is released at commit,
before the transaction is built, before it is signed, and before it is sent. The
pipeline is `quote -> build -> sign -> send -> confirm` across five pg-boss jobs.
The lock protects the status flip and nothing else.

Worse, `status: 'signing'` is a lock held in a data column with no owner, no
lease, and no expiry. If the signing job dies — OOM, deploy, network — the
session is stuck in `signing` forever and the user cannot trade until someone
manually resets it. A stuck-state bug in a trading system reads exactly like a
freeze to the user.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT — atomic compare-and-set plus a lease
```typescript
/** Atomic CAS: the WHERE clause is the guard. Either exactly one caller flips
 *  the row and gets it back, or nobody does. No read-then-write window. */
export async function claimSessionForTrade(
  sessionId: string,
  ownerToken: string,           // uuid identifying this worker+attempt
  leaseSeconds = 60
): Promise<TradingSession | null> {
  const rows = await db
    .update(tradingSessions)
    .set({
      status: "signing",
      leaseOwner: ownerToken,
      leaseExpiresAt: sql`now() + make_interval(secs => ${leaseSeconds})`,
      updatedAt: sql`now()`,
    })
    .where(
      and(
        eq(tradingSessions.id, sessionId),
        // claimable if active, OR if a previous lease has expired
        or(
          eq(tradingSessions.status, "active"),
          and(
            eq(tradingSessions.status, "signing"),
            lt(tradingSessions.leaseExpiresAt, sql`now()`)
          )
        )
      )
    )
    .returning();
  return rows[0] ?? null;   // null == somebody else holds it
}

/** Release must also be a CAS, so a worker whose lease expired cannot clobber
 *  the new owner's state. */
export async function releaseSession(sessionId: string, ownerToken: string) {
  await db.update(tradingSessions)
    .set({ status: "active", leaseOwner: null, leaseExpiresAt: null })
    .where(and(
      eq(tradingSessions.id, sessionId),
      eq(tradingSessions.leaseOwner, ownerToken)
    ));
}
```
Schema additions: `lease_owner text`, `lease_expires_at timestamptz`, plus
`index on (status, lease_expires_at)` for the reaper.
A reaper job every 30s logs any lease that expired without release — that is a
crash signal, and it should be a metric, not silence.

AND, decisively: even if all of the above is wrong, the signer's per-wallet rate
limit and per-request `requestId` deduplication (CTL-102 P6) make a duplicate
signature impossible at the last layer. Two mechanisms, two systems (INV-2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-029  [S1]  Session revocation is not the fastest path; it is not even a
               reliable path
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Research package section 10 `revokeSession`; ADDENDUM K Part 2
          "Session State Caching (Critical Path)".
CLASS     The kill switch does not kill.

WHAT IS WRONG
Three failures compound:

  1. Revocation writes to Postgres. Session state is *cached in Redis* per
     ADDENDUM K with a TTL. Workers that read the cache continue to see
     `active` until the TTL expires. Revocation is therefore eventually
     consistent, with the eventual bounded by a cache TTL, during a window in
     which the user is pressing a panic button because they believe they are
     being robbed.
  2. `await boss.cancel('trade:%', { sessionId })` is not a pg-boss API. There
     is no wildcard-name cancellation and no metadata-predicate cancellation.
     This line does not compile against pg-boss's signature, or if coerced,
     cancels nothing. In-flight jobs are not cancelled.
  3. Every enforcement point is inside the application. If the application host
     is compromised — the case where you most want revocation — the attacker
     simply does not honor it.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT — revocation as a monotonic epoch, enforced at the signer
```typescript
export async function revokeSession(
  sessionId: string, userId: string, reason: string, isPanic = false
): Promise<void> {
  const t0 = performance.now();

  // STEP 1 — the signer. Do this FIRST, before anything else, because this is
  // the only step that binds an attacker who controls this host. It is one
  // HTTPS call to a Cloudflare KV write; it completes in tens of milliseconds.
  await signerClient.revoke({ sessionId, userId, scope: isPanic ? "user" : "session" });

  // STEP 2 — Redis tombstone. Tombstones are checked BEFORE the cached session
  // object and are never TTL'd shorter than the session itself, so a stale
  // cached "active" cannot win.
  await redis.set(`revoked:session:${sessionId}`, reason, "EX", 60 * 60 * 24 * 8);
  if (isPanic) await redis.incr(`epoch:user:${userId}`);   // invalidates all

  // STEP 3 — durable record.
  await db.update(tradingSessions).set({
    status: "revoked", revokedAt: new Date(), revokedReason: reason,
  }).where(eq(tradingSessions.id, sessionId));

  // STEP 4 — best-effort: cancel queued jobs by their real ids, broadcast.
  const ids = await db.select({ id: tradeJobs.pgBossId })
    .from(tradeJobs).where(eq(tradeJobs.sessionId, sessionId));
  await Promise.allSettled(ids.map((r) => boss.cancel(r.id)));
  broadcastToSession(sessionId, { type: "SESSION_REVOKED", reason, isPanic });

  metrics.observe("revocation_latency_ms", performance.now() - t0);
}
```
```typescript
/** The ONLY sanctioned session read. Tombstone first, always. */
export async function readSession(sessionId: string) {
  if (await redis.exists(`revoked:session:${sessionId}`)) return null;
  const cached = await redis.get(`session:${sessionId}`);
  const s = cached ? JSON.parse(cached) : await loadFromDb(sessionId);
  if (!s) return null;
  const epoch = Number(await redis.get(`epoch:user:${s.userId}`) ?? 0);
  if (epoch > s.epoch) return null;   // panic invalidated everything older
  return s;
}
```
PANIC BUTTON, restated: the panic path must NOT "bypass normal auth middleware"
as the research package says — an unauthenticated panic endpoint is a free DoS
where anyone who learns a session id can halt a stranger's trading. It must
authenticate, but with the *cheapest sufficient* check (valid session cookie OR
a pre-issued single-purpose panic token the user can keep in their phone's
notes), and it must skip everything else: no rate limiter lookup, no analytics,
no anomaly scoring. Fast because it does less, not because it checks less.
TEST-105 asserts that after `revoke`, a signer request for that session is
rejected by the *signer*, with the application deliberately patched to ignore
revocation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-030  [S3]  `singletonKey` misused twice, in opposite directions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 3.6 item 3 (`singletonKey: trade:${sessionId}`,
          `singletonSeconds: 60`); research package section 2
          (`singletonKey: "copy-trade"` — a constant).
CLASS     One config blocks legitimate work; the other serializes all users
          globally.

WHAT IS WRONG
  - `singletonKey: 'trade:' + sessionId` with `singletonSeconds: 60` means a
    user cannot place a second trade in the same session for 60 seconds. On a
    memecoin bot that is a product-breaking constraint sold as a security
    control. It also does not prevent the actual bug (two intents for one
    click); it prevents two intents for two clicks.
  - `singletonKey: "copy-trade"` is a literal constant in the job *definition*,
    so every copy trade for every user shares one singleton slot. Only one copy
    trade in the entire system can be queued at a time. One stuck job halts copy
    trading for all users — an availability single point of failure created by a
    typo-level mistake.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Separate the two concerns. Idempotency belongs to the intent; concurrency
control belongs to the resource.
```typescript
// 1. Idempotency at the intent level. The CLIENT generates the key.
export const tradeIntents = pgTable("trade_intents", {
  idempotencyKey: text("idempotency_key").primaryKey(),   // client uuid v4
  userId:  text("user_id").notNull(),
  sessionId: text("session_id").notNull(),
  requestHash: text("request_hash").notNull(),  // sha256 of normalized params
  tradeId: text("trade_id"),
  createdAt: timestamp("created_at").defaultNow().notNull(),
});
// Insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Zero rows inserted => duplicate intent:
// return the existing tradeId instead of creating a second trade. If the key
// matches but requestHash differs, that is a client bug or an attack: reject
// with 409, never silently execute either version.

// 2. Concurrency at the resource level: the session lease from DEF-028.

// 3. Per-invocation singleton keys, not per-definition:
await boss.send("copy:execute", data, {
  singletonKey: `copy:${userId}:${targetWallet}:${targetSignature}`,
  singletonSeconds: 300,   // dedupes a replayed webhook, blocks nobody else
});
```
Move `singletonKey` out of the job *definition* object entirely so it cannot be
a constant by accident. TEST-501 fires the same intent twice concurrently and
asserts exactly one trade row.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-031  [S4]  PM2 cluster mode and Docker `deploy.replicas: 4` multiply
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM K Part 4 (PM2 cluster) vs ADDENDUM L Layer 3
          (`deploy: replicas: 4`).
CLASS     Contradiction producing 4x oversubscription; also a port conflict.

WHAT IS WRONG
  - ADDENDUM K runs PM2 in cluster mode with instances per core. ADDENDUM L runs
    4 container replicas. Together: 4 containers x N PM2 workers on a 4-OCPU
    box. Context-switch thrash, memory exhaustion, and the `max_memory_restart`
    setting causing cascading restarts under load — which is Red Team attack 1.3
    achieved without an attacker.
  - `deploy.replicas` combined with a published host port cannot work: N
    containers cannot bind the same host port. Compose will error or start one.
  - Several `deploy` subkeys behave differently in Compose versus Swarm.
    `deploy.resources.reservations.cpus` and `deploy.placement` are Swarm
    concepts. Do not rely on a key whose behaviour you have not observed on the
    version you run.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Pick one process manager. For a single host, PM2 inside one container is
simpler, keeps the port model trivial, and gives zero-downtime reloads.
```yaml
app:
  image: osiris-app@sha256:<PIN>
  # exactly one container; PM2 handles process-level concurrency
  # bind to loopback: Caddy runs on the host and proxies to it
  ports: ["127.0.0.1:3000:3000"]
  # Use the unambiguous, non-Swarm keys so behaviour does not depend on mode:
  mem_limit: 2g
  mem_reservation: 512m
  cpus: 2.0
  pids_limit: 512
  restart: unless-stopped
  user: "1000:1000"
  read_only: true
  tmpfs: ["/tmp:noexec,nosuid,size=64m"]
  security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
  cap_drop: ["ALL"]
  networks: [backend]
```
```javascript
// ecosystem.config.cjs — instances sized to the box, leaving room for
// Postgres, Redis, Caddy, and the OS. Do not use "max".
module.exports = {
  apps: [{
    name: "osiris-web",
    script: "server.js",
    instances: 2,
    exec_mode: "cluster",
    max_memory_restart: "700M",
    node_args: "--disable-proto=delete --max-old-space-size=640",
    kill_timeout: 10000,
    listen_timeout: 8000,
  }],
};
```
Whatever numbers are chosen must be validated with a load test before launch and
recorded. A resource limit nobody has tested is a guess.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-032  [S4]  `ignore-scripts=true` plus native modules on arm64 will not build
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 8 `.npmrc`; ADDENDUM M Scenario 5; war game 4.5
          item 4; combined with the recommendation to use `re2` (war game 3.10)
          and `@node-rs/argon2` (DEF-004).
CLASS     Mutually exclusive requirements shipped together.

WHAT IS WRONG
`ignore-scripts=true` is a genuinely strong supply-chain control — install-time
script execution is the most common npm attack vector. But it also disables the
`install` and `postinstall` steps that native modules use to download or compile
prebuilt binaries. On arm64 the prebuild coverage is thinner than on x64, so the
modules most likely to break are exactly the ones the corpus recommends.

Result: a developer hits an obscure "cannot find module .node" error, searches,
finds "delete ignore-scripts", and the supply-chain control is gone permanently.
The control is lost not because it was wrong but because it was shipped without
the accompanying procedure.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Keep the control; add the procedure.
```ini
# .npmrc
ignore-scripts=true
package-lock=true
registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/
audit=true
fund=false
save-exact=true          # no ^ or ~ ever, at install time, automatically
engine-strict=true
```
```json
// package.json — explicit, reviewed allowlist of packages permitted to run
// install scripts. Adding to this list is a code review event.
{
  "scripts": {
    "postinstall": "node scripts/run-allowed-build-scripts.mjs"
  }
}
```
```javascript
// scripts/run-allowed-build-scripts.mjs
// Runs `npm rebuild <pkg>` for a short, explicit allowlist AFTER `npm ci
// --ignore-scripts` has completed. Every entry must have a comment explaining
// why it is native and who reviewed it.
const ALLOWED = [
  "@node-rs/argon2",   // native argon2; prebuilds published for linux-arm64-gnu
  // "re2",            // see DEF-032b: prefer NOT to use re2
];
```
DEF-032b: prefer avoiding `re2` entirely. The ReDoS problem it solves is better
solved by not writing catastrophic regexes and by bounding input length before
any regex runs (see DEF-033). Adding a native dependency to the trusted compute
base in order to avoid a class of bug you can avoid by construction is a bad
trade on arm64. If `re2` is genuinely needed, verify a linux-arm64 prebuild
exists for the pinned version before adding it.

Additional supply-chain controls that cost nothing and are missing entirely:
```bash
npm ci --ignore-scripts        # never `npm install` in CI
npm audit signatures           # verifies registry signatures on the tree
npx --yes @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json   # SBOM
```
plus image digest pinning (DEF-052) and secret scanning (DEF-053).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-033  [S3]  Solana address validation accepts things that are not wallets
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 3.10 item 1; ADDENDUM L Layer 4 `SolanaAddressSchema`.
CLASS     Incomplete validation.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
/^[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{32,44}$/
new PublicKey(address)
```
  - The character-count check is not a byte-length check. Base58 is not
    fixed-ratio: a 32-character base58 string can decode to fewer than 32 bytes.
    `new PublicKey()` will accept some of these and produce a key that is not
    what the user typed.
  - `PublicKey` accepts any 32 bytes, including points not on the ed25519 curve.
    A PDA is a valid `PublicKey` and is not a wallet — it has no private key and
    cannot receive a transfer the way a user expects. For a *destination
    address* field, off-curve is a red flag; for a program-derived account it is
    expected. The schema must distinguish, and the corpus's single schema is
    used for both.
  - The regex is applied without a prior length bound, so a 10 MB string is
    handed to the regex engine. This one is linear-time so it will not
    catastrophically backtrack, but it is still 10 MB of work per request and it
    is the same pattern that DOES bite on other regexes.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```typescript
import { PublicKey } from "@solana/web3.js";
import bs58 from "bs58";

/** Bound BEFORE the regex, always. This ordering is the general rule. */
const base58Shape = z.string().min(32).max(44).regex(/^[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]+$/);

function decodesTo32Bytes(s: string): boolean {
  try { return bs58.decode(s).length === 32; } catch { return false; }
}

/** Any 32-byte account: mints, PDAs, program ids, token accounts. */
export const SolanaAccountSchema = base58Shape.refine(decodesTo32Bytes, "not 32 bytes");

/** A user-controlled wallet. Must be on-curve: a PDA cannot sign or be safely
 *  sent to as a system account, and accepting one in a withdrawal destination
 *  field is a way to burn funds. */
export const WalletAddressSchema = SolanaAccountSchema.refine((s) => {
  try { return PublicKey.isOnCurve(new PublicKey(s).toBytes()); } catch { return false; }
}, "address is off-curve (not a wallet)");

/** A token mint. On-curve-ness is not meaningful; existence is. Do the
 *  on-chain existence check in a separate async layer, never inside a Zod
 *  refine (see DEF-033b). */
export const MintSchema = SolanaAccountSchema;
```
DEF-033b [S3]: `TokenMintSchema` in ADDENDUM L uses an `async` refine that calls
`connection.getAccountInfo`. That puts an unbounded, unauthenticated, uncached
network call to the RPC provider inside input validation — before authentication,
before rate limiting. An attacker sends 10,000 random base58 strings and burns
the RPC quota, and every request blocks on network I/O. Existence checking is a
business rule, not a validation rule: it belongs after auth, after the rate
limiter, behind a cache, with a timeout.

################################################################################
GROUP D — DETECTION, RESPONSE, AND OPERATIONS
################################################################################

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-034  [S3]  Device-fingerprint session binding is brittle and
               counterproductive
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 5.1 item 3.
CLASS     High false-positive control; privacy hazard.

WHAT IS WRONG
Canvas, WebGL, and font fingerprints change on browser updates, GPU driver
updates, OS updates, window resizes on some implementations, and whenever the
user enables privacy protections — which security-conscious users do. Binding a
session to that value means logging people out semi-randomly, most often the
users who care most about security. It also builds a tracking-grade identifier
into a financial product, which is a regulatory and reputational liability, and
it is defeated by any attacker who has XSS (they can read and replay the
fingerprint from the same page).

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Bind to things that are stable and meaningful:
  - A rotating session token. Rotate on every privilege elevation and on a
    fixed schedule; detect reuse of a superseded token, which is a strong
    theft signal (this is the standard refresh-token-reuse detection and it is
    genuinely high-signal).
  - Coarse network context: ASN and country, not IP. Alert on change; do not
    auto-revoke, because mobile users change ASN legitimately.
  - Re-authenticate with a passkey for Trust Tier 2 and 3 actions
    (ARGUMENT 9). Possession of a stolen cookie does not give possession of
    the authenticator.
  - Show the user their active sessions with device, ASN, country, and last
    seen, and let them revoke. Users are excellent at spotting "Chrome on
    Windows in a country I have never visited."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-035  [S3]  The anomaly detector fires on the product's normal behaviour
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 5 `AnomalyDetector`.
CLASS     Alert fatigue by construction. See ARGUMENT 10.
FIX       Delete `OFF_HOURS_TRADING`, `NEW_TOKEN_TRADE`, and the 3x-average
          `UNUSUAL_TRADE_SIZE` and 10/min `RAPID_TRADING` thresholds as paging
          alerts. Retain them as non-paging risk scores stored on the trade row
          for forensics and for the user's own activity view. Replace paging
          detection with CTL-705 through CTL-709, whose defining property is
          that a benign explanation is rare rather than typical.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-036  [S2]  The critical incident response damages users and creates
               liability
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 6 `criticalResponse`.
CLASS     Wrong mechanism; conflates billing with security; unbounded blast
          radius.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
await db.update(users).set({ tier: "free" }).where(inArray(users.id, ids));
await db.update(accounts).set({ password: null }).where(inArray(...));
```
  - Downgrading a paying user's `tier` to disable trading destroys billing
    state. Restoring it requires knowing what they had. Users who paid for Pro
    are silently on Free with no record of the change beyond an incident log.
    Security containment must never mutate commercial state.
  - `password: null` in Better Auth's `account` row is not a documented
    "force reset" mechanism. Depending on version it either leaves the account
    unauthenticatable with no reset path, or — worse — leaves it in a state some
    code path treats as "no password required."
  - `.where(eq(tradingSessions.userId, userId))` inside a loop over
    `affectedUserIds` with no bound: if the incident detector produces a large
    affected set (and a false positive will), this mass-revokes and mass-locks
    a large fraction of the user base. Red Team attack 12.3 is literally
    "trigger security features to make the system block legitimate users." The
    automation is the weapon.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```typescript
// Dedicated, reversible, security-only state. Never touch `tier`.
export const userSecurityHolds = pgTable("user_security_holds", {
  userId: text("user_id").primaryKey(),
  level: text("level").notNull(),      // 'trading_paused' | 'full_lock'
  reason: text("reason").notNull(),
  incidentId: text("incident_id").notNull(),
  placedAt: timestamp("placed_at").defaultNow().notNull(),
  expiresAt: timestamp("expires_at"),  // auto-expiring holds by default
  releasedAt: timestamp("released_at"),
  releasedBy: text("released_by"),
});
```
```typescript
const AUTOMATION_BLAST_RADIUS = 25;   // hard cap on automated containment

async function criticalResponse(incident: SecurityIncident) {
  if (incident.affectedUserIds.length > AUTOMATION_BLAST_RADIUS) {
    // Above the cap, automation stops and a human decides. An automated action
    // affecting hundreds of users is itself an incident.
    await pageOncall("CONTAINMENT_EXCEEDS_BLAST_RADIUS", incident);
    await globalHalt(incident.id);   // signer HALT: stops signing, breaks
                                     // nothing else, fully reversible
    return;
  }
  for (const userId of incident.affectedUserIds) {
    await placeHold(userId, "trading_paused", incident.id, { expiresIn: "24h" });
    await revokeAllSessions(userId, `INCIDENT:${incident.id}`);   // DEF-029
  }
  // Force re-auth by rotating the session-signing epoch, NOT by nulling
  // credentials. The user logs in normally with their existing password/passkey.
  await bumpAuthEpoch(incident.affectedUserIds);
  await notifyAffectedUsers(incident);
}
```
Principles, stated so they are not re-derived incorrectly later:
  - Containment actions must be reversible and must auto-expire.
  - Containment must never destroy commercial or credential state.
  - Automated containment has a blast-radius cap; above it, a human decides.
  - The globally-safe action (stop signing) is always preferred over the
    locally-destructive one (lock accounts).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-037  [S3]  `isSessionSuspicious` detects unprofitable trading
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 6.
CLASS     Detector measuring the wrong variable.

WHAT IS WRONG
```typescript
const allLosses = trades.every((t) => Number(t.executedPrice) < Number(t.quotedPrice) * 0.95);
return allLosses && trades.length > 5;
```
This says: "if the last 5+ trades all executed more than 5% worse than quoted,
the session is compromised." What that actually detects is high slippage —
i.e. thin liquidity, volatile markets, or a slippage setting that is too tight.
On a memecoin bot it will fire on ordinary bad conditions and revoke sessions
mid-trade. It will never fire on an attacker, because an attacker executing a
sandwich or a forced swap has no reason to produce five consecutive
worse-than-quote fills — and a profitable attacker produces the opposite signal.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
Replace with signals that describe control, not outcome:
```typescript
async function sessionRiskSignals(session): Promise<Signal[]> {
  return [
    // A signing request whose transaction the policy engine rejected. Normal
    // clients never produce these; a compromised host produces many.
    await signerRejectionsInWindow(session.id, "15m"),      // >0 is notable
    // Trades whose output mint has no route back to SOL on any allowlisted
    // AMM: the shape of a forced dump into an attacker's token.
    await unsellableOutputMintCount(session.id, "1h"),      // >0 is severe
    // Session used from a new ASN AND a security setting changed within 10min.
    await asnChangeFollowedBySettingsChange(session.userId, "10m"),
    // Trade rate exceeding the user's own p99 by 5x, not a global constant.
    await rateVsPersonalBaseline(session.userId),
  ];
}
```
Every one of these is rare when benign. That is the selection criterion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-038  [S4]  Retention policy names tables that do not exist
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 7 `RETENTION_POLICIES`.
CLASS     Runtime error; plus it deletes from the audit log.

WHAT IS WRONG
  - The policy list contains `"sessions"`. The Drizzle schema names that table
    `"session"` (Better Auth's convention). `sql.identifier("sessions")` produces
    `DELETE FROM "sessions"` -> `relation "sessions" does not exist`. The whole
    job throws on that entry and every later policy is skipped, silently, in a
    cron job nobody watches.
  - `"rate_limits"` is not in the schema at all.
  - `{ table: "audit_logs", retentionDays: 2555 }` issues DELETE against the
    append-only, hash-chained audit log, which breaks the chain at the tail and
    contradicts DEF-042's requirement that the app role hold no DELETE grant on
    that table. If the grant is correctly revoked, this job fails; if the job
    succeeds, the grant is wrong.
  - Deleting a `trades` row with `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `tax_lots` destroys
    tax basis history that the product promises to keep for seven years.

CORRECTED ARTIFACT
```typescript
// Reference the Drizzle table objects, not strings. A renamed table then
// becomes a compile error instead of a 3am cron failure.
const RETENTION: Array<{ table: PgTable; column: PgColumn; days: number; mode: "delete" | "anonymize" }> = [
  { table: notifications, column: notifications.createdAt, days: 90,  mode: "delete" },
  { table: webhookEvents, column: webhookEvents.createdAt, days: 30,  mode: "delete" },
  { table: sessions,      column: sessions.expiresAt,      days: 90,  mode: "delete" },
  // trades and tax_lots: NEVER deleted. Anonymize the user linkage only, and
  // only after the account is closed and the tax window has passed.
  // audit_logs: NEVER deleted by the application. Archived off-box, then
  // pruned by a separate operator-run process that also re-anchors the chain.
];
```
Add a CI test that asserts every entry in the retention list corresponds to a
table present in the schema (TEST-403), because this is a class of bug that
recurs.

DEF-039  [S5]  ".npmrc audit=true" does not do what the comment says
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 8; ADDENDUM M Scenario 5.
CLASS     Mislabeled control.
WHAT IS WRONG
The comment says `# Verify package signatures` above `audit=true`. `audit=true`
enables the vulnerability audit during install; it does not verify registry
signatures. Signature verification is `npm audit signatures`, a separate
command that must be run explicitly and that fails if any package in the tree
lacks a valid registry signature.
FIX       Keep `audit=true`, correct the comment, and add
          `npm audit signatures` as a required CI step that fails the build.
          Also note that `ignore-scripts` interacts with native modules — see
          DEF-032.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-052  [S2]  Mutable image tags
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 3 docker-compose (`postgres:16-alpine`,
          `redis:7-alpine`).
CLASS     Supply-chain gap.
WHAT IS WRONG
`postgres:16-alpine` resolves to whatever the registry serves today. A rebuild
six months from now pulls different bits with no record of the change. If an
upstream image is ever compromised, or simply ships a breaking change, the
deployment changes underneath you with no diff and no approval.
FIX
```yaml
image: postgres:16-alpine@sha256:<digest>
```
Digest-pin every image including the base images in every Dockerfile. Add a
scheduled job that checks for newer digests and opens a PR — updates become
reviewed events rather than silent drift. Scan pinned images with Trivy (free)
in CI and fail on HIGH/CRITICAL with a documented, expiring exception file.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-053  [S2]  No secret scanning anywhere
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Absent from both documents.
CLASS     Missing control against the most common real-world key leak.
WHAT IS WRONG
The corpus worries extensively about npm supply chain, kernel exploits, and BGP
hijacking, and never mentions the mechanism that actually leaks production
credentials most often: someone commits a `.env`, a private key, or an API token
to git. Once pushed to a remote — even to a private repo, even force-pushed away
— treat it as public.
FIX
```yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks: [{ id: gitleaks }]
```
Plus a CI job running `gitleaks detect --no-git --redact` on the working tree
and `gitleaks detect --log-opts="--all"` on history, both failing the build.
Plus a custom rule matching this project's own shapes: base58 strings of length
87-88 (Solana secret keys), `helius` URLs containing `api-key=`, Telegram bot
tokens (`\d{8,10}:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{35}`), and the signer request-key format.
Plus: `.gitignore` must contain `.env*`, `secrets/`, `*.pem`, `*.key`,
`aide.db*`, and a `.gitattributes` marking them as binary so a diff never
renders them. TEST-801.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-051  [S2]  Backups are encrypted with a key the server holds, never leave
               the server, and are never restored
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 7.3; ADDENDUM M Scenario 12.
CLASS     Three independent failures in one control.
WHAT IS WRONG
  - `gpg --symmetric --cipher-algo AES256 backup.sql` with a passphrase the
    backup script must possess means the host can decrypt its own backups. An
    attacker with the host has the backups too. The stated mitigation
    ("password stored separately from backup") is not achievable for an
    unattended nightly job.
  - "Backup to offline location / air-gapped machine" describes an intention,
    not a mechanism. Nothing in the corpus moves a byte off the host.
  - Nothing tests restoration. An untested backup is a hypothesis.
  - Ransomware (Scenario 12) deletes backups reachable with the host's
    credentials, which is all of them.
FIX — CTL-405
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
# age encrypts to a PUBLIC key. The server can create backups and is
# mathematically unable to read them. The private key never touches this host.
RECIPIENT="age1qz..."          # public key, safe to commit
STAMP="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
OUT="/var/backups/osiris-${STAMP}.sql.age"

pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner --no-privileges "$DATABASE_URL" \
  | age -r "$RECIPIENT" > "$OUT"

sha256sum "$OUT" > "${OUT}.sha256"

# Upload with a credential scoped to write-only on a bucket with Object Lock /
# immutability enabled. Even full host compromise cannot delete or alter
# previous backups.
rclone copy "$OUT" "immutable:osiris-backups/" --immutable
rclone copy "${OUT}.sha256" "immutable:osiris-backups/"

rm -f "$OUT" "${OUT}.sha256"   # do not keep plaintext-adjacent artifacts local
```
```
KEY CUSTODY for the age identity (this is the whole control):
  - generated offline on a machine that has never been on the internet, or on
    the operator's hardware-encrypted machine
  - stored in a password manager guarded by a hardware key
  - printed on paper (an age identity is one short line) and stored physically
  - NEVER present on the Oracle host, in CI, or in any environment variable

RESTORE DRILL (CTL-406) — monthly, automated, and it must actually fail loudly:
  1. Pull the newest object from the immutable bucket.
  2. Verify sha256.
  3. Decrypt with the identity on the operator machine (this step is manual by
     design; it is the one moment the private key is used).
  4. Restore into a scratch Postgres container.
  5. Assert: expected table set present, row counts within tolerance of
     production, the audit chain verifies from GENESIS, and a canonical query
     returns a known-good result.
  6. Record the drill result in the audit log. A month with no recorded drill
     is a paging alert.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-054  [S3]  MFA secret stored as a Better Auth `additionalField`
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L Layer 2 (`mfaSecret: { type: "string" }` on the users
          model, alongside `twoFactor: { enabled: true }`).
CLASS     Two competing mechanisms; secret at risk of serialization.
WHAT IS WRONG
Better Auth's two-factor plugin manages its own storage. Declaring a parallel
`mfaSecret` field on the user model creates a second, unmanaged copy. Worse,
fields declared as `additionalFields` on the user model are part of the user
object the library serializes into session responses — so the TOTP seed can be
returned to the client, at which point the second factor is not a factor.
FIX
  - Use the two-factor plugin's own storage. Do not declare `mfaSecret`.
  - If any secret must live on the user row, it must be encrypted with the
    envelope service under its own `CryptoContext` (DEF-027) and explicitly
    excluded from every serializer, with a test asserting it never appears in
    an API response body (TEST-106).
  - Prefer passkeys (CTL-502) over TOTP as the primary second factor; TOTP is
    the fallback for users without a passkey-capable device.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-056  [S3]  The Telegram IP allowlist cannot work as written
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 8.1 item 2.
CLASS     Control that rejects all legitimate traffic (or none).
WHAT IS WRONG
Comparing Telegram's published ranges (149.154.160.0/20, 91.108.4.0/22) against
the connecting IP fails behind Cloudflare, where the connecting IP is always
Cloudflare (DEF-025). If the developer instead compares against
`CF-Connecting-IP`, the check works — but only if that header is trusted, which
requires the DEF-025 plumbing. Neither document establishes it. Additionally,
Telegram's ranges are not contractually stable, so a change silently breaks the
bot with a 403 that looks like a Telegram outage.
FIX
Make the secret token the control (DEF-001) and the IP check a low-severity
signal:
```typescript
const TELEGRAM_RANGES = ["149.154.160.0/20", "91.108.4.0/22"];
export function handleTelegramWebhook(req: Request) {
  if (!verifyTelegramWebhook(req.headers.get("x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token")))
    return new Response(null, { status: 401 });        // THE control
  const ip = clientIp(req.headers);                     // DEF-025
  if (!inAnyCidr(ip, TELEGRAM_RANGES)) {
    // Do not reject: a valid secret from an unexpected IP more likely means
    // Telegram changed ranges than that someone guessed a 256-bit secret.
    securityLog("TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_UNEXPECTED_SOURCE", { severity: "low", ip });
  }
  // ...
}
```
Better still — and this removes the whole class of problem — put the webhook
behind a Cloudflare WAF rule that only allows Telegram's ranges to reach
`/api/telegram/webhook`. Then the enforcement happens where the true source IP
is known, and the origin never sees the traffic at all.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-057  [S1]  Withdrawals are never specified
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Absent from both documents.
CLASS     The actual money-out path has no design and therefore no controls.
WHAT IS WRONG
Both documents extensively secure the trading path — quotes, slippage, MEV,
token safety — and never describe how a user gets funds *out*. But withdrawal is
the only operation an attacker actually wants: forcing bad swaps destroys value,
transferring funds captures it. A system that can transfer to an arbitrary
address has a drain path regardless of how good its swap security is.
FIX — CTL-605, withdrawal as a distinct, hard-gated operation
```
1. SEPARATE SIGNER MODE. The signer's default policy (CTL-102 P4) forbids all
   top-level token and SOL transfers. Withdrawals use a distinct request type
   that the signer evaluates under a stricter policy, and that policy requires
   the destination to be on a per-user allowlist held in the SIGNER's storage —
   not in Postgres, not writable by the application host.

2. ALLOWLIST ENROLLMENT.
   - Add destination -> requires passkey re-authentication.
   - Enters a 24-hour pending state. Notification to every channel on file.
   - Any session can CANCEL a pending addition; only the enrolling session can
     confirm it. Cancellation is easier than confirmation, deliberately.
   - Becomes usable 24h after confirmation.
   - Rationale: an attacker with full session control still needs 24 hours
     during which the real user is being told, repeatedly, that a new
     destination is being added.

3. CAPS. Per-transaction and rolling-24h caps per user, enforced in the signer.
   Raising a cap is itself a Trust Tier 3 action with the same 24h delay.

4. FIRST-WITHDRAWAL FRICTION. The first withdrawal to any destination is capped
   at a small notional regardless of the user's limit. A test transaction is a
   normal expectation in this space and it converts a total loss into a small
   one.

5. NO WITHDRAWAL VIA TELEGRAM. Ever. Trust Tier 3 (ARGUMENT 9).

6. ADDRESS ANTI-POISONING (war game 6.5, correctly identified there): show the
   full destination address, never truncated, alongside a deterministic
   identicon; on paste, diff against every address the user has ever used and
   warn on high-similarity-but-not-equal; require the user to retype the last
   six characters for a new destination.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-041  [S3]  The referral system has no abuse controls
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Schema has `referralCode`/`referredBy` and a referral economics
          section; no controls anywhere.
CLASS     Missing control on a value-bearing subsystem.
WHAT IS WRONG
Self-referral (create account B with account A's code), sybil farms, and
circular referral chains all extract real value. The schema even permits
`referredBy` to point at a user who is themselves referred by the target,
creating a cycle. Fraud in a referral program is a certainty, not a risk.
FIX
```sql
-- Structural: no self-reference, ever.
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_no_self_referral CHECK (referred_by <> id);
```
```
Plus, in application logic:
  - referred_by is immutable after first set (enforced by trigger, not by code)
  - cycle detection with a recursive CTE at set time; reject cycles
  - referral rewards accrue but do not vest until the referred account has
    (a) completed a verified payment, and (b) traded on N distinct days
  - one referral credit per (payment instrument, device, ASN) cluster per window
  - rewards paid from a capped pool with a per-referrer ceiling
  - reversal path: a clawback procedure that exists before launch, not after
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-048  [S2]  Token metadata images are fetched from attacker-controlled URLs
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Implied by the token metadata features; never addressed.
CLASS     SSRF (server side) and tracking/deanonymization (client side).
WHAT IS WRONG
Token metadata contains a URI chosen by whoever created the token, which is
often the attacker. Two failure modes:
  - If the SERVER fetches it to cache or resize: that is a user-triggered fetch
    of an arbitrary URL, i.e. SSRF. `http://169.254.169.254/` returns Oracle
    instance metadata. The corpus's own SSRF section (3.4) says "never accept
    URLs from users" and then the product accepts URLs from tokens, which is the
    same thing with extra steps.
  - If the BROWSER fetches it directly: every user who views a token page makes
    a request to the token creator's server, disclosing IP, user agent, and
    timing. A malicious token becomes a beacon that enumerates the user base.
FIX
```
1. CSP img-src 'self' data: only. The browser never fetches a third-party
   image. (Already in the canonical CSP, DEF-018.)
2. Server-side image proxy, hardened:
   - allowlist schemes: https and ipfs only (ipfs via your own gateway)
   - resolve DNS FIRST, then check the resolved IP against a blocklist of
     private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, and metadata ranges — and re-check
     after every redirect, because DNS rebinding defeats a pre-resolution check
   - maximum 2 redirects, all re-validated
   - hard limits: 5s total timeout, 2 MB response cap, Content-Type must be an
     image type, verify magic bytes rather than trusting the header
   - re-encode through sharp to a fixed size and format; never serve the
     original bytes (this also strips EXIF and any polyglot payload)
   - cache by content hash; serve from your own origin
   - the proxy runs with no credentials and no access to the internal network
3. Default to NOT displaying token images at all in Phase 0. An identicon
   derived from the mint address is more useful for spoofing resistance than the
   attacker-supplied logo, which is usually a copy of a legitimate project's
   logo anyway.
```

################################################################################
GROUP E — FALSE PREMISES
Wrong beliefs that produce wrong decisions downstream.
################################################################################

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-044  [S5]  "Oracle Cloud free tier is dedicated / no noisy neighbors"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 13.3 item 1.
WHAT IS WRONG
The Always Free ARM shape is a virtual machine on shared Ampere hardware. Only
bare-metal shapes are dedicated, and they are not in the Always Free tier. The
side-channel section's primary defence therefore does not exist. Correct
mitigations for cross-tenant side channels are: keep the kernel patched, keep
key material off this host entirely (which CTL-100 does), and accept the
residual (RISK-005).

Related, and operationally more important: Oracle documents that Always Free
compute instances may be reclaimed when, over a 7-day window, the 95th
percentile of CPU utilization is below 20%, network utilization is below 20%,
and (on A1 shapes) memory utilization is below 20% — all three. A low-volume
trading bot plausibly meets that definition. There is also no SLA on Always Free
resources. For a system holding user funds this is a real availability risk that
neither document records. Mitigations: keep a documented, tested rebuild
procedure and current off-box backups (CTL-405/406) so reclamation is a
two-hour restore rather than an extinction event; monitor for the reclamation
warning; and consider that a paid instance is a $5-10/month answer to a
single-point-of-failure that the "$0" framing has been hiding.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-045  [S3]  "Multi-RPC confirmation: all must agree"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 11.2 item 1.
WHAT IS WRONG
Requiring three providers to agree adds latency to the critical path and adds
three failure modes for one benefit. It also misidentifies the authority: the
question "did this transaction land" is answered by the *ledger*, and any
correct RPC reporting `finalized` for a signature is reporting a fact about a
supermajority-rooted slot. Two honest providers agreeing does not add
information; one dishonest provider is caught by checking the *content*, not by
polling more endpoints.
FIX
```
1. Confirm with commitment "confirmed" for UX, and require "finalized" before
   any state change that is economically irreversible (crediting a deposit,
   marking a payment received, releasing a referral reward).
2. Verify the CONTENT, not just the status: fetch the transaction, assert it
   contains the expected instruction set, the expected accounts, and — for
   payment verification (PAY-01) — the exact recipient and lamport delta from
   pre/post balances. A lying RPC must forge a whole transaction, and a forged
   transaction fails these checks.
3. Keep a provider pool for AVAILABILITY (failover on error/timeout/rate limit),
   which is the real reason to have several, and record which provider answered
   on the trade row.
4. Cross-check with a second provider only for high-value operations and only on
   the finalized confirmation, not on every poll.
5. Never let a user supply an RPC URL (the corpus gets this right; keep it).
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-046  [S5]  The reorg threat model is written for proof of work
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 6.7 ("I control significant hash power"); also the
          "double spend" framing in 3.6.
WHAT IS WRONG
Solana has no hash power and no PoW reorgs. Forks resolve by stake-weighted
voting; a slot with supermajority root ("finalized") is not reversible without a
consensus failure of a completely different character. And a signed Solana
transaction cannot execute twice — the signature is the identity, and a
duplicate submission of the same signed transaction is a no-op. So "double
spend" in the PoW sense does not apply.
Why this matters: an agent implementing the war game's model builds a
confirmation-depth counter and a double-spend detector, both of which are
meaningless here, while the actual risk — building two *different* transactions
for one user intent — gets no control at all.
FIX
Restate correctly and control the real risk:
```
- Use "processed" for optimistic UI only, never for state.
- Use "confirmed" for normal trade completion.
- Use "finalized" for anything irreversible (deposit crediting, payouts).
- The real duplicate risk is two distinct transactions for one user intent.
  Control it with the intent-level idempotency key (DEF-030), the session lease
  (DEF-028), and the signer's requestId dedupe (CTL-102 P6).
- Blockhash expiry (~150 slots, roughly 60-90s) means a stale unsigned
  transaction becomes unsendable rather than dangerous. Treat expiry as the
  natural timeout for the pipeline and size job TTLs below it.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-047  [S2]  Token safety checks omit the most common honeypot mechanism
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  War game 6.1; SAF-05 in the research package.
WHAT IS WRONG
SAF-05 focuses on Token-2022 extensions: transfer fees, permanent delegate,
transfer hooks. Those matter. But the most common way a token traps buyers is
much simpler and lives on classic SPL Token: a live `freezeAuthority`. The
authority freezes the buyer's token account and the buyer can never sell.
Nothing in the corpus checks it.
FIX — the complete pre-trade token check
```
CLASSIC SPL AND TOKEN-2022, BOTH:
  [ ] freezeAuthority is None  (if Some: severe warning, block by default)
  [ ] mintAuthority is None    (if Some: supply can be inflated; warn)
  [ ] decimals are sane (0-9); unusual decimals are a display-spoofing vector

TOKEN-2022 EXTENSIONS (block or require explicit typed confirmation):
  [ ] transferFeeConfig      -> current AND scheduled future fee; a 0% fee that
                                becomes 100% later is the classic bait
  [ ] permanentDelegate      -> can seize tokens at any time. Block.
  [ ] transferHook           -> arbitrary program on every transfer. Block
                                unless the hook program is on an allowlist.
  [ ] defaultAccountState=Frozen -> new accounts are born frozen. Block.
  [ ] nonTransferable        -> cannot ever be sold. Block.
  [ ] mintCloseAuthority     -> mint can be closed. Warn.
  [ ] confidentialTransfer   -> balances opaque; PNL and safety checks break.
  [ ] pausable (where present) -> transfers can be halted globally. Block.

MARKET STRUCTURE:
  [ ] LP tokens burned or locked, and by whom
  [ ] top-holder concentration
  [ ] a route back to SOL exists on an allowlisted AMM RIGHT NOW — the single
      most predictive sellability signal, and cheap to check with a reverse
      quote for a dust amount
  [ ] pool age and liquidity depth versus intended trade size

PRESENTATION: the check result is shown before the trade, not after. Blocking
defaults are on. The override for a warn-level finding is a typed confirmation,
not a checkbox. Whatever the result, the trade is recorded with the check
snapshot so a later dispute has evidence.
```

DEF-040  [S1]  Telegram is used as an authenticator while SMS 2FA is banned

LOCATION  ADDENDUM M Scenario 3 ("NO SMS 2FA. Ever.") versus the entire Telegram
          authentication design.

FIX       The four-tier Telegram trust model in ARGUMENT 9, enforced in code by
          a single `requireTrustTier(n)` guard that every mutation declares.

DEF-058  [S3]  A public real-time security dashboard is a reconnaissance feed

DEF-059  [S5]  The bug bounty contradicts the stated scope
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Round 0 of the war game ("No bug bounty") versus ADDENDUM N Part 6 and
          the ADDENDUM L Phase 1 checklist ("Bug bounty program launched").
CLASS     Contradiction; also a cost the "$0" framing cannot absorb.
FIX       Phase 0 and Phase 1 ship a `security.txt` and a
          responsible-disclosure policy with a clear scope, a contact, a safe
          harbour statement, and an explicit "we currently offer recognition,
          not cash." That is free, honest, and gets you reports. A funded bounty
          is a Phase 3+ decision that requires a budget line and a triage
          capacity that does not exist yet. Promising a bounty you cannot pay is
          worse than not having one.

DEF-060  [S5]  "Insurance policy for user funds" and "third-party penetration
               test" on a $0 budget
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  ADDENDUM L "Before Phase 1" checklist.
CLASS     Unachievable checklist items that will be silently dropped.
FIX       Remove both from the Phase 1 gate. Crypto custody insurance is not
          available to an unregistered individual operator at any accessible
          price. A third-party pentest is $8k-30k. Replace with what is
          achievable and honest: (a) the automated verification suite in PART 5,
          (b) a structured self-directed review against this document's control
          list with written findings, (c) a public statement of exactly what has
          and has not been independently verified. Users can evaluate an honest
          "no third-party audit yet" far better than they can evaluate a
          checklist item that was quietly deleted.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEF-061  [S5]  "BUDGET: $0. ONGOING COST: $0. TIME: 2-3 days."
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LOCATION  Blue Team final assessment.
CLASS     False cost claim that will cause controls to be dropped. See
          ARGUMENT 14.
FIX       PART 9.

================================================================================
PART 3 — THE SEVEN EASIEST ENTRY POINTS: STRUCTURAL FIXES
================================================================================

The Red Team's final assessment:

    EASIEST ENTRY POINTS (Fix First):
    1. SSH on port 22 with password auth = owned in hours
    2. Docker running as root with writable filesystem = easy escape
    3. Missing auth check on ONE tRPC endpoint = total compromise
    4. Telegram webhook without signature check = arbitrary bot control
    5. Raw SQL query somewhere = database dump
    6. XSS in token name display = session theft
    7. No rate limiting = DoS for free

Each is addressed below with a STRUCTURAL fix. The distinction matters and it is
the organizing principle of this part:

    A PROCEDURAL fix says "always remember to do X."
    A STRUCTURAL fix makes the vulnerable state unreachable, or makes reaching
    it require a deliberate, reviewed, logged act.

The Blue Team's answers were mostly procedural. Procedural controls decay: the
person who wrote them leaves, the deadline compresses, an AI agent generates a
new endpoint from a pattern it saw elsewhere. Structural controls do not decay,
because violating them breaks the build.

Format for each entry point:
  ATTACK        what the Red Team does
  WHY THE
  EXISTING FIX
  IS NOT ENOUGH what the corpus proposed and where it falls short
  STRUCTURAL FIX the design change
  ARTIFACTS     exact configuration and code
  RESIDUAL      what is still possible afterwards, stated honestly
  TESTS         what fails the build

================================================================================
EP-1 — SSH ON PORT 22
================================================================================

ATTACK
"Oracle Cloud ARM VM has SSH on port 22. nmap the IP. Port 22 open. hydra with a
password list, or leaked keys from prior breaches. If password auth is enabled I
own the server in hours."

WHY THE EXISTING FIX IS NOT ENOUGH
The Blue Team proposed: disable password auth, move to port 2222, fail2ban,
ed25519 keys, `ufw limit`, and a custom bash monitor. Assessed individually:

  - `PasswordAuthentication no` is correct and necessary. Keep it.
  - Port 2222 is noise reduction, not security, and it conflicts with the
    ADDENDUM L UFW rule that allows only 22 — apply both documents and you are
    locked out (DEF-013).
  - fail2ban as configured does not start (DEF-012).
  - `ufw limit` on 443 breaks the site behind Cloudflare (DEF-009).
  - The bash monitor is a root-run shell-injection sink that duplicates fail2ban
    and amplifies load (DEF-014).
  - A key with no passphrase on a compromised laptop is game over, and the
    corpus's own "one thing that worries us" says exactly this.

But the deeper problem is the frame. Every item answers "how do I survive an
exposed SSH daemon." The daemon does not need to be exposed. As long as port 22
answers the internet, you are betting on OpenSSH having no pre-auth
vulnerability for the lifetime of the project, and on your key management being
perfect. Both are decent bets. Neither is necessary.

STRUCTURAL FIX
Remove SSH from the internet entirely. The host has no inbound listener for
administration. Access is an outbound-initiated tunnel gated by an identity
provider and a hardware authenticator. There is nothing to scan, nothing to
brute force, and no pre-auth attack surface.

  Layer 1  Oracle VCN Security List: no ingress rule for 22, from anywhere.
  Layer 2  UFW: no allow rule for 22.
  Layer 3  sshd listens on 127.0.0.1 only.
  Layer 4  cloudflared makes an outbound-only tunnel to Cloudflare.
  Layer 5  Cloudflare Access policy: a specific email, WebAuthn hardware key
           required, short session, every authentication logged.
  Layer 6  Break glass: Oracle serial console (out-of-band, Oracle-authenticated,
           independent of Cloudflare, the network stack, and sshd).

An attacker must now compromise the Cloudflare Zero Trust account AND possess
the physical hardware key. Note this is the *site* Cloudflare account; the
signer lives in a different account (ARGUMENT 2), so this compromise does not
reach key material either.

ARTIFACTS

```bash
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-osiris.conf
# sshd binds loopback only. Even if a firewall rule is wrong, there is no
# listener on a routable address.
ListenAddress 127.0.0.1
ListenAddress ::1

PasswordAuthentication no
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
PermitEmptyPasswords no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AuthenticationMethods publickey
MaxAuthTries 3
MaxSessions 4
MaxStartups 3:50:10
LoginGraceTime 20
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2
AllowUsers ubuntu
X11Forwarding no
AllowAgentForwarding no
AllowTcpForwarding no
PermitTunnel no
PermitUserEnvironment no
# Modern algorithms only.
HostKeyAlgorithms ssh-ed25519,ssh-ed25519-cert-v01@openssh.com
PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms ssh-ed25519,sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com,ssh-ed25519-cert-v01@openssh.com
KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org,sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com
Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com
MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com
```

```
  Session duration:   1 hour  (short; you can re-auth in seconds)
  Policy: ALLOW
    - Include:  Emails -> <the one admin email>
    - Require:  Authentication Method -> Hardware key (WebAuthn/FIDO2)
    - Require:  Country -> <your country>       [optional, adds friction for
                                                 an attacker abroad]
  Policy: BLOCK (evaluated first)
    - Everyone else. Explicit, so the intent is visible in the UI.
  Enable: "Browser rendering: SSH" only if you want browser access; if not,
          leave it off to reduce surface.
  Logs:   Zero Trust -> Logs -> Access. Every attempt, allowed or denied.
```

```
    HostName ssh.osiris.trade

    ProxyCommand cloudflared access ssh --hostname %h
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk_osiris
```

```bash
# The SSH key itself is hardware-bound. This is what makes laptop theft
# survivable (the Red Team's "one thing that worries us").
ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident -O verify-required \
           -C "osiris-admin" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk_osiris
# -O resident        : the key can be recovered from the token onto a new
#                      machine, so losing the laptop is not losing access
# -O verify-required : a PIN or biometric is required per use, so stealing the
#                      token alone is also insufficient
# Requires a FIDO2 security key. This is NOT free (~$25-50). It is the single
# highest-value purchase in this entire plan. See PART 9.
# Enroll TWO keys. One lives somewhere else, physically.
```

BREAK GLASS (must be tested before it is needed, not during)
```
Oracle Cloud Console -> Compute -> Instances -> <instance> -> Console connection
  -> Create local connection (upload an SSH public key)
  -> Connect with a serial console connection
This path does not use sshd, does not use the network stack, does not use
Cloudflare, and is authenticated by the Oracle tenancy (which must itself have
hardware-key MFA — see CTL-901). Test it during setup. A break-glass path that
has never been exercised is a story you tell yourself.
```

RESIDUAL
  - Compromise of the site Cloudflare account plus the hardware key gives shell.
    Mitigated by hardware-key-only account MFA and by the signer living in a
    separate account.
  - `cloudflared` itself is software running as a privileged service and could
    have a vulnerability. It is outbound-only, which is a materially smaller
    surface than an inbound daemon, and it is kept updated by unattended
    upgrades.
  - Oracle tenancy compromise gives serial console access. Mitigated by hardware
    MFA on the Oracle account.
  - Recorded as RISK-006.

TESTS
  TEST-201  External `nmap -Pn -p 22,2222,5432,6379,3000 <public-ip>` reports
            no open ports. Run from outside the VCN.
  TEST-205  `ss -tlnp` on the host shows sshd bound to loopback only.
  TEST-206  `cloudflared` has no listening socket.
  TEST-207  An Access-authenticated SSH session succeeds; a request to
            ssh.osiris.trade without Access authentication is refused by
            Cloudflare (asserted by response, not by manual observation).
  TEST-208  Break-glass serial console connection succeeds. Run quarterly.
            Recorded in the audit log.

================================================================================
EP-2 — DOCKER AS ROOT WITH A WRITABLE FILESYSTEM
================================================================================

ATTACK
"Docker defaults run as root. If I get RCE in the Next.js app I escape the
container. I check for --privileged, a mounted Docker socket, kernel
capabilities. If the socket is mounted I make a container with host PID
namespace and read /proc/1/root/etc/shadow. Game over."

WHY THE EXISTING FIX IS NOT ENOUGH
The Blue Team's list (non-root, cap_drop ALL, read_only, no-new-privileges, no
socket mount, seccomp, resource limits, internal networks) is a good list. Six
problems with it as delivered:

  1. It publishes Postgres and Redis ports, and Docker's published ports bypass
     UFW entirely (DEF-010). The strongest container hardening in the world does
     not help when the database is directly reachable from the internet.
  2. `user: "999:999"` is the wrong UID for the Alpine postgres image (DEF-005).
     The container will not start, and the first fix a frustrated developer
     reaches for is removing the `user:` key.
  3. `userns-remap` in daemon.json, enabled after volumes exist, breaks
     everything (DEF-011) — and again the fix people reach for is removing it.
  4. `seccomp:./seccomp-default.json` points at a file the corpus never
     provides. A missing seccomp profile prevents the container (or dockerd)
     from starting, and the fix people reach for is deleting the security_opt.
  5. `deploy.replicas: 4` cannot coexist with a published port and contradicts
     the PM2 cluster design (DEF-031).
  6. Every one of these is a *config* that a future change can silently drop.
     Nothing verifies at runtime that the container is actually unprivileged.

Notice the pattern: four of the six failures end with "and so the security
control gets removed." A control that breaks the app is a control with a
deletion timer on it.

STRUCTURAL FIX
Three parts:
  (a) A compose file whose every value has been verified against the actual
      image, with ports that are not publishable to the internet by
      construction.
  (b) A runtime self-check: the application refuses to start if it finds itself
      running as root, with a writable root filesystem, with the Docker socket
      present, or with capabilities it should not have. The check is in the
      application, so it cannot be lost when someone edits the compose file.
  (c) A CI test that asserts the compose file's security posture, so a
      regression fails the build before it reaches the host.

ARTIFACTS

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml — canonical. Replaces ADDENDUM L Layer 3 in full.
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine@sha256:PIN_ME              # DEF-052
    user: "70:70"                                        # DEF-005
    restart: unless-stopped
    # NO ports: block. Reached as postgres:5432 on the internal network only.
    read_only: true

      - /tmp:noexec,nosuid,nodev,size=64m
      - /var/run/postgresql:size=16m
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]

    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER_FILE: /run/secrets/db_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password

                                 # the remote signer. The ONLY key on this host,
```
