================================================================================
EP-BONUS — "THE ONE THING THAT WORRIES US"
================================================================================

The Red Team's closing worry, quoted in full:

    "If the developer's laptop is compromised, everything is compromised. SSH
    keys, .env files, browser cookies. Physical security of the developer is the
    weakest link. Full disk encryption + SSH passphrase + no local secrets is
    mandatory."

They are right, and the three mitigations they name are the weakest three
available. Full disk encryption protects a powered-off stolen laptop and does
nothing against malware on a running one. An SSH passphrase is typed on the
compromised keyboard. "No local secrets" is an intention with no enforcement.

The laptop is the highest-value target in this system because it holds the
authority to change everything else. Treat it accordingly.

STRUCTURAL FIX — CTL-901 through CTL-906

CTL-901  NO SECRET IS EVER TYPED OR STORED IN SOFTWARE THE ATTACKER CAN READ.
  Every credential that matters is bound to a hardware authenticator:
    - SSH:            ed25519-sk resident key, verify-required (EP-1)
    - Cloudflare:     WebAuthn hardware key, TOTP fallback DISABLED, no SMS
    - Oracle Cloud:   hardware MFA
    - Domain registrar: hardware MFA + registry lock
    - GitHub:         hardware key, and "require 2FA" on the org
    - Password manager: hardware key as second factor
  A keylogger captures nothing usable, because nothing usable is a string.
  Two keys enrolled everywhere. One lives off-site. Enrollment of a third key is
  itself an alert.

CTL-902  ADMIN AUTHORITY IS NOT ON THE DAILY-DRIVER MACHINE.
  Ideal: a separate machine that does nothing but administer this system — no
  email, no browsing, no npm install, no Discord. A $200 used laptop or a
  Raspberry Pi is sufficient and is the cheapest meaningful risk reduction in
  this entire document.
  Minimum acceptable: a separate OS user account on the same machine, with its
  own browser profile containing no extensions, used for nothing else, plus full
  disk encryption, plus the hardware keys above. This is weaker — same kernel,
  same running malware — but it defeats the common case of a browser-profile
  credential stealer.
  Never: administering production from the machine that runs `npm install` on
  untrusted repositories.

CTL-903  THE TREASURY IS NOT REACHABLE BY ANY CODE IN THIS SYSTEM.
  The operator's own holdings — the $1.8M in the threat model — live in a Squads
  multisig with hardware signers, on addresses the application has never seen
  and cannot construct. The application's hot wallets hold operational balances
  with a documented cap. There is no code path, no environment variable, and no
  database row that connects the two. Compromising OSIRIS entirely does not
  reach the treasury, because the treasury is not part of OSIRIS.
  This single decision does more for the stated threat model than every other
  control in this document combined, and it is free.

CTL-904  RECOVERY PATHS ARE THE REAL ATTACK SURFACE.
  Enumerate every account and write down its recovery path. Then remove the weak
  ones. Concretely:
    - Remove the phone number from every account that permits it. SMS recovery
      converts a SIM swap into total compromise and bypasses the hardware key
      entirely — which makes SMS recovery strictly worse than no MFA at all,
      because it creates the illusion of protection.
    - The email account used for these registrations is used for NOTHING else,
      is protected by a hardware key, has no SMS recovery, and its own recovery
      address is a second such account.
    - Print recovery codes. Store them physically. Delete the digital copies.
    - Domain registrar: registry lock, so a support-desk social engineer cannot
      transfer the domain.
  The attacker does not need to beat your hardware key if they can ask the
  provider to remove it.

CTL-905  DEVELOPMENT HYGIENE, ENFORCED RATHER THAN INTENDED.
    - gitleaks as a pre-commit hook AND a CI job (DEF-053).
    - `npm ci --ignore-scripts` with the reviewed allowlist (DEF-032).
    - Dependencies installed in a container or a devcontainer, not on the host,
      so a malicious postinstall lands in a sandbox.
    - No production credential is ever present on a developer machine. Local
      development uses devnet and a local signer explicitly gated on
      `NODE_ENV !== "production"` plus a runtime assertion that the RPC endpoint
      is devnet.
    - Separate browser profile for anything touching production consoles.

CTL-906  ASSUME IT HAPPENS ANYWAY, AND MAKE IT SURVIVABLE.
  The whole point of CTL-100 is that laptop compromise no longer means key
  compromise:
    - The laptop holds no wallet keys (they never leave the signer).
    - The laptop holds no KEK (it is a Cloudflare Worker secret).
    - The laptop's SSH access requires a physical key touch per use.
    - Cloudflare Access logs every administrative authentication with time, IP,
      and method; an authentication the operator did not perform is a
      high-signal alert.
    - The global HALT switch is reachable from a phone, independent of the
      laptop, and stops all signing in under a second.
  So the honest revised statement of the Red Team's worry is: "If the
  developer's laptop is compromised, the attacker gets a shell on the trading
  host, can grief users within the signer's policy and rate limits, and is
  visible in the Access log — and the keys are still safe." That is a
  fundamentally different sentence from the one they wrote, and getting there is
  the point of this document.

================================================================================
PART 4 — THE CANONICAL STACK
================================================================================

Ten layers. Every control has an ID, the invariant it serves, the artifact, the
failure mode if it is absent, and its test. Where PART 2 or PART 3 already gave
the artifact in full, this part references rather than repeats it, so that there
is exactly one copy of every configuration in this document.

Layer index:
  L1  Key custody and signing        CTL-100 .. CTL-109   (the core change)
  L2  Host and container             CTL-200 .. CTL-209
  L3  Network and edge               CTL-300 .. CTL-309
  L4  Data                           CTL-400 .. CTL-409
  L5  Identity, session, application CTL-500 .. CTL-509
  L6  Blockchain-specific            CTL-600 .. CTL-609
  L7  Detection and response         CTL-700 .. CTL-709
  L8  Supply chain and build         CTL-800 .. CTL-809
  L9  Operator security              CTL-900 .. CTL-906   (in PART 3, EP-BONUS)

################################################################################
LAYER 1 — KEY CUSTODY AND SIGNING
The load-bearing layer. Everything else is defence in depth around this.
################################################################################

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-100  THE REMOTE SIGNER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SERVES    INV-1. Rulings from ARGUMENT 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
REPLACES  ADDENDUM L Layer 1 as deployed on the application host.

ARCHITECTURE

```
                 OSIRIS APPLICATION HOST (Oracle Cloud)
                 ─────────────────────────────────────
                 Holds: encrypted wallet blobs (in Postgres)
                        signer request-signing private key (Docker secret)
                 Never holds: KEK, DEK, any wallet private key

                          │  1. build unsigned VersionedTransaction
                          │  2. load blob {ciphertext, iv, tag, wrappedDek}
                          │  3. build SigningRequest
                          │  4. sign the request with the request key (Ed25519)
                          ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
                 │  HTTPS POST  signer.osiris-sign.workers.dev
                 └────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          ▼
                 OSIRIS SIGNER (Cloudflare Worker, SEPARATE ACCOUNT)
                 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
                 Holds: KEK (Worker Secret)
                        app request-signing PUBLIC key
                        rate-limit counters, revocation flags, HALT flag,
                        session policies, withdrawal allowlists   (KV / DO)
                 Never holds: wallet blobs, user data, the database

                 Per request, in order:
                   P0  HALT flag        -> if set, refuse everything
                   P1  request signature verify (Ed25519)
                   P2  timestamp freshness (±30s) + requestId replay check
                   P3  revocation: session, user epoch
                   P4  rate limits: wallet / user / global
                   P5  unwrap DEK with KEK, decrypt secret key (AAD-bound)
                   P6  derive public key; assert == declared wallet == fee payer
                   P7  POLICY ENGINE: parse the transaction message and refuse
                       anything outside the permitted shape
                   P8  sign; zero; append to signing log
                   P9  return { signature } and nothing else
                          │
                          ▼
                 base58 signature string  ->  app sends it to Solana
```

WHY THIS SHAPE
  - The app host cannot steal a key because it never receives one.
  - The signer cannot steal a key on its own because it has no ciphertext.
  - Neither can act alone; the attacker needs both, plus the request key.
  - The policy engine means that even both-compromised does not yield an
    arbitrary transfer (ARGUMENT 5), only a bounded, rate-limited, alarmed
    degradation.
  - HALT is one KV write from a phone and stops everything globally in under a
    second, with no dependency on the compromised host.

MANDATORY DEPLOYMENT CONSTRAINTS (all three, or the design is not what it claims)
  1. The signer Worker lives in a DIFFERENT Cloudflare account from the one
     hosting DNS, the WAF, and the tunnel. Different email, different hardware
     key, no shared API tokens.
  2. That account's API tokens are scoped to the single Worker and are stored
     only in the operator's password manager, never in CI. Deployment is manual
     or gated behind a separate hardware-key approval.
  3. `wrangler secret put KEK` is the only way the KEK enters the Worker. It is
     never in a file, never in `wrangler.toml`, never in git, never in an env
     var on the app host.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-101  SIGNING REQUEST PROTOCOL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

```typescript
// shared/signer-protocol.ts — imported by BOTH the app and the Worker.
// A single source of truth for the wire format prevents the classic bug where
// the signer verifies a different canonical form than the app signed.

export interface SigningRequest {
  v: 1;
  requestId: string;         // UUID v7 — time-ordered, used for replay defence
  ts: number;                // ms since epoch, at request construction
  mode: "trade" | "withdraw";
  userId: string;
  sessionId: string;
  walletId: string;          // base58 public key; must equal derived pubkey
  txBase64: string;          // serialized unsigned VersionedTransaction
  blob: {
    ciphertext: string; iv: string; tag: string;
    encryptedDek: string; kekVersion: string;
  };
  // Declared expectations. The signer verifies these against the parsed
  // transaction rather than trusting them; they exist so that a mismatch is a
  // detectable lie rather than a silent difference.
  expect: {
    programIds: string[];    // every top-level program the app believes is used
    outputMint?: string;     // for trade mode
    destination?: string;    // for withdraw mode
    maxLamportsOut: number;  // top-level SOL leaving the wallet (tip + rent)
  };
}

/**
 * Canonical serialization. Deterministic key order, no whitespace, no
 * floating-point ambiguity. Both sides MUST use this exact function.
 */
export function canonicalize(r: SigningRequest): Uint8Array {
  const ordered = JSON.stringify(r, Object.keys(r).sort());
  return new TextEncoder().encode(ordered);
}

export interface SignedEnvelope {
  request: SigningRequest;
  sig: string;               // base64 Ed25519 over canonicalize(request)
}
```

App side:
```typescript
// src/server/signer/client.ts
import { sign } from "@noble/ed25519";

const REQUEST_KEY = readFileSync("/run/secrets/signer_request_key");  // 32 bytes

export async function requestSignature(req: SigningRequest): Promise<string> {
  const sig = await sign(canonicalize(req), REQUEST_KEY);
  const res = await fetch(process.env.SIGNER_URL!, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ request: req, sig: Buffer.from(sig).toString("base64") }),
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000),
  });
  if (res.status === 423) throw new SignerHaltedError();       // HALT is set
  if (res.status === 403) throw new PolicyRejectedError(await res.text());
  if (res.status === 429) throw new SignerRateLimitedError();
  if (!res.ok) throw new SignerUnavailableError(res.status);
  const { signature } = await res.json();
  return TxSignatureSchema.parse(signature);                   // base58, DEF-050
}
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-102  THE POLICY ENGINE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SERVES    INV-1, INV-2. Ruling from ARGUMENT 3 and ARGUMENT 5.

This is the control that distinguishes this architecture from "KMS plus hope."
It reads the transaction and refuses anything outside a narrow permitted shape.

CRITICAL IMPLEMENTATION FACT — AND HOW TO VERIFY IT
The v0 message sanitization in the Solana runtime requires an instruction's
`program_id_index` to fall within the transaction's STATIC account keys; program
IDs are not resolved from address lookup tables. This is what makes P2 complete
without resolving ALTs and without any RPC call from the Worker, which is what
keeps the Worker inside the free tier's CPU budget.

DO NOT TAKE THIS ON FAITH. Verify it against the runtime version in use before
shipping, two ways:
  (a) Read `Message::sanitize()` for the v0 message in the solana-sdk version
      you depend on and confirm the bounds check against the static key count.
  (b) Empirically: on devnet, construct a v0 transaction whose instruction
      program_id_index points into the ALT-loaded region and submit it. It must
      be rejected by the cluster. Record the result in the repo.

The design is safe either way, because it fails closed: `resolveKey()` returns
null for any index outside the static keys, and P2 returns
`program_id_outside_static_keys`. If the constraint ever ceases to hold, the
engine refuses those transactions rather than mis-evaluating them. That is the
correct behaviour for an assumption you cannot continuously re-verify.

```typescript
// worker/policy.ts

const ALLOWED_PROGRAMS = new Set([
  "11111111111111111111111111111111",              // System
  "ComputeBudget111111111111111111111111111111",   // ComputeBudget
  "TokenkegQfeZyiNwAJbNbGKPFXCWuBvf9Ss623VQ5DA",   // SPL Token
  "TokenzQdBNbLqP5VEhdkAS6EPFLC1PHnBqCXEpPxuEb",   // Token-2022
  "ATokenGPvbdGVxr1b2hvZbsiqW5xWH25efTNsLJA8knL",  // Associated Token
  "JUP6LkbZbjS1jKKwapdHNy74zcZ3tLUZoi5QNyVTaV4",   // Jupiter v6 aggregator
  "MemoSq4gqABAXKb96qnH8TysNcWxMyWCqXgDLGmfcHr",   // Memo
  // DEX programs, scoped per the research package's decision to ship 3:
  "675kPX9MHTjS2zt1qfr1NYHuzeLXfQM9H24wFSUt1Mp8",  // Raydium AMM v4
  "pAMMBay6oceH9fJKBRHGP5D4bD4sWpmSwMn52FMfXEA",   // PumpSwap
]);

// SystemProgram instruction discriminators (first 4 bytes, little-endian u32)
const SYS_TRANSFER = 2;
const SYS_CREATE_ACCOUNT = 0;
const SYS_ASSIGN = 1;
const SYS_CREATE_WITH_SEED = 3;
const SYS_ADVANCE_NONCE = 4;

// SPL Token instruction discriminators (first byte)
const TOK_TRANSFER = 3, TOK_APPROVE = 4, TOK_REVOKE = 5, TOK_SET_AUTHORITY = 6,
      TOK_MINT_TO = 7, TOK_BURN = 8, TOK_CLOSE_ACCOUNT = 9, TOK_FREEZE = 10,
      TOK_THAW = 11, TOK_TRANSFER_CHECKED = 12, TOK_APPROVE_CHECKED = 13,
      TOK_SYNC_NATIVE = 17;

const TIP_ACCOUNTS = new Set([
  // Helius Sender / Jito tip accounts. Verify against the provider's current
  // published list at implementation time and pin them here.
  "4ACfpUFoaSD9bfPdeu6DBt89gB6ENTeHBXCAi87NhDEE",
  "D2L6yPZ2FmmmTKPgzaMKdhu6EWZcTpLy1Vhx8uvZe7NZ",
  // ... remaining published accounts
]);

const MAX_TIP_LAMPORTS  = 2_000_000;   // 0.002 SOL. Sender Max minimum is
                                       // 0.001 SOL; this leaves headroom and
                                       // still caps the drain-by-tip vector.
const MAX_RENT_LAMPORTS = 10_000_000;  // ~0.01 SOL, covers several ATAs

export interface PolicyResult { ok: boolean; reason?: string; }

export function evaluate(
  msg: ParsedMessage,             // from the minimal parser, CTL-103
  req: SigningRequest,
  signerPubkey: string,
  sessionPolicy: SessionPolicy    // pushed to the Worker by the USER, not the app
): PolicyResult {

  // P1 — exactly one signer, and it is us, and it is the fee payer.
  if (msg.numRequiredSignatures !== 1) return no("multiple_signers");
  if (msg.staticKeys[0] !== signerPubkey) return no("fee_payer_mismatch");
  if (req.walletId !== signerPubkey)      return no("wallet_id_mismatch");

  // P2 — every invoked program is allowlisted. Program IDs are always in the
  // static keys, so this is complete without ALT resolution.
  for (const ix of msg.instructions) {
    const pid = msg.staticKeys[ix.programIdIndex];
    if (pid === undefined) return no("program_id_outside_static_keys");
    if (!ALLOWED_PROGRAMS.has(pid)) return no(`program_not_allowed:${pid}`);
  }

  // P3/P4/P5 — per-instruction rules.
  let lamportsOut = 0;
  for (const ix of msg.instructions) {
    const pid = msg.staticKeys[ix.programIdIndex];

    if (pid === "11111111111111111111111111111111") {
      const disc = readU32LE(ix.data, 0);
      if (disc === SYS_TRANSFER) {
        const dstIdx = ix.accounts[1];
        const dst = msg.resolveKey(dstIdx);              // may be from an ALT
        const lamports = Number(readU64LE(ix.data, 4));
        if (dst === null) return no("transfer_destination_from_alt");
        if (TIP_ACCOUNTS.has(dst)) {
          if (lamports > MAX_TIP_LAMPORTS) return no("tip_exceeds_cap");
        } else if (dst === signerPubkey) {
          // moving lamports to self is a no-op; allow
        } else {
          return no(`sol_transfer_to_unapproved:${dst}`);
        }
        lamportsOut += lamports;
      } else if (disc === SYS_CREATE_ACCOUNT) {
        lamportsOut += Number(readU64LE(ix.data, 4));
        if (lamportsOut > MAX_RENT_LAMPORTS + MAX_TIP_LAMPORTS)
          return no("lamports_out_exceeds_cap");
      } else if (disc === SYS_ASSIGN || disc === SYS_CREATE_WITH_SEED ||
                 disc === SYS_ADVANCE_NONCE) {
        return no(`system_ix_not_allowed:${disc}`);
      }
      continue;
    }

    if (pid === "TokenkegQfeZyiNwAJbNbGKPFXCWuBvf9Ss623VQ5DA" ||
        pid === "TokenzQdBNbLqP5VEhdkAS6EPFLC1PHnBqCXEpPxuEb") {
      const disc = ix.data[0];
      // A legitimate Jupiter swap performs its token movements by CPI from
      // inside the aggregator. A TOP-LEVEL token transfer is the drain shape.
      switch (disc) {
        case TOK_SYNC_NATIVE:
          break;                                   // wSOL wrapping: fine
        case TOK_CLOSE_ACCOUNT: {
          const dst = msg.resolveKey(ix.accounts[1]);
          const owner = msg.resolveKey(ix.accounts[2]);
          if (dst !== signerPubkey || owner !== signerPubkey)
            return no("close_account_to_third_party");
          break;                                   // unwrapping wSOL: fine
        }
        case TOK_TRANSFER:
        case TOK_TRANSFER_CHECKED:
        case TOK_APPROVE:
        case TOK_APPROVE_CHECKED:
        case TOK_SET_AUTHORITY:
        case TOK_BURN:
        case TOK_MINT_TO:
        case TOK_FREEZE:
        case TOK_THAW:
        case TOK_REVOKE:
          if (req.mode !== "withdraw") return no(`top_level_token_ix:${disc}`);
          // withdraw mode is evaluated separately, below
          break;
        default:
          break;                                   // ATA create, initialize etc.
      }
      continue;
    }
  }

  // P6 — trade mode: the output mint must be permitted by the session policy
  // that the USER established, not by whatever the app host claims now.
  if (req.mode === "trade") {
    if (req.expect.outputMint && sessionPolicy.deniedMints.has(req.expect.outputMint))
      return no("output_mint_denied");
    if (sessionPolicy.allowedMints && req.expect.outputMint &&
        !sessionPolicy.allowedMints.has(req.expect.outputMint))
      return no("output_mint_not_allowed");
  }

  // P7 — withdraw mode: destination must be on the signer-held allowlist, past
  // its 24h maturity, and within caps. See CTL-605.
  if (req.mode === "withdraw") {
    const dst = req.expect.destination;
    if (!dst) return no("withdraw_without_destination");
    const entry = sessionPolicy.withdrawalAllowlist.get(dst);
    if (!entry) return no("withdraw_destination_not_allowlisted");
    if (entry.maturesAt > Date.now()) return no("withdraw_destination_immature");
    if (req.expect.maxLamportsOut > entry.perTxCapLamports) return no("withdraw_over_cap");
  }

  // P8 — the app's declared expectations must match what we actually parsed.
  // A mismatch means the app is lying or buggy; either way, refuse and alert.
  const actualPrograms = new Set(msg.instructions.map((i) => msg.staticKeys[i.programIdIndex]));
  for (const p of req.expect.programIds)
    if (!actualPrograms.has(p)) return no("declared_program_absent");
  for (const p of actualPrograms)
    if (!req.expect.programIds.includes(p!)) return no("undeclared_program_present");
  if (lamportsOut > req.expect.maxLamportsOut) return no("lamports_exceed_declared");

  return { ok: true };
}

const no = (reason: string): PolicyResult => ({ ok: false, reason });
```

P8 deserves a note. Requiring the application to *declare* what it believes the
transaction does, and then checking the declaration against the parse, turns
every discrepancy into a signal. A compromised app host that crafts a hostile
transaction must also craft a matching honest-looking declaration — and the
declaration is checked against the bytes, so it cannot. Every
`declared_program_absent` or `undeclared_program_present` rejection is
near-certain evidence of compromise, which makes it one of the highest-signal
detectors in the system (CTL-709).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-103  MINIMAL TRANSACTION PARSER (Worker-side)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WHY      Cloudflare Workers on the free plan have a 10ms CPU budget per request.
         Importing @solana/web3.js to deserialize a message would be both large
         and slow. A purpose-written parser is roughly 150 lines and runs in
         microseconds. It also has no dependencies, which matters for a
         component whose entire job is to be trustworthy.

```typescript
// worker/parse-message.ts
// Parses a serialized v0 (and legacy) Solana transaction MESSAGE. Deliberately
// strict: anything it does not fully understand is a parse error, which the
// caller treats as a policy rejection. Fail closed on ambiguity.

export interface ParsedInstruction {
  programIdIndex: number;
  accounts: number[];
  data: Uint8Array;
}

export interface ParsedMessage {
  version: "legacy" | 0;
  numRequiredSignatures: number;
  numReadonlySigned: number;
  numReadonlyUnsigned: number;
  staticKeys: string[];               // base58
  recentBlockhash: string;
  instructions: ParsedInstruction[];
  altWritable: number[][];            // per-table writable index lists
  altReadonly: number[][];
  /** Resolves an account index to a base58 key, or null if it comes from an
   *  address lookup table (whose contents we deliberately do not fetch). A null
   *  return is a signal to the policy engine to refuse, not to guess. */
  resolveKey(i: number): string | null;
}

function readCompactU16(buf: Uint8Array, off: number): [number, number] {
  let value = 0, shift = 0, o = off;
  for (;;) {
    const b = buf[o++];
    if (b === undefined) throw new Error("truncated compact-u16");
    value |= (b & 0x7f) << shift;
    if ((b & 0x80) === 0) break;
    shift += 7;
    if (shift > 21) throw new Error("compact-u16 too long");
  }
  return [value, o];
}

export function parseMessage(raw: Uint8Array): ParsedMessage {
  if (raw.length > 1232) throw new Error("message exceeds max transaction size");
  let o = 0;
  const first = raw[o];
  const isV0 = (first & 0x80) !== 0;
  if (isV0 && (first & 0x7f) !== 0) throw new Error("unsupported message version");
  if (isV0) o += 1;

  const numRequiredSignatures = raw[o++];
  const numReadonlySigned     = raw[o++];
  const numReadonlyUnsigned   = raw[o++];

  let n: number;
  [n, o] = readCompactU16(raw, o);
  if (n > 64) throw new Error("too many static keys");
  const staticKeys: string[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    staticKeys.push(bs58encode(raw.subarray(o, o + 32)));
    o += 32;
  }

  const recentBlockhash = bs58encode(raw.subarray(o, o + 32));
  o += 32;

  let ixCount: number;
  [ixCount, o] = readCompactU16(raw, o);
  if (ixCount > 32) throw new Error("too many instructions");
  const instructions: ParsedInstruction[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < ixCount; i++) {
    const programIdIndex = raw[o++];
    let aCount: number; [aCount, o] = readCompactU16(raw, o);
    if (aCount > 64) throw new Error("too many accounts in instruction");
    const accounts: number[] = [];
    for (let j = 0; j < aCount; j++) accounts.push(raw[o++]);
    let dLen: number; [dLen, o] = readCompactU16(raw, o);
    if (dLen > 1232) throw new Error("instruction data too long");
    const data = raw.subarray(o, o + dLen);
    o += dLen;
    instructions.push({ programIdIndex, accounts, data });
  }

  const altWritable: number[][] = [];
  const altReadonly: number[][] = [];
  if (isV0) {
    let tCount: number; [tCount, o] = readCompactU16(raw, o);
    if (tCount > 8) throw new Error("too many lookup tables");
    for (let t = 0; t < tCount; t++) {
      o += 32;                                    // table account key
      let wc: number; [wc, o] = readCompactU16(raw, o);
      const w: number[] = []; for (let i = 0; i < wc; i++) w.push(raw[o++]);
      let rc: number; [rc, o] = readCompactU16(raw, o);
      const r: number[] = []; for (let i = 0; i < rc; i++) r.push(raw[o++]);
      altWritable.push(w); altReadonly.push(r);
    }
  }
  if (o !== raw.length) throw new Error("trailing bytes after message");

  const resolveKey = (i: number): string | null =>
    i < staticKeys.length ? staticKeys[i] : null;

  return { version: isV0 ? 0 : "legacy", numRequiredSignatures,
           numReadonlySigned, numReadonlyUnsigned, staticKeys,
           recentBlockhash, instructions, altWritable, altReadonly, resolveKey };
}
```
Note the deliberate strictness: unknown version, trailing bytes, oversized
counts, and truncation are all errors. A parser that guesses is a parser an
attacker can confuse into disagreeing with the runtime — and a policy engine
that disagrees with the runtime about what a transaction does is worthless.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-104  THE WORKER (assembled)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

```typescript
// worker/index.ts
import { verify } from "@noble/ed25519";

export default {
  async fetch(req: Request, env: Env): Promise<Response> {
    if (req.method !== "POST") return new Response(null, { status: 405 });

    // P0 — global HALT. Checked first, cheapest, and it is the panic button.
    if (await env.KV.get("HALT") === "1")
      return new Response("halted", { status: 423 });

    const body = await req.json<SignedEnvelope>().catch(() => null);
    if (!body?.request || !body.sig) return new Response(null, { status: 400 });
    const r = body.request;
    if (r.v !== 1) return new Response("bad version", { status: 400 });

    // P1 — request authenticity.
    const appPub = base64ToBytes(env.APP_REQUEST_PUBKEY);
    const ok = await verify(base64ToBytes(body.sig), canonicalize(r), appPub);
    if (!ok) {
      await logSecurity(env, "SIGNER_BAD_REQUEST_SIGNATURE", r);
      return new Response(null, { status: 401 });
    }

    // P2 — freshness and replay. Both directions: a far-future ts is as
    // suspicious as a stale one.
    const skew = Date.now() - r.ts;
    if (skew > 30_000 || skew < -5_000) return new Response("stale", { status: 400 });
    // put with expirationTtl doubles as the dedupe record.
    const seen = await env.KV.get(`req:${r.requestId}`);
    if (seen) return new Response("replay", { status: 409 });
    await env.KV.put(`req:${r.requestId}`, "1", { expirationTtl: 300 });

    // P3 — revocation, checked at the signer so a compromised app cannot ignore
    // it (DEF-029).
    if (await env.KV.get(`revoked:session:${r.sessionId}`))
      return new Response("session revoked", { status: 403 });
    const epoch = Number(await env.KV.get(`epoch:user:${r.userId}`) ?? 0);
    if (epoch > (await sessionEpoch(env, r.sessionId)))
      return new Response("epoch revoked", { status: 403 });

    // P4 — rate limits, in the signer's own storage.
    const rl = await checkRateLimits(env, r);
    if (!rl.ok) {
      await logSecurity(env, "SIGNER_RATE_LIMITED", r);
      if (rl.trip) await env.KV.put("HALT", "1");    // velocity auto-halt
      return new Response(rl.reason, { status: 429 });
    }

    // P5 — unwrap and decrypt, AAD-bound to (user, wallet, purpose, kekVersion).
    let secret: Uint8Array;
    try {
      secret = await decryptWalletKey(env, r);
    } catch {
      await logSecurity(env, "SIGNER_DECRYPT_FAILED", r);   // CRITICAL alert
      return new Response("decrypt failed", { status: 403 });
    }

    try {
      // P6 — derived key must equal the declared wallet.
      const pub = await ed25519PublicFromSecret(secret);
      if (pub !== r.walletId) {
        await logSecurity(env, "SIGNER_KEY_WALLET_MISMATCH", r);  // CRITICAL
        return new Response("key mismatch", { status: 403 });
      }

      // CTL-707 — canary. A wallet no legitimate path ever signs for.
      if (await env.KV.get(`canary:${r.walletId}`)) {
        await env.KV.put("HALT", "1");
        await pageOncall(env, "CANARY_WALLET_SIGN_ATTEMPT", r);
        return new Response("halted", { status: 423 });
      }

      // P7 — the policy engine.
      const msg = parseMessage(extractMessage(base64ToBytes(r.txBase64)));
      const policy = await loadSessionPolicy(env, r.userId, r.sessionId);
      const verdict = evaluate(msg, r, pub, policy);
      if (!verdict.ok) {
        await logSecurity(env, "SIGNER_POLICY_REJECT", { ...r, reason: verdict.reason });
        return new Response(verdict.reason ?? "policy", { status: 403 });
      }

      // P8 — sign.
      const sig = await ed25519Sign(secret, extractMessage(base64ToBytes(r.txBase64)));
      await appendSigningLog(env, r, msg, verdict);
      return Response.json({ signature: bs58encode(sig) });
    } finally {
      secret.fill(0);       // best effort; the isolate is short-lived anyway
    }
  },
};
```
```toml
# wrangler.toml — the signer. SEPARATE ACCOUNT.
name = "osiris-signer"
main = "worker/index.ts"
compatibility_date = "2026-01-01"

kv_namespaces = [{ binding = "KV", id = "..." }]

# Secrets set with `wrangler secret put`, never here:
#   KEK
#   APP_REQUEST_PUBKEY
#   ALERT_WEBHOOK
```

WORKER RUNTIME NOTES
  - Cloudflare Workers' SubtleCrypto supports Ed25519 for sign and verify, and
    AES-GCM for the envelope decryption, so no third-party crypto is strictly
    required. `@noble/ed25519` is a reasonable alternative if the key-format
    handling is simpler; it is small and auditable. Do not add a large
    dependency to this Worker for any reason.
  - Verify the CPU budget with a load test before launch. Signing plus AES-GCM
    plus a 150-line parse is well within 10ms, but measure rather than assume.
  - The Worker must not log request bodies, blobs, or any key material. The
    signing log records: requestId, ts, userId (hashed), walletId, mode,
    program IDs, lamportsOut, verdict. Nothing else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-105  GLOBAL HALT (the panic button that works)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```
Setting KV key "HALT" = "1" stops all signing globally, immediately, from any
device with the signer account credential. It does not require the Oracle host,
the database, Redis, or the application to be functioning or trustworthy.

Reachable three ways:
  1. Cloudflare dashboard on a phone (KV editor).
  2. `wrangler kv:key put --binding=KV HALT 1` from any machine with the token.
  3. A dedicated one-route Worker with a long random path and a hardware-key
     Access policy in front of it, so the operator can HALT with one tap.

Automatic triggers (the Worker sets it itself):
  - canary wallet signing attempt                    (CTL-707)
  - decrypt failure rate above threshold             (a KEK problem or an attack)
  - key/wallet mismatch                              (blob tampering, DEF-027)
  - signing velocity above 3x rolling baseline       (CTL-706)
  - more than N policy rejections in a window        (CTL-709)

Clearing HALT is deliberately manual and requires the hardware key. A system
that can un-halt itself has no halt.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-106  KEK ROTATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```
Because the KEK never leaves the Worker, rotation happens there:
  1. `wrangler secret put KEK_NEXT`  (new 32-byte key)
  2. The Worker accepts both: unwrap tries kekVersion's key; new wraps use NEXT.
  3. A background job on the app host walks wallets in batches and, for each,
     calls a dedicated /rewrap endpoint that unwraps under the old KEK and
     re-wraps under the new one, returning the new blob. The plaintext DEK never
     leaves the Worker. The app stores the returned blob.
  4. When zero rows remain at the old version, promote KEK_NEXT to KEK and
     delete the old secret.
  5. Verify: a query asserting no wallet row references a retired kekVersion.

Emergency rotation additionally sets HALT first, so nothing signs during the
window, and notifies users. Rotation is exercised on devnet before launch; a
rotation procedure that has never been run is not a procedure.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-107  WALLET GENERATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```
The wallet is generated INSIDE the Worker, not on the app host. The app host
calls /generate with (userId, walletId [DEFINE IN ENV]) and receives back
{ publicKey, blob }. It never sees the secret key, not even for a moment, not
even at creation. This closes the one window where the old design would
otherwise have had key material on the host.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-108  LOCAL DEVELOPMENT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```
A LocalSignerProvider exists for development. It is gated by THREE independent
checks, all of which must pass, because this is the obvious way to accidentally
ship a local signer to production:
  1. process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production"
  2. process.env.OSIRIS_ALLOW_LOCAL_SIGNER === "yes-i-am-on-devnet"
  3. a runtime assertion that the configured RPC endpoint resolves to a devnet
     cluster (getGenesisHash() matches the devnet genesis)
If any check fails, the process exits. TEST-108 asserts that setting
NODE_ENV=production with the local signer configured causes a non-zero exit.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CTL-109  WHAT THE APPLICATION HOST STILL HOLDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```
Exactly one secret with security value: the Ed25519 request-signing key, in a
Docker secret at /run/secrets/signer_request_key, mode 400, root-owned.

What it can do if stolen: construct valid signing requests. Which then still
face the policy engine, the rate limits, revocation, and HALT. It is an
authorization to ASK, not an authorization to TAKE.

Rotation: generate a new pair, `wrangler secret put APP_REQUEST_PUBKEY` with the
new public key, then swap the private key on the host. Brief overlap is handled
by the Worker accepting two public keys during a rotation window.
```

LAYER 7 — DETECTION AND RESPONSE
################################################################################

CTL-700  ALERT BUDGET. At most five pages per week in steady state. Every page
         has a documented action. Anything without an action is a dashboard
         metric, not a page. Reviewed monthly: any alert that fired more than
         twice without leading to an action is retuned or deleted.
                                                                (ARGUMENT 10)
CTL-701  Structured JSON logging only; a redaction allowlist so that only known
         fields are logged (never a spread of a request body); no shell ever
         parses a log.                                          (DEF-002)
CTL-702  Log shipping off-box within seconds to an immutable sink; local logs
         size-capped and rotated normally.                      (DEF-015)
CTL-703  Hash-chained audit log with daily external anchoring and a verification
         job.                                                   (DEF-042)
CTL-704  Alert transport: two independent channels (Telegram admin channel plus
         email), because a single channel is a single point of failure on the
         worst day. Critical alerts additionally set HALT where appropriate.
CTL-705  DETECTOR — signer decrypt failure or key/wallet mismatch. Near-zero
         false positive rate. CRITICAL. Auto-HALT.
CTL-706  DETECTOR — signing velocity above 3x the rolling baseline, per wallet
         and globally. CRITICAL. Auto-HALT at the global threshold.
CTL-707  DETECTOR — canary wallet. A wallet row that exists in the database,
         looks entirely ordinary, and that no legitimate code path ever signs
         for. Any signing attempt means someone is enumerating wallets.
         False-positive rate is zero by construction. CRITICAL. Auto-HALT.
         Deploy several, and also deploy: a decoy `/api/admin/export-keys` route
         that 404s and alerts; a decoy `.env.backup` file on the host containing
         a canary token; a decoy user row whose email address, if it ever
         receives mail, proves database exfiltration.
CTL-708  DETECTOR — audit chain anchor mismatch, AIDE baseline mutation, or an
         `ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` event trigger firing.
         CRITICAL.
CTL-709  DETECTOR — signer policy rejections, especially
         `declared_program_absent` / `undeclared_program_present` (CTL-102 P8).
         A correct client never produces these. HIGH; auto-HALT above a small
         threshold.
CTL-710  DETECTOR — Cloudflare Access authentication that the operator did not
         perform; new hardware key enrollment; API token creation. HIGH.
CTL-711  INCIDENT RESPONSE — reversible, auto-expiring containment; never mutate
         commercial or credential state; a hard blast-radius cap above which a
         human decides; prefer the globally safe action (HALT) over the locally
         destructive one (account lock).                        (DEF-036)
CTL-712  Risk scores retained on trade rows for forensics and for the user's own
         activity view; they never page.                        (DEF-035)

================================================================================
PART 5 — THE VERIFICATION SUITE
================================================================================

INV-3 says every control has a test that fails the build when the control is
removed. This part is that list. It is the deliverable that makes the rest of
this document real rather than aspirational.

RULE C-2 RESTATED, BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE PEOPLE SKIP
A test that has never been observed to fail is not a test. For each entry below,
the implementing agent must (1) write the test, (2) deliberately break the
control, (3) observe the test fail, (4) restore the control, (5) observe the
test pass, and (6) record that it did so. A test suite where step 2 was skipped
is a suite of assertions about a system nobody has probed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUITE 1 — SIGNER AND KEY CUSTODY  (blocking; runs on every commit)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TEST-101  Telegram webhook: missing / wrong / 1-char / correct secret header
          returns 401/401/401/200, and the 1-char case throws nothing.
TEST-102  Mini App initData: valid fixture accepts; flipped byte rejects; stale
          auth_date rejects; Login-Widget key derivation rejects.
TEST-103  Replayed Telegram update returns 200 and enqueues nothing.
TEST-104  Envelope encryption: ciphertext encrypted under CryptoContext A fails
          to decrypt under CryptoContext B (AAD binding, DEF-027).
TEST-105  With the application deliberately patched to ignore revocation, a
          signing request for a revoked session is still rejected — by the
          signer. Proves DEF-029's independence.
TEST-106  No API response body, in any route, contains an MFA secret, a private
          key, a KEK, a DEK, a session token, or a blob field. Implemented as a
          response-shape scanner over an integration run, not as spot checks.
TEST-107  A 1 MB webhook body returns 413 without proportional allocation.
TEST-108  Local signer with NODE_ENV=production causes a non-zero process exit.
TEST-110  Signature format: signer output matches
          /^[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{86,88}$/ and round-trips through
          getSignatureStatuses on devnet (DEF-050).
TEST-111  POLICY ENGINE, table-driven. Each case is a serialized transaction
          and an expected verdict:
            accept  — Jupiter swap: ComputeBudget x2 + ATA create + Jupiter
                      route + SyncNative + CloseAccount(self) + tip transfer
            accept  — same, without the optional ATA create
            reject  — top-level SPL Transfer to a third party
            reject  — top-level SPL TransferChecked to a third party
            reject  — SetAuthority on the wallet's token account
            reject  — Approve (delegate) to any address
            reject  — SystemProgram Transfer to a non-tip address
            reject  — tip transfer above MAX_TIP_LAMPORTS
            reject  — CloseAccount with a third-party lamport destination
            reject  — an unknown program ID in the static keys
            reject  — fee payer is not the wallet
            reject  — numRequiredSignatures = 2
            reject  — declared programIds omit a program that is present
            reject  — declared programIds include one that is absent
            reject  — lamportsOut exceeds the declared maximum
            reject  — trailing bytes after the message
            reject  — truncated compact-u16
            reject  — a transaction larger than 1232 bytes
          Every reject case must return the specific reason string, not a
          generic failure, so that CTL-709 can distinguish "buggy client" from
          "compromised client."
TEST-112  HALT: with KV HALT=1, every signing request returns 423, including a
          perfectly valid one.
TEST-113  Canary wallet: a signing request for a canary walletId sets HALT and
          pages.
TEST-114  Request replay: the same requestId twice returns 409 on the second.
TEST-115  Clock skew: ts 60s in the past and 60s in the future both reject.
TEST-116  KEK rotation on devnet: rotate, rewrap all wallets, assert zero rows
          at the retired version, assert signing still works throughout.

TEST-401  Every tRPC procedure carries the auth marker except those in
          INTENTIONALLY_PUBLIC; the allowlist has no stale entries; the walker
          finds a plausible number of procedures.
TEST-402  RLS, four assertions: cross-user read returns nothing without an
          app-layer check; cross-user write is refused; no user context sees
          nothing; 200 concurrent interleaved identities never cross over.
TEST-403  Every retention-policy entry corresponds to a table in the schema.
TEST-404  The ESLint restriction on `@trpc/server` imports fails on a
          deliberate violation.
TEST-405  `osiris_app` has rolsuper=false, rolbypassrls=false, rolcreatedb=false,
          rolcreaterole=false, no DDL grants, and no UPDATE/DELETE on
          audit_logs.
TEST-406  An intentionally injectable test procedure given `' OR 1=1 --`
          returns only the current user's rows.
TEST-407  `no-raw-sql.sh` exits non-zero when a `sql.raw` is introduced.
TEST-408  Every user-scoped table reports relrowsecurity AND relforcerowsecurity.
TEST-409  Audit chain: append 1000 entries concurrently, then verify the chain
          from GENESIS with no forks and no gaps.
TEST-410  Backup restore drill assertions run green against a fresh restore.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUITE 5 — APPLICATION AND FRONTEND
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TEST-501  The same idempotency key submitted twice concurrently produces exactly
          one trade row; the same key with a different request hash returns 409.
TEST-502  Session lease: two workers racing to claim one session, exactly one
          wins; an expired lease is reclaimable; a stale owner cannot release.
TEST-601  Token label normalizer fixtures: RTL override, Cyrillic homoglyph,
          zero-width joiner, Zalgo, 1 MB input, lone surrogate, empty string,
          emoji-only, "OSIRIS Official", fullwidth characters, combining-mark
          run. Each asserts display and flags.
TEST-602  CSP present, nonce-based, no unsafe directives (also SUITE 3).
TEST-603  Bundle grep: no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, no `.innerHTML =` outside
          the sanctioned Trusted Types policy file.
TEST-604  Playwright: a token named `<img src=x onerror=fetch('//evil')>`
          renders as literal text, executes nothing, and produces no outbound
          request.
TEST-605  Playwright: a token name containing U+202E does not reorder
          surrounding interface text.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUITE 6 — RATE LIMITING AND RESILIENCE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TEST-701  With Redis stopped: /api/auth/signIn returns 503, /api/price/* returns
          200.
TEST-702  200 concurrent auth attempts from one identity: at most 5 succeed.
TEST-703  `caddy validate` succeeds with the custom build and fails with stock
          Caddy.
TEST-704  A free-tier user issuing fullTokenAnalyze three times in one minute is
          refused by cost budget.
TEST-705  AIDE baseline mutation produces an alert from the OFF-BOX comparison,
          not from the host.
TEST-706  auditd rules loaded and immutable (also SUITE 2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUITE 7 — SUPPLY CHAIN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TEST-801  gitleaks detects a planted fake Solana secret key, a planted Telegram
          bot token, and a planted Helius URL — in the working tree and in
          history.
TEST-802  `npm audit signatures` passes; the build fails if it does not.
TEST-803  Every image reference in compose and every Dockerfile FROM is
          digest-pinned.
TEST-804  Trivy reports no unexpired HIGH/CRITICAL findings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAOS DRILLS  (quarterly, manual, recorded in the audit log)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DRILL-1  Kill Redis in production-like staging. Confirm auth fails closed,
         reads fail open, and the fail-open metric pages after 60 seconds.
DRILL-2  Set HALT. Confirm every signing path stops within one second, the UI
         degrades gracefully with an honest message, and no data is corrupted.
         Clear HALT and confirm recovery.
DRILL-3  Revoke a session mid-trade. Confirm the in-flight pipeline aborts, the
         signer refuses, and the session lease is released cleanly.
DRILL-4  Restore the newest backup to a scratch environment and pass every
         assertion. Time it. The number is the recovery-time objective.
DRILL-5  Rotate the KEK end to end on devnet.
DRILL-6  Simulate app-host compromise: from a shell in the app container, try to
         (a) read a wallet private key, (b) sign a transfer to an attacker
         address, (c) read another user's rows, (d) delete an audit log row.
         All four must fail. Record exactly how each failed and which control
         caught it. If any succeeds, that is a Gate 1 blocker, not a finding.
DRILL-7  Simulate signer-account compromise: with the Worker's KV and secrets
         but no database access, attempt to produce a usable key. Confirm the
         absence of ciphertext makes it impossible.

PART 6 — IMPLEMENTATION ORDER
================================================================================

Three gates. Gate 1 is mandatory before a mainnet private key exists. Nothing in
Gate 1 is optional, and there is no partial launch of a custody system (C-5).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GATE 0 — PREREQUISITES (before any code)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [ ] Two FIDO2 hardware security keys purchased and in hand.
  [ ] Two Cloudflare accounts created: `site` and `signer`. Different emails.
      Hardware key MFA on both. TOTP fallback disabled. No SMS recovery.
  [ ] Oracle Cloud account with hardware MFA.
  [ ] Domain registered; registry lock enabled; hardware MFA at the registrar.
  [ ] A dedicated email account, used for nothing else, hardware-key protected,
      as the registration address for all of the above.
  [ ] Recovery codes for every account printed and stored physically; digital
      copies deleted.
  [ ] The admin machine (or admin OS user + browser profile) set up per CTL-902.
  [ ] The `age` identity for backups generated offline; public key committed;
      private key in the password manager AND on paper. Never on any server.
  [ ] Squads multisig created for the operator treasury, with hardware signers,
      on addresses this application will never see.        (CTL-903)

ACCEPTANCE: a written inventory of every account, its MFA method, and its
recovery path, with SMS appearing nowhere.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GATE 1 — MANDATORY BEFORE A MAINNET KEY EXISTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ordered by dependency, not by importance.

  1.  Host baseline
      [ ] Oracle VCN security list closed; iptables-persistent removed; UFW
          baseline + DOCKER-USER rules; verified from outside.   (CTL-200/202)
      [ ] SSH loopback-only; Cloudflare Tunnel + Access + WebAuthn; break-glass
          serial console tested.                                 (CTL-201)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-201, 202, 205, 206, 207, 208 pass.

  2.  Container baseline
      [ ] Hardened compose with verified UIDs, no published internal ports,

      [ ] Runtime hardening self-assertion in the app.           (CTL-205)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-203, 209, 210, 211 pass.

  3.  Edge and origin
      [ ] Single origin; Cloudflare proxy; Authenticated Origin Pulls; correct
          client IP resolution end to end.                (CTL-300/302/304)
      [ ] Canonical headers; nonce-based strict CSP with Trusted Types, deployed
          report-only for 48h first, then enforced.              (CTL-303)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-212, 301, 302, 304, 305, 306 pass.

  4.  Data layer
      [ ] Roles and grants; RLS ENABLE + FORCE on every user-scoped table;
          `withUser()` as the only query path; lint enforcement.  (CTL-401/402)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-402, 405, 406, 408 pass, including the concurrency case.

  5.  The signer                                            <-- the long pole
      [ ] Worker deployed in the separate account; KEK set via `wrangler secret`.
      [ ] Protocol, canonicalization, and request signing shared between app and
          Worker from one module.                                (CTL-101)
      [ ] Minimal parser.                                        (CTL-103)
      [ ] Policy engine with the full TEST-111 table green.      (CTL-102)
      [ ] Rate limits, revocation, replay dedupe, HALT.     (CTL-104/105)
      [ ] Wallet generation moved inside the Worker.             (CTL-107)
      [ ] Local signer triple-gated.                             (CTL-108)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-104, 105, 108, 110, 111 (every row), 112, 113, 114, 115
      pass. DRILL-6 and DRILL-7 pass.

  6.  Application authorization
      [ ] `t` not exported; only guarded procedure builders; ESLint restriction.
      [ ] Runtime router assertion test with the public allowlist. (CTL-501)
      [ ] Idempotency keys; session lease CAS; revocation epoch.
                                                     (CTL-504, DEF-028, DEF-030)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-401, 404, 501, 502 pass.

  7.  Telegram
      [ ] Correct secret-token verification; crash-proof comparison; replay
          dedupe; bounded body; WAF rule.                        (PART 3 EP-4)
      [ ] Trust tier guard on every mutation.                    (CTL-509)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-101, 102, 103, 107 pass.

  8.  Frontend hostile-input handling
      [ ] Token label normalizer; TokenIdentity as the only render path; lint
          bans; safeHref.                                        (CTL-603)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-601, 603, 604, 605 pass.

  9.  Rate limiting
      [ ] Five tiers; per-class fail policy; cost budget; WebSocket limits.
                                                                 (CTL-305)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-701, 702, 703, 704 pass.

 10.  Backups and the first drill
      [ ] `age`-encrypted, immutable off-box backups; restore drill executed and
          timed.                                                 (CTL-405/406)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-410 passes; DRILL-4 recorded with a real RTO number.

 11.  Minimum viable detection
      [ ] Structured logging with a redaction allowlist; off-box shipping.
      [ ] Canary wallet deployed; decoy admin route; decoy `.env.backup`.
      [ ] Velocity, decrypt-failure, key-mismatch, and policy-rejection
          detectors wired to two alert channels.        (CTL-705/706/707/709)
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-113 passes; a synthetic trigger of each detector reaches
      both channels within 60 seconds.

 12.  Supply chain minimum
      [ ] gitleaks pre-commit and CI; `npm ci --ignore-scripts` with allowlist;
          digest-pinned images; `npm audit signatures` in CI.
      ACCEPTANCE: TEST-801, 802, 803 pass.

GATE 1 EXIT CRITERIA
  - Every acceptance test above is green in CI.
  - Every test has been observed to fail with its control removed (C-2).
  - DRILL-2, DRILL-6, and DRILL-7 have been executed and recorded.
  - The written account inventory from Gate 0 exists and is current.
  Only then may a mainnet wallet be generated.

================================================================================
PART 7 — WHAT WE ARE DELIBERATELY NOT DOING
================================================================================

Recorded with reasons so that nobody re-adds them in month three because they
sound impressive. Each of these was in the corpus.

7.1  BEHAVIORAL BIOMETRICS (keystroke dynamics, mouse movement)
     Removed. Enrollment is slow, drift is constant, accuracy on a population
     of a few hundred is poor, and the failure mode is locking out a legitimate
     user mid-trade. It is also trivially replayed by an attacker who has script
     execution on the page, which is the scenario it is aimed at. The passkey
     requirement on Tier 2/3 actions does the same job correctly.

7.2  VIRTUAL / ON-SCREEN KEYBOARD as anti-keylogger
     Removed. Screen-capturing malware defeats it, it degrades accessibility
     badly, and it signals security theater to exactly the technical users this
     product needs. The correct answer to keyloggers is that nothing worth
     stealing is ever typed (CTL-901).

7.3  DEVICE FINGERPRINT SESSION BINDING
     Removed. See DEF-034.

7.4  ANTI-SCREEN-RECORDING / UI OBFUSCATION
     Removed. Not achievable in a browser. Any partial measure degrades
     accessibility and legitimate screenshotting while stopping no attacker who
     controls the machine.

7.5  PUBLIC REAL-TIME SECURITY DASHBOARD AND SECURITY SCORE
     Removed. See ARGUMENT 12 and DEF-058. Replaced with attestations and a
     per-user security page.

7.6  FUNDED BUG BOUNTY IN PHASE 0/1
     Deferred. Contradicts the stated scope, requires a budget line that does
     not exist, and requires triage capacity that does not exist. Replaced with
     `security.txt` plus an honest disclosure policy. Revisit when there is
     both money and a person to triage.

7.7  THIRD-PARTY PENETRATION TEST AS A PHASE 1 GATE
     Deferred. $8k-30k. Keeping it on a "$0 budget" checklist guarantees it gets
     silently dropped and the checklist becomes a lie. Replaced with the
     verification suite in PART 5 and an honest public statement of what has and
     has not been independently reviewed.

7.8  INSURANCE FOR USER FUNDS
     Removed. Not obtainable by an unregistered individual operator at any
     accessible price. Listing it creates an expectation that cannot be met.

7.9  MULTI-RPC "ALL MUST AGREE" CONFIRMATION
     Removed as a security control, retained as an availability pool. See
     DEF-045.

7.10 SIEM INTEGRATION
     Deferred. The corpus's `SIEM_WEBHOOK_URL` posts every security event to an
     arbitrary URL from an environment variable, which is an exfiltration
     primitive if that variable is ever wrong. Off-box immutable log shipping
     (CTL-702) covers the actual need. A real SIEM is a Gate 3+ decision.

7.11 `userns-remap` IN PHASE 0
     Deferred. Good control, hazardous ordering. See DEF-011.

7.12 `re2`
     Avoided. See DEF-032b. Bound input length and write linear regexes.

7.13 PORT KNOCKING
     Removed. With SSH not internet-reachable at all (EP-1), there is no port to
     knock on. Port knocking is a weaker version of what the tunnel already
     does.

7.14 IPv6 DISABLED AT THE KERNEL
     Removed. Breaks Cloudflare IPv6 origin connectivity and outbound resolution
     on IPv6-preferring networks. Filter, do not disable.

================================================================================
PART 8 — RESIDUAL RISK REGISTER
================================================================================

Risks that are accepted rather than mitigated. Each has an owner decision, a
bound, and a review date. A risk register that only contains solved problems is
marketing.

RISK-001  SIGNER CLOUDFLARE ACCOUNT COMPROMISE COMBINED WITH DATABASE ACCESS
  Impact: total. Both are required; neither alone suffices.
  Bound:  requires two independent compromises across two providers and two
          hardware keys.
  Accept: yes. Mitigated by account separation, hardware MFA, no SMS recovery,
          and the fact that the signer account is used for nothing else and is
          touched rarely.
  Review: on any change to the signer deployment process.

RISK-002  FORCED-SWAP VALUE DESTRUCTION AFTER APP-HOST COMPROMISE
  Impact: an attacker with app-host RCE can force swaps into a worthless token
          within the signer's policy and rate limits. Value is destroyed even
          though it is not transferred to the attacker's address directly.
  Bound:  per-wallet signing rate limit, session policy mint constraints
          (CTL-604), loss circuit breaker, velocity auto-HALT, and the fact that
          it is loud.
  Accept: yes, explicitly. This is the honest residual of ARGUMENT 5 and it must
          be stated to users rather than hidden behind "non-custodial."
  Review: quarterly; tighten per-wallet rate limits as real volume data arrives.

RISK-003  A QUERY PATH THAT BYPASSES `withUser()`
  Impact: RLS does not apply; an application-layer authorization bug becomes
          exploitable.
  Bound:  lint restriction, the "no user context sees nothing" test, and the
          fact that `withSystemContext` is restricted to `src/jobs/**` and logs
          every use.
  Accept: yes. Review on every new data-access module.

RISK-004  AUTHENTIC MALICIOUS TELEGRAM UPDATES
  Impact: Telegram's infrastructure, or an insider there, could deliver
          authentic-looking updates.
  Bound:  Trust Tier 0/1 only. Cannot authorize a withdrawal, a settings change,
          or a limit increase.
  Accept: yes.

RISK-005  CROSS-TENANT SIDE CHANNELS ON SHARED ORACLE HARDWARE
  Impact: theoretical extraction of memory contents from a co-tenant.
  Bound:  no key material is on this host at all (CTL-100), so the highest-value
          target is absent. Kernel kept patched.
  Accept: yes. This replaces the corpus's false claim that the free tier is
          dedicated (DEF-044).

RISK-006  CLOUDFLARE ZERO TRUST OUTAGE BLOCKS ADMINISTRATIVE ACCESS
  Impact: no SSH during a Cloudflare outage.
  Bound:  Oracle serial console break-glass, tested quarterly.
  Accept: yes.

RISK-007  CONTAINER ESCAPE VIA A KERNEL VULNERABILITY
  Impact: host root.
  Bound:  no key material on the host; distroless runtime; unattended security
          upgrades with a scheduled reboot window (Livepatch is unavailable on
          22.04 arm64, so reboots are the mechanism and must actually happen).
  Accept: yes, with the reboot cadence as a tracked operational metric.

RISK-008  SQL INJECTION INSIDE `withSystemContext`
  Impact: RLS does not bound the blast radius for that code path.
  Bound:  the same lint and CI grep controls apply; the surface is `src/jobs/**`
          only; every use is audit-logged.
  Accept: yes.

RISK-009  TRUSTED TYPES IS CHROMIUM-ONLY
  Impact: Firefox and Safari users do not get the DOM-XSS sink protection.
  Bound:  strict nonce CSP and the lint bans apply to all browsers; Trusted
          Types is additive, not the sole control.
  Accept: yes. Re-review when Firefox and Safari ship support.

RISK-010  SUSTAINED DISTRIBUTED L7 ATTACK
  Impact: availability. Cloudflare's free plan gives one rate-limiting rule with
          a fixed 10-second window.
  Bound:  Under Attack mode, managed challenges, per-identity limits, cost
          budgets.
  Accept: for now. The honest escalation is Cloudflare Pro, which costs money.

RISK-011  ORACLE ALWAYS FREE INSTANCE RECLAMATION
  Impact: total loss of the host with limited notice. Oracle may reclaim an
          Always Free instance whose 95th-percentile CPU, network, and memory
          utilization are all below 20% over a 7-day window. There is no SLA.
  Bound:  off-box immutable backups, a tested restore procedure with a known
          RTO, and infrastructure that is reproducible from the repository.
  Accept: for Phase 0. This is a genuine single point of failure that the "$0"
          framing conceals, and a paid instance is the honest fix once there is
          real money in the system.

RISK-012  UPGRADEABLE ALLOWLISTED PROGRAMS
  Impact: a program on the signer's `ALLOWED_PROGRAMS` list whose upgrade
          authority is live can change behaviour after allowlisting.
  Bound:  record the verified build and upgrade authority at allowlist time;
          re-check on a schedule; prefer immutable programs; alert on change.
  Accept: yes, with the scheduled re-check as the mitigation.        (CTL-809)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CORRECTED "HARDEST TARGETS" LIST
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Red Team's original list, corrected. Three of their five were resting on
claims that were not true as built.

  ORIGINAL                                    CORRECTED
  1. Envelope encryption with HSM-backed KEK  -> Remote signer: the app host
     "we can't decrypt keys"                     never possesses key material,
                                                 so RCE yields no key. TRUE, but
                                                 only after CTL-100. It was NOT
                                                 true as specified; see
                                                 ARGUMENT 1.
  2. Zero-memory signing, keys < 50ms         -> DELETED. Not achievable in
                                                 Node. Replaced by "keys are
                                                 never on that host at all,"
                                                 which is stronger and real.
  3. Multi-RPC confirmation                   -> Replaced by content
                                                 verification at the correct
                                                 commitment level (DEF-045).
                                                 Stronger, and cheaper.
  4. Token-2022 safety checks                 -> Extended to include classic-SPL
                                                 freezeAuthority, which was the
                                                 larger hole (DEF-047).
  5. Circuit breaker                          -> Retained, and joined by the
                                                 signer's own rate limits, which
                                                 the application cannot disable.

  NEW, and the one that matters most:
  6. Signer policy engine                     -> Even with the app host fully
                                                 compromised, the attacker
                                                 cannot produce a transaction
                                                 that transfers SOL or tokens to
                                                 an address they control. This
                                                 is the control that changes the
                                                 economics of attacking this
                                                 system.

================================================================================
PART 9 — TRUE COST
================================================================================

The Blue Team's assessment claimed "BUDGET: $0. TOOLS: 100% free and open
source. TIME TO IMPLEMENT: 2-3 days. ONGOING COST: $0." Every clause was wrong,
and the wrongness is expensive: a plan that claims zero cost will, on meeting a
$50 cost, either stall or quietly drop the control — and the control most likely
to be dropped is the hardware security key, which is the fix for the Red Team's
single biggest worry.

Verify every figure below against the provider's current pricing at
implementation time (C-4). These are the values as of this document's date.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GENUINELY FREE, WITH LIMITS THAT MATTER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Cloudflare DNS, proxy, universal SSL       $0
  Cloudflare WAF custom rules (free tier)    $0   limited rule count
  Cloudflare rate limiting                   $0   ONE rule, IP-only, fixed
                                                  10-second window. Pro is
                                                  needed for anything richer.
  Cloudflare Zero Trust (Tunnel + Access)    $0   up to 50 users; 24h log
                                                  retention on free
  Cloudflare Workers                         $0   100k requests/day, 10ms CPU
                                                  per invocation. Ample here;
                                                  the CPU limit dictates the
                                                  no-web3.js decision (CTL-103).
  Cloudflare R2                              $0   10 GB storage tier
  Oracle Cloud Always Free ARM               $0   NO SLA. Subject to idle
                                                  reclamation when CPU, network,
                                                  and memory 95th-percentile
                                                  utilization are all under 20%
                                                  over 7 days. Verify the
                                                  current OCPU/RAM allowance in
                                                  the console rather than
                                                  assuming the spec's figures.
  Ubuntu Pro (personal)                      $0   up to 5 machines. NOTE:
                                                  Livepatch on arm64 arrived
                                                  with Ubuntu 26.04; a 22.04
                                                  arm64 host does NOT get it, so
                                                  kernel CVEs require reboots.
  Helius RPC free tier                       $0   rate-limited; the pool exists
                                                  for availability (CTL-607)
  fail2ban, UFW, AIDE, auditd, age, rclone,
    gitleaks, Trivy, Caddy, PostgreSQL,
    Redis, Docker                            $0
  Let's Encrypt certificates                 $0
  Backblaze B2 (Object Lock backups)         $0   10 GB free tier

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2 x FIDO2 hardware security keys       $50 - 100
      Required for: SSH (ed25519-sk), Cloudflare account MFA, Oracle MFA,
      registrar MFA, GitHub, password manager. This is the fix for "the one

  Dedicated admin machine (optional but

      A used laptop or a Raspberry Pi. The cheapest meaningful risk reduction

      unacceptable)                      $5 - 15 / month, contingent (RISK-011)

  Solana base transaction fee            ~0.000005 SOL
  Priority fee                           variable with congestion
  Helius Sender tip                      0.001 SOL minimum for the priority

  MEV protection (`?mev-protect=true`)   included in the above, but it rides on

HONEST TOTAL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Year one, minimum viable:      ~$60 - 140
     (2 hardware keys + a domain)
  Year one, recommended:         ~$110 - 400
     (adds a dedicated admin machine)
  Ongoing:                       ~$10 - 40 / year plus per-trade tips
  Contingent:                    +$25 - 35 / month if Cloudflare Pro and a paid
                                 instance become necessary

TIME
  "2-3 days" describes typing the configurations. Implementing, testing, and
  verifying Gate 1 — including writing the verification suite, observing each
  test fail with its control removed, and running the drills — is realistically
  two to three focused weeks, of which the signer Worker is roughly a third.

  That is still an extraordinarily cheap security posture for a system holding
  user funds. It does not need to be exaggerated to be impressive, and
  exaggerating it is how controls get dropped.

================================================================================
CLOSING — WHAT CHANGED, IN ONE PAGE
================================================================================

The corpus was strong on breadth and weak on load-bearing detail. Fifty-seven
defects, of which eleven were code that cannot run and nine were controls that
do not control the attack they are filed under. The five changes that matter
most:

  1. KEY MATERIAL LEAVES THE APPLICATION HOST ENTIRELY.
     Envelope encryption with the KEK on the same box as the ciphertext is a
     filing system, not a boundary. A remote signer with a policy engine means
     RCE on the trading host does not yield a private key and cannot produce a
     transaction that moves value to the attacker. This single change is what
     makes the Red Team's "we need to break 5+ layers" true rather than
     flattering.

  2. AUTHORIZATION IS ENFORCED IN THE DATABASE, NOT ONLY IN THE APPLICATION.
     "Never forget the auth check" is not a control. Postgres row-level security
     with FORCE, plus procedure builders that make an unauthenticated endpoint
     unconstructible, plus a test that enumerates every procedure, means the
     Red Team's "one missing check" is a bug rather than a breach.

  3. SSH IS NOT ON THE INTERNET.
     Every mitigation in the corpus answered "how do I survive an exposed SSH
     daemon." The daemon does not need to be exposed.

  4. THE THINGS THAT DO NOT WORK ARE GONE.
     Two wrong Telegram verifiers, a comparison that crashes on attacker input,
     a UFW rule that opens the database, a Caddy directive that prevents the
     server from starting, a CSP that disarms itself, a Docker interaction that
     makes the firewall irrelevant, a rate limiter that keys on Cloudflare's IP,
     an anomaly detector that fires on the product's normal behaviour, and a
     backup scheme with no off-box copy and no restore test.

  5. THE CLAIMS ARE HONEST NOW.
     Not $0. Not 2-3 days. Zero-memory signing was not a hard control. Oracle
     free tier is not dedicated and can be reclaimed. MEV protection costs a tip
     per trade. Cloudflare's free rate limiting is one rule with a 10-second
     window. Each of these was a place where a comfortable claim would have
     produced a bad decision later.

The Red Team's closing line was: "The architecture is defense-in-depth. We need
to break 5+ layers to get keys. That's expensive. We'll move on to easier
targets."

That was aspirational when they wrote it. After Gate 1 it is accurate, and the
layers are: the Cloudflare edge, the origin firewall and origin-pull
certificate, the container boundary, the application authorization layer, the
database RLS policy, the request-signing key, the signer's rate limits and
revocation, the signer's KEK, and the policy engine that reads the transaction
and refuses. Breaking all of them from one position is not possible, because
they do not all live in one place — which was the entire point.

================================================================================
END OF ADDENDUM O

PART 0 — DECISIONS RECORDED

## 0.1 Three decisions taken by the operator

  D-1  THE SIGNER MOVES OFF CLOUDFLARE ENTIRELY.
       ADDENDUM O placed the signer in a second Cloudflare account. That is
       now superseded: the signer runs on a different vendor. The reason is
       correlated failure — a Cloudflare-wide outage, a Cloudflare-side
       security incident, or a Cloudflare support-desk social engineering
       attack should not be able to touch both the edge and the keys. See
       PART 4.

  D-2  STRICT $0 RECURRING SPEND.
       No Cloudflare Pro. No paid Oracle instance. No managed database. This
       is a legitimate choice and it is workable, but it means two residual
       risks from ADDENDUM O are accepted rather than mitigated, and a third
       becomes more important. PART 7 states exactly where this hurts and
       what free measures partially compensate. Nothing in this document
       pretends the free tier is equivalent to the paid one.

  D-3  FUNDS UNDER MANAGEMENT ARE UNKNOWN BUT REAL.
       The operator expects meaningful money to flow through the system
       without a firm projection. Designing for a guess is how systems end up
       either over-built and unshipped or under-built and drained. Instead,
       PART 9 defines balance tripwires: specific thresholds that
       mechanically force specific actions. The system measures its own risk
       and tells you when the posture must change.

================================================================================
PART 1 — THE LAYERING DOCTRINE
================================================================================

Your instinct is right: breach is a question of when, and depth beats height.
But there is one correction that determines whether the depth is real, and it
is the single most useful idea in this document.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LAYER-1  THE INDEPENDENCE TEST
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Layers only count if they fail independently.

    Ten controls that all stop working the moment the application host is
    compromised are not ten layers. They are one layer, drawn ten times.

This is the most common way defence-in-depth becomes theatre. A team lists
twenty controls, feels protected, and every one of those controls is code
running on the same box, reading the same config, trusting the same session,
enforced by the same process. An attacker who gets that box gets all twenty at
once. The list was long; the depth was one.

THE TEST, stated so it can be applied mechanically:

    For any two controls A and B, ask: is there a single compromise that
    disables both?

    If yes, A and B are ONE layer for that compromise. Count them once.
    If no, they are genuinely two.

Applied to the original corpus, this is devastating and clarifying. Consider
the controls that were filed against "attacker steals private keys":

    - Zod input validation            } all of these are
    - tRPC auth middleware            } code running in the
    - ownership checks on mutations   } app process, reading
    - rate limiting                   } app config, on the
    - CSRF tokens                     } app host
    - envelope encryption             }
    - zero-memory signing             }
    - the KEK in a Docker secret      } on the same host

    Single compromise that disables all eight: RCE in the Node process.

Eight controls. One layer. That is why ADDENDUM O moved key material off the
host entirely — not because envelope encryption is bad, but because it was
sitting inside the same blast radius as everything else, so it added a line to
the list and nothing to the depth.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LAYER-2  THE FOUR DIMENSIONS OF INDEPENDENCE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Two controls are independent to the degree that they differ along these axes.
Use this when designing a new control: if it scores the same as an existing
