control on all four, you have not added a layer.

  1. LOCATION      Different machine, network, or provider.
                   app host / edge / signer vendor / user's device / offline
  2. MECHANISM     Different technology enforcing it.
                   TypeScript / SQL policy / packet filter / TLS / hardware
  3. CREDENTIAL    Different secret or key required to bypass it.
                   session cookie / DB password / KEK / hardware key / age key
  4. OPERATOR      Different party must fail.
                   you / Cloudflare / Deno / Oracle / the user

Worked example — Red Team entry point 3, "one missing auth check":

  Control                        Location      Mechanism     Credential
  -----------------------------  ------------  ------------  ---------------
  protectedProcedure middleware  app host      TypeScript    session
  router assertion test          CI            test runner   repo write
  Postgres RLS policy            database      SQL           DB role
  AAD binding on the blob        signer        AES-GCM       KEK
  policy engine wallet check     signer vendor JS parse      signer account

Five controls, four locations, five mechanisms, five credentials. No single
compromise takes more than two of them. That is genuine depth, and it is why
the fix works.

Counter-example, from the corpus, same attack:

  Control                        Location      Mechanism     Credential
  -----------------------------  ------------  ------------  ---------------
  auth middleware                app host      TypeScript    session
  ownership check in mutation    app host      TypeScript    session
  Zod validation                 app host      TypeScript    session
  rate limit                     app host      TypeScript    session

Four controls. One location, one mechanism, one credential. One layer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LAYER-3  ORDERING: WHICH LAYER SHOULD BE STRONGEST
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Not all layers deserve equal investment. Rank them by what they protect, in
this order, and spend accordingly:

  TIER A — IRREVERSIBLE LOSS. Private keys, fund movement.
           Every control here must be independent of the application host,
           because the application host is the most likely thing to fall.
           This is the signer, the policy engine, HALT, and the treasury
           multisig. Over-invest here.

  TIER B — RECOVERABLE LOSS. User data, session integrity, service integrity.
           Controls may live on the app host, but must be doubled at a second
           location where cheap (RLS at the database, headers at the edge).

  TIER C — AVAILABILITY. Rate limits, DoS resistance, uptime.
           Cheapest to accept partial failure. An outage is survivable; a
           drain is not. When forced to choose, fail toward unavailable.

The corpus inverted this in places: it spent enormous effort on Tier C
controls (kernel tuning, connection limits, sysctl) and had a Tier A control
(the KEK) sitting in a file next to the ciphertext. Effort should follow
consequence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LAYER-4  THE AUDIT PROCEDURE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Run this quarterly, and any time a control is added or removed. It takes about
an hour and it is the only way to know your depth is real.

  STEP 1  List every asset an attacker could compromise (PART 2 has the list).
  STEP 2  For each, write down what it yields with NO other compromise.
  STEP 3  For each attacker objective (PART 3), list every control that must
          fail. Mark any two that share a location, mechanism, credential, AND
          operator — those collapse into one.
  STEP 4  Count the true depth per objective. Anything that reaches depth 1 or
          2 for a Tier A objective is a finding and must be fixed before other
          work.
  STEP 5  Record the result with the date. Depth that decreases between audits
          is the signal you are looking for — it means a control was removed,
          or a new dependency created a shared failure mode.

PART 2 and PART 3 are the current output of this procedure. Re-run them; do
not trust them indefinitely.

================================================================================
PART 2 — THE SINGLE-COMPROMISE MAP
================================================================================

For each asset: what an attacker gets by owning ONLY that, what stops them
going further, and whether it is a single point of failure. This is the honest
answer to "how bad is it if X falls."

Objectives referenced:
  A  steal user private keys      E  persist undetected
  B  move user funds out          F  deny service
  C  destroy user value           G  steal the operator treasury
  D  exfiltrate user data

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 1 — THE APPLICATION HOST (RCE in the Node process, or root on Oracle)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      D (full user data), C (forced swaps within limits), F.
          Read of the request-signing key, so it can ASK the signer to sign.
DOES NOT GET
          A — key material is never on this host, at any point, including
              wallet creation (CTL-107).
          B — the policy engine refuses every top-level SOL and token transfer
              (CTL-102 P3/P4). It can swap; it cannot send.
          G — the treasury is a Squads multisig this system has never seen.
STOPPED BY
          Signer policy engine; signer-side rate limits; HALT; RLS limits what
          a stolen DB session sees to the acting user unless the attacker also
          takes the DB role; canary wallet fires if they enumerate.
DEPTH TO A  3 (signer account + KEK + policy engine — none reachable from here)
DEPTH TO B  2 (policy engine + signer rate limits)
SPOF?     No for A/B/G. Yes for D and F — this is the single point of failure
          for data confidentiality and for uptime, and that is accepted.
NOTE      This is the most likely compromise in the whole list. Everything in
          ADDENDUM O is arranged so that the most likely compromise is not the
          most costly one.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 2 — POSTGRES, READ ACCESS ONLY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      D. Encrypted wallet blobs — which are useless without the KEK.
DOES NOT GET
          A — blobs are AES-GCM sealed under a DEK wrapped by a KEK held at a
              different vendor. No offline attack is available.
STOPPED BY Envelope encryption with AAD binding (CTL-407).
DEPTH TO A  1 more (the signer vendor account). This is RISK-001.
SPOF?     No.
NOTE      This is why the blobs deliberately do NOT live with the KEK. Keep it
          that way. Any future "cache the unwrapped DEK in Redis for
          performance" proposal collapses this to depth 0 and must be refused.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 3 — POSTGRES, WRITE ACCESS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      Everything in ASSET 2, plus the ability to tamper with rows.
ATTEMPTS  Move a victim's ciphertext blob into an attacker-owned wallet row so
          the system signs with the victim's key while every application-layer
          ownership check passes.
STOPPED BY Two independent mechanisms:
          (i)  AAD binds the ciphertext to (userId, walletId, purpose,
               kekVersion). A moved blob fails the GCM tag check and does not
               decrypt (DEF-027).
          (ii) The signer derives the public key from the decrypted secret and
               asserts it equals the declared wallet and the fee payer
               (CTL-102 P1/P6).
DEPTH TO A  2 (AAD + derived-key assertion), both at the signer.
SPOF?     No. But note both blocking mechanisms live at the signer, so they
          share an OPERATOR. Acceptable, because the alternative — checking at
          the app host — is checking at the place the attacker already owns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 4 — THE CLOUDFLARE (SITE) ACCOUNT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      Control of DNS, the proxy, the WAF, the tunnel, and Access policies.
          Can serve malicious JavaScript to every user, which is severe: a
          fake confirmation screen is a real path to user-approved bad actions.
          Can remove the WebAuthn requirement from the Access policy.
DOES NOT GET
          Shell on the host — removing the Access requirement gets an attacker
          to sshd, but sshd requires the resident ed25519-sk key with
          verify-required, which lives on physical hardware the Cloudflare
          account does not hold. Two independent factors: Access gates
          REACHING sshd; the security key gates AUTHENTICATING to it.
          A or B — the signer is at a different vendor (D-1) and requires the
          request-signing key from the host.
STOPPED BY Hardware-key-only MFA on the account with TOTP disabled; Cloudflare
          audit-log alerting on Access policy changes and API token creation
          (CTL-710); the separate SSH factor; the separate signer vendor.
DEPTH TO A  3.
SPOF?     For F (availability) and for frontend integrity, yes. This is the
          largest single concentration in the design and it is the direct cost
          of using one provider for DNS, edge, and remote access. PART 6.4
          states what that buys and what it costs.
NOTE      Because this account is a concentration, its own protection is
          disproportionate: hardware key, no TOTP fallback, no SMS recovery,
          a dedicated email, and audit-log alerts. Treat any unexpected
          authentication as a Tier A incident.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 5 — THE SIGNER VENDOR ACCOUNT (Deno Deploy)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      The KEK. The ability to edit the policy engine — including replacing
          it with "sign anything."
DOES NOT GET
          A or B on its own. There is no ciphertext at the signer. Wallet blobs
          live in Postgres on Oracle. A decryption oracle with nothing to
          decrypt yields nothing.
          It also cannot produce a valid signing request: requests must carry an
          Ed25519 signature from the request key held on the app host.
STOPPED BY The deliberate split of material (blobs stay in Postgres) and the
          split of authority (request signing). Both are load-bearing; neither
          may be "simplified away."
DEPTH TO A  1 more (Postgres read OR app host). This is the other half of
          RISK-001.
SPOF?     For signing availability, yes — if the signer is down, nothing
          trades. That is the intended fail-closed direction.
NOTE      This account is used for nothing else, touched rarely, and protected
          by a hardware key. Its deploy pipeline is manual (PART 4.4), because
          an automated deploy path is an automated compromise path.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 6 — THE OPERATOR'S LAPTOP
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      Browser sessions, source code, whatever is on disk, keylogging, and
          the ability to ride an authenticated session while the operator is
          working.
DOES NOT GET
          Any credential that is hardware-bound: SSH (ed25519-sk,
          verify-required), Cloudflare, Deno Deploy, Oracle, the registrar, the
          password manager. A keylogger captures nothing usable because nothing
          usable is a string (CTL-901).
          The age backup identity, if it is stored per CTL-405 (password
          manager behind a hardware key, plus paper).
STOPPED BY Hardware binding of every credential that matters; short Access
          session duration (1h) limiting ride-along windows; per-use touch on
          the SSH key; admin work isolated per CTL-902.
RESIDUAL  Session ride-along is the real risk: the attacker acts while the
          operator is authenticated. Mitigated by 1-hour Access sessions,
          per-use SSH key touch, and by the fact that the laptop cannot reach
          user keys through any path.
DEPTH TO A  3. This is the correction to the Red Team's closing worry.
SPOF?     No — which is the whole point of ADDENDUM O.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 7 — THE PASSWORD MANAGER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      Recovery codes, API tokens, the age backup identity, account
          passwords.
DOES NOT GET
          Hardware-key second factors. Passwords alone do not authenticate
          anywhere that matters.
STOPPED BY Hardware key as the password manager's second factor; hardware key
          on every account it holds a password for.
SPOF?     Close to it, if hardware second factors were ever removed. This is
          the reason CTL-904 (recovery-path inventory) exists: the password
          manager plus a weak recovery path is a total compromise, and the weak
          recovery path is usually SMS.
ACTION    The age backup identity should ALSO exist on paper, offline, so that
          losing the password manager is not losing the ability to restore.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 8 — THE DOMAIN REGISTRAR
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      The ability to repoint DNS, obtain certificates for the domain, and
          impersonate the site completely.
DOES NOT GET
          A, B, or G. Users can be phished at a convincing fake site, but the
          real system's keys and funds are untouched.
STOPPED BY Registry lock (blocks transfers even with account access); hardware
          MFA; DNSSEC; CT monitoring via crt.sh, which alerts within minutes of
          a certificate being issued for your domain by anyone (CTL-307).
SPOF?     For user-facing trust, effectively yes. CT monitoring is the detection
          layer and it is free — make sure it is actually running and actually
          alerting to a channel you read.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 9 — THE TELEGRAM BOT TOKEN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      The ability to send messages as the bot. That is a phishing channel
          aimed directly at your users, which is not nothing.
DOES NOT GET
          Anything in the application. Inbound webhook authenticity depends on
          the secret token, not the bot token, and Telegram identity is capped
          at Trust Tier 0/1 (ARGUMENT 9).
STOPPED BY The Telegram trust tiers; CTL-802 (no secret, code, or full address
          ever travels over Telegram, so a convincing message cannot ask for
          one because users have been told it never happens); token rotation.
SPOF?     No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 10 — A SINGLE USER'S SESSION COOKIE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      That user's Tier 0/1 capabilities: view balances, trade within
          existing session limits.
DOES NOT GET
          Tier 2/3: raising limits, changing copy targets, adding a withdrawal
          destination, changing security settings. All require passkey
          re-authentication, which a cookie cannot satisfy.
STOPPED BY Passkey re-auth on Tier 2/3; session rotation with reuse detection;
          RLS scoping; signer session policy caps.
SPOF?     No. This is the correct outcome: stealing a session should let you
          annoy one user, not drain them.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 11 — AN NPM DEPENDENCY IN THE APPLICATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      Equivalent to ASSET 1 (app host RCE), with the same bounds.
STOPPED BY Everything that bounds ASSET 1, plus `npm ci --ignore-scripts`,
          exact pinning, `npm audit signatures`, and the reviewed
          install-script allowlist.
SPOF?     No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 12 — A DEPENDENCY IN THE SIGNER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      EVERYTHING. A malicious dependency inside the signer runs in the
          process that holds the KEK and performs the signing. It can exfiltrate
          keys, or silently sign an attacker's transaction while returning a
          plausible response.
STOPPED BY Nothing, once it is there. This is the one place in the architecture
          with no meaningful second layer.
SPOF?     YES. Unambiguously. This is the most important finding in PART 2.
ACTION    The signer must have ZERO install-time dependencies. Crypto source is
          vendored into the repository, hash-pinned, and reviewed line by line.
          The dependency count is a tracked security metric (CTL-111). See
          PART 4.3.
NOTE      This is a good example of the independence test doing real work: the
          signer's depth is excellent against every external attack and is
          exactly 1 against its own supply chain. Depth is per-path, never
          global.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 13 — AN UPSTREAM API (Helius, Jupiter)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      The ability to return bad quotes, bad routes, or false confirmations.
DOES NOT GET
          A or B. The signer's program allowlist means a malicious route
          through an unknown program is refused. Bad quotes are bounded by
          slippage and by `otherAmountThreshold` enforced on-chain.
STOPPED BY Program allowlist (CTL-102 P2); slippage and minimum-output
          enforcement; content verification of confirmations at the right
          commitment level (DEF-045); server-to-server SPKI pinning (CTL-307).
SPOF?     For availability, partially — mitigated by the provider pool.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSET 14 — THE ORACLE CLOUD TENANCY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GETS      Serial console access to the host, the ability to snapshot the boot
          volume, and the ability to destroy the instance.
DOES NOT GET
          A or B — a boot volume snapshot contains the database and the
          request-signing key, which together equal ASSET 1 + ASSET 2, still
          short of the KEK.
STOPPED BY Hardware MFA on the Oracle account; the signer at a separate vendor;
          off-box immutable backups so instance destruction is recoverable.
SPOF?     For availability, yes. See RISK-011 and PART 7.2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY OF THE MAP
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Objective                       Minimum compromises required
  ------------------------------  ---------------------------------------------
  A  steal user private keys      2  (signer vendor + [app host OR Postgres])
                                     — or 1, via a signer dependency (ASSET 12)
  B  move user funds out          2  (same as A) — the policy engine means even
                                     app-host compromise alone cannot transfer
  C  destroy user value           1  (app host) — bounded, rate-limited, alarmed
  D  exfiltrate user data         1  (app host or Postgres)
  E  persist undetected           1  (app host) but detection is off-box, so
                                     persistence does not mean invisibility
  F  deny service                 1  (app host, Cloudflare, Oracle, or signer)
  G  steal operator treasury      not reachable from this system at all

The two numbers that matter: A and B both require two independent vendors to
fail. C and D require one. That asymmetry is deliberate — it puts the depth
where the loss is irreversible, and accepts depth 1 where recovery is possible.

The one place the map is unacceptable is ASSET 12, and PART 4.3 fixes it.

================================================================================
PART 3 — KILL CHAINS: WHAT MUST FAIL, IN ORDER
================================================================================

PART 2 asked "what does owning X give you." This part asks the inverse: for
each thing an attacker wants, what is the complete list of controls that must
fail, and are they genuinely independent?

Read the LOC / MECH / CRED columns as the independence audit. Two rows sharing
all three collapse into one layer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAIN A — STEAL A USER'S PRIVATE KEY
Tier A. Irreversible. The chain that matters most.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  #  Control that must fail                LOC        MECH        CRED
  -  ------------------------------------  ---------  ----------  -------------
  1  Cloudflare edge (WAF, TLS, origin     edge       proxy       CF account
     hiding, origin-pull cert)
  2  Origin firewall: UFW + DOCKER-USER    host net   iptables    host root
     + Oracle security list
  3  Container boundary: non-root,         host       namespaces  host root
     read-only, cap_drop ALL, distroless
  4  App authorization: protectedProcedure app        TypeScript  session
     + ownership + trust tier
  5  Postgres RLS (ENABLE + FORCE)         database   SQL policy  DB role
  6  Envelope encryption AAD binding       signer     AES-GCM     KEK
  7  Signer request signature              signer     Ed25519     request key
     (Ed25519 over canonical request)                             (on host)
  8  Signer rate limits + revocation       signer     KV state    signer acct
  9  KEK confidentiality                   signer     secret      signer acct
 10  Policy engine wallet/fee-payer        signer     JS parse    signer acct
     assertion

  TRUE DEPTH: rows 8, 9, 10 share LOC and CRED (signer account) — count as one.
  Rows 2 and 3 share CRED (host root) — count as one.
  Collapsed: edge / host / app / database / AAD-KEK / request-key / signer-acct
  = SIX independent layers, spanning THREE operators (you, Cloudflare, Deno).

  SHORTEST REAL PATH: skip 1-5 entirely by stealing the Postgres blobs (ASSET
  2), then compromise the signer vendor account. Two compromises, two vendors.
  That is RISK-001 and it is the design's floor.

  THE ONE-STEP PATH: a malicious dependency inside the signer (ASSET 12).
  Depth 1. Fixed by PART 4.3 and nothing else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAIN B — MOVE USER FUNDS TO AN ATTACKER ADDRESS
Tier A. This is the chain the policy engine was built for.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume the attacker already has full app-host RCE — the most likely single
compromise. They now try to construct a transaction that sends value out.

  Attempt                                  Refused by            Reason string
  ---------------------------------------  --------------------  ---------------
  SystemProgram::Transfer to attacker      CTL-102 P3            sol_transfer_to_
                                                                 unapproved
  Inflate the Helius tip to drain SOL      CTL-102 P3 tip cap    tip_exceeds_cap
  Top-level SPL Transfer / TransferChecked CTL-102 P4            top_level_token_ix
  Approve a delegate, drain later          CTL-102 P4            top_level_token_ix
  SetAuthority on the token account        CTL-102 P4            top_level_token_ix
  CloseAccount with attacker as lamport    CTL-102 P4            close_account_to_
  destination                                                    third_party
  Route through an attacker-controlled     CTL-102 P2            program_not_allowed
  program
  Hide the program ID in a lookup table    CTL-102 P2 + parser   program_id_outside_
                                           returns null          static_keys
  Sign for a different user's wallet       CTL-102 P1 + P6       wallet_id_mismatch /
                                           + AAD (DEF-027)       decrypt failure
  Declare an honest-looking request and    CTL-102 P8            undeclared_program_
  send a hostile transaction                                     present
  Withdraw to a new address                CTL-605 allowlist     withdraw_destination_
                                           + 24h maturity        not_allowlisted
  Grind attempts until one passes          CTL-102 P6 rate       429 + CTL-706
                                           limits + velocity     auto-HALT
                                           auto-HALT

  RESULT: with full app-host compromise, CHAIN B does not complete. Every
  refusal is generated at the signer, which the attacker does not control, and
  every refusal is a high-signal alert (CTL-709) because a correct client never
  produces one.

  WHAT REMAINS: CHAIN C.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAIN C — DESTROY USER VALUE WITHOUT TRANSFERRING IT
Tier A consequence, depth 1. The honest residual.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The attacker cannot send funds out, so they force swaps into a token they
created and then rug it. Economically this is theft; structurally it is not,
which is why the policy engine does not catch it.

  Bound                                   Control          Effect
  --------------------------------------  ---------------  ---------------------
  Per-wallet signing rate limit           CTL-102 P6       caps swaps per hour
  Session policy allowed/denied mints     CTL-604          the mint list is
                                                           written by the USER,
                                                           not the app host
  Output-mint sellability probe           CTL-602          a token with no route
                                                           back to SOL is refused
                                                           before the swap
  Loss circuit breaker                    ADDENDUM C       halts on rolling loss
  Velocity auto-HALT                      CTL-706          3x baseline stops
                                                           everything globally
  Time to contain                         CTL-713          target under 60s from
                                                           detection

  DEPTH: 1 to start the attack, but the attacker's yield is a function of TIME,
  and every bound above is a time bound. This is why CTL-713 (time-to-contain)
  is a real control here and not a metric. Halving TTC halves the loss.

  STATED PLAINLY: this is RISK-002. It is not solved. It is bounded and loud.
  Users should be told this in plain language rather than sold "non-custodial"
  as if it meant "cannot be harmed."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAIN D — EXFILTRATE USER DATA
Tier B. Depth 1 by design.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

App host or Postgres read gives user data. There is no second layer, and
adding one would cost more than it is worth for this data class.

  What is exposed:   identities, balances, positions, trade history, Telegram
                     IDs, email addresses.
  What is NOT:       private keys (encrypted, KEK elsewhere), passwords
                     (Argon2id), passkey credentials (public keys only), MFA
                     secrets (encrypted and never serialized, DEF-054),
                     withdrawal allowlists (held at the signer, not in Postgres).

  ACCEPTED with three compensations, all cheap:
    - Data minimization: do not store what you do not need. No phone numbers,
      no addresses, no KYC documents unless a regulator forces it — and if one
      does, that is a different architecture conversation, not a column.
    - The audit log records reads of sensitive tables so an exfiltration leaves
      a trace (CTL-703), anchored off-box so the trace cannot be erased.
    - The decoy user row (CTL-707): a user record whose email address is
      monitored and used nowhere else. Mail arriving at it is proof of
      exfiltration, with a zero false-positive rate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAIN E — PERSIST UNDETECTED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Attacker action                     Detected by              Independent of
                                                               the host?
  ----------------------------------  -----------------------  ---------------
  Modify a binary or config           AIDE with off-box        YES
                                      baseline comparison
  Add a cron job or systemd unit      auditd rules on          Partly — the
                                      /etc/cron.d,             rules are on-host
                                      /etc/systemd/system      but logs ship off
  Load a kernel module                auditd init_module rule  Partly
  Delete or rewrite logs              off-box shipping +       YES
                                      daily anchored root hash
  Rewrite the audit chain             external anchor          YES
                                      mismatch (CTL-708)
  Enumerate wallets                   canary wallet (CTL-707)  YES — the signer
                                                               detects it
  Sit quietly and wait                canary + anchor +        YES
                                      periodic restore drill

  KEY PROPERTY: every detection that matters is verified OFF the compromised
  host. An attacker with root can silence local logging; they cannot un-send
  yesterday's anchored root hash, and they cannot stop the signer from noticing
  a canary. This is the independence test applied to detection, and it is the
  reason CTL-702 (ship logs off-box within seconds) is not optional.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAIN F — DENY SERVICE
Tier C. Depth 1 in several places. Accepted.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Any one of: app host down, Cloudflare down, Oracle reclaims the instance,
  Deno Deploy down, Postgres corrupted, Redis down (auth fails closed).

  ACCEPTED because the alternative — failing open to preserve uptime — trades
  an inconvenience for a loss. The design deliberately fails toward
  unavailable. What is NOT accepted is slow recovery, which is why PART 8
  specifies the runbook and PART 7 specifies the free availability measures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAIN G — STEAL THE OPERATOR TREASURY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Not reachable. The treasury is a Squads multisig with hardware signers, on
addresses this system has never seen and cannot construct (CTL-903). There is
no code path, no environment variable, and no database row connecting them.

This is worth stating explicitly because it is the cheapest control in the
entire document — it costs nothing, it takes an afternoon, and it removes the
largest single number from the threat model. If only one thing from these two
addenda gets done this week, make it this one.

================================================================================
PART 3.5 — WHERE THE DEPTH IS THIN
================================================================================

An honest register of the places where layering is nominal rather than real.
These are the findings from running the LAYER-4 audit on the current design.

  FINDING P-1  [must fix]  SIGNER SUPPLY CHAIN IS DEPTH 1
      A malicious or compromised dependency inside the signer defeats every
      other control at once. Fix: zero install-time dependencies, vendored and
      hash-pinned crypto, manual review. PART 4.3. This is a Gate 1 blocker.

  FINDING P-2  [must fix]  SIGNER DEPLOY PIPELINE IS DEPTH 1
      Anything that can deploy to the signer can replace the policy engine. An
      automated CI deploy with a stored token means the CI system is now a
      Tier A asset. Fix: manual deploy only, hardware-key gated, with the
      deployed hash recorded and verified. PART 4.4.

  FINDING P-3  [accepted]  THREE SIGNER CONTROLS SHARE ONE CREDENTIAL
      The KEK, the rate limits, the revocation state, and the policy engine all
      live behind the signer vendor account. They are one layer, not four.
      Accepted: the alternative is enforcing them at the app host, which is the
      place most likely to be compromised. Better to have one strong layer in a
      safe place than four weak ones in a dangerous one.

  FINDING P-4  [accepted]  CLOUDFLARE IS A CONCENTRATION
      DNS, edge, WAF, tunnel, and Access are one account. See PART 6.4 for what
      that buys and the compensating controls. The SSH hardware key is the
      factor that keeps it from being depth 0 to the host.

  FINDING P-5  [monitor]  THE OPERATOR IS A SINGLE HUMAN
      One person holds every hardware key and every recovery path. Illness,
      travel, or a lost bag is an availability event with no second operator.
      Free mitigations: two hardware keys with one stored off-site; printed
      recovery codes in a second physical location; a written runbook a
      technical friend could follow; and — when there is a second person —
      splitting the signer account from the edge account across two humans.

  FINDING P-6  [monitor]  DETECTION DEPENDS ON THE OPERATOR READING ALERTS
      Every off-box detection ends at a Telegram channel and an email. If the
      operator is asleep, TTC is hours. Free mitigation: the auto-HALT triggers
      (CTL-705/706/707/709) do not require a human — they are the reason TTC
      can be under a minute for the highest-signal events. Anything not on the
      auto-HALT list has human-latency TTC, and that should inform which
      detectors get promoted to auto-HALT.

================================================================================
PART 4 — THE SIGNER MOVES OFF CLOUDFLARE
================================================================================

Decision D-1. ADDENDUM O's signer becomes a Deno Deploy application. Everything
about the protocol, the policy engine, and the parser is unchanged — those were
written against a small runtime surface precisely so this move would be cheap.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.1  WHY A DIFFERENT VENDOR, NOT JUST A DIFFERENT ACCOUNT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ADDENDUM O ARGUMENT 2 required three separations: material (blobs stay in
Postgres), authority (requests are signed), and account. The account separation
was the weakest of the three, because two accounts at one vendor share:

  - one company's security posture and one company's breach
  - one support organization, therefore one social-engineering path
  - one outage, therefore correlated availability
  - one legal/compliance action, therefore correlated account termination
  - one set of platform-wide policy changes

Moving to a second vendor upgrades that separation from "two accounts" to "two
companies." The cost is one more account in the CTL-904 recovery-path
inventory, which is real but small, and one more free tier to monitor for
changes.

There is a second, less obvious benefit. Cloudflare already holds an enormous
amount in this design — DNS, edge, WAF, tunnel, remote access (FINDING P-4).
Adding the KEK to that account would have made a Cloudflare compromise close to
total. Moving the signer out means the largest concentration in the system does
not also hold the keys.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.2  DENO DEPLOY: WHY IT FITS, AND ITS LIMITS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

WHY IT FITS
  - Free tier is comfortably sufficient: 1M requests/month, 20GB egress, 15
    hours of CPU time per month, 350 GB-h memory, 1 GiB Deno KV storage with
    450,000 read units and 300,000 write units per month, 5 team members.
    Phase 0 signing volume is in the hundreds to low thousands per day. Three
    orders of magnitude of headroom on requests.
  - Deno KV replaces Cloudflare KV for HALT, revocation, rate counters, session
    policies, withdrawal allowlists, and request dedupe. Same shape, same code
    structure.
  - Generally available since 5 February 2026, not beta.
  - Web-standard APIs (`fetch`, `Request`, `Response`, `crypto.subtle`), so the
    Worker code ports with an adapter rather than a rewrite.
  - Far more generous CPU allowance than Workers' 10ms-per-request, which
    removes the tightest constraint on the policy engine. Keep the minimal
    parser anyway — it is a security asset, not just a performance one.

LIMITS, STATED HONESTLY
  - No SLA and community-only support on the free tier. If the signer is down,
    trading is down and there is nobody to call. This is the fail-closed
    direction and it is intentional, but it must be communicated to users as an
    availability characteristic, not discovered by them during an outage.
  - 1-day log retention on free. Therefore the signer MUST ship its own signing
    log off-platform (CTL-702) rather than relying on the vendor's. This was
    already required; the short retention makes it non-negotiable.
  - 512MB memory ceiling per application. Irrelevant here — the signer's
    working set is a few kilobytes.
  - Free tiers change. That is precisely why CTL-110 exists.

VERIFY BEFORE BUILDING
  - Ed25519 support in Deno's `crypto.subtle` for `importKey`/`sign`/`verify`.
    It is not clearly enumerated in the public API reference. Do not assume it.
    Run the probe in 4.3 first. If it is absent or awkward, the vendored
    implementation is used — which is the recommended path regardless.
  - Deno KV availability and current quotas on the GA platform.
  - Whether Deno Deploy exposes the deployed artifact hash for verification
    (needed by CTL-112).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.3  CTL-110 / CTL-111 — THE PORTABILITY CONTRACT AND THE ZERO-DEPENDENCY RULE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This section fixes FINDING P-1, which is the only depth-1 path to the keys.

THE RULE
    The signer has ZERO install-time dependencies. Not "few." Zero.
    No `npm install`. No `deno add`. No remote imports resolved at deploy time.
    All cryptographic code is vendored into the repository as reviewed source,
    hash-pinned, and imported by relative path.

WHY THIS IS NOT PARANOIA
  Every other component in this system has a second layer behind it. The signer
  does not: code running inside the signer process holds the KEK and performs
  the signing. A single malicious dependency version, published at 3am to a
  package the signer imports transitively, defeats the policy engine, the rate
  limits, the AAD binding, and HALT simultaneously — because it runs inside all
  of them. There is no control that catches this after the fact.
  The dependency count of the signer IS its attack surface, and it is the one
  number in this architecture that should be zero.

WHAT GETS VENDORED
  - Ed25519 sign/verify. Either `@noble/ed25519` source (small, auditable,
    single-purpose, widely reviewed) copied into `signer/vendor/ed25519.ts`, or
    `crypto.subtle` if the runtime supports it natively — which is better still,
    because then there is no vendored crypto at all.
  - Base58 encode/decode. About 40 lines. Write it; do not import it.
  - The compact-u16 / message parser from ADDENDUM O CTL-103. Already
    dependency-free.
  - AES-GCM: use `crypto.subtle`. Universally available, no vendoring needed.

RUNTIME PROBE — run this first, on Deno Deploy, before writing anything else:
```typescript
// signer/probe.ts — determines whether any vendoring is required at all.
const results: Record<string, unknown> = {};

// 1. Ed25519 via WebCrypto?
try {
  const kp = await crypto.subtle.generateKey("Ed25519", true, ["sign", "verify"]);
  const sig = await crypto.subtle.sign("Ed25519", (kp as CryptoKeyPair).privateKey,
                                        new TextEncoder().encode("probe"));
  results.ed25519_webcrypto = sig.byteLength === 64;
} catch (e) { results.ed25519_webcrypto = `unsupported: ${e}`; }

// 2. Raw private key import (needed to load the wallet secret)?
try {
  const raw = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32));
  await crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", raw, "Ed25519", false, ["sign"]);
  results.ed25519_raw_import = true;
} catch (e) { results.ed25519_raw_import = `unsupported: ${e}`; }

// 3. AES-GCM with a 96-bit nonce and AAD?
try {
  const key = await crypto.subtle.generateKey({ name: "AES-GCM", length: 256 },
                                              true, ["encrypt", "decrypt"]);
  const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12));
  const aad = new TextEncoder().encode("ctx");
  const ct = await crypto.subtle.encrypt({ name: "AES-GCM", iv, additionalData: aad },
                                          key, new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]));
  await crypto.subtle.decrypt({ name: "AES-GCM", iv, additionalData: aad }, key, ct);
  results.aes_gcm_aad = true;
} catch (e) { results.aes_gcm_aad = `unsupported: ${e}`; }

console.log(JSON.stringify(results, null, 2));
```
  If `ed25519_webcrypto` and `ed25519_raw_import` are both true, vendor nothing
  and use `crypto.subtle` throughout. That is the ideal outcome: a signer whose
  entire cryptographic surface is the platform's own, with zero third-party
  code of any kind.
  If raw import is unsupported, note that Solana secret keys are 64 bytes
  (secret seed || public key); the seed is the first 32. Try PKCS#8 wrapping of
  the 32-byte seed before concluding it cannot be done.

CTL-111 — DEPENDENCY BUDGET AS A TRACKED METRIC
```
signer/DEPENDENCIES.md must exist and must read, in full:

    Install-time dependencies: 0
    Vendored source files: <list, with sha256 of each, and the reviewer's
                            initials and date>
    Platform APIs used: crypto.subtle, Deno.openKv, fetch, Request, Response

CI check (TEST-P01): fail the build if signer/ contains package.json,
deno.json with an "imports" map pointing at a remote registry, node_modules/,
any `import ... from "https://..."`, or any `import ... from "npm:..."`.
Fail if any vendored file's sha256 differs from DEPENDENCIES.md.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.4  CTL-112 — MANUAL, VERIFIED DEPLOYMENT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This fixes FINDING P-2.

  RULE: the signer is deployed manually, from the admin machine, authenticated
  by hardware key. There is no CI deploy token for the signer anywhere.

  Rationale: a CI system with deploy rights to the signer becomes a Tier A
  asset — anything that compromises CI can replace the policy engine with
  `return sign(everything)` and the change is invisible to every other control.
  A CI pipeline is exactly the kind of thing that gets a token stored in it, a
  third-party action added to it, and a dependency updated in it. Keep it away
  from the one component with no second layer.

  PROCEDURE, every deploy:
```bash
# 1. Clean checkout at a specific commit. Never deploy from a dirty tree.
git -C signer status --porcelain   # must be empty
git -C signer rev-parse HEAD       # record this

# 2. Verify vendored file hashes against DEPENDENCIES.md.
./scripts/verify-signer-vendor.sh

# 3. Compute the artifact hash of exactly what will be uploaded.
find signer -type f -name '*.ts' | sort | xargs sha256sum | sha256sum

# 4. Deploy, authenticated by hardware key.
deployctl deploy --project=osiris-signer --prod signer/main.ts

# 5. Verify the running code answers with the expected build id.
curl -s https://<signer-host>/version   # returns { commit, artifactHash }
#    Assert it matches steps 1 and 3.

# 6. Append commit, artifact hash, timestamp, and deployer to the audit log.
#    A signer deploy is a Tier A event and must be visible in the anchored
#    chain (CTL-703).
```

  DETECTION: a nightly job calls `/version` and compares against the last
  recorded deploy. A mismatch means the signer was deployed by something other
  than the documented procedure. CRITICAL alert, auto-HALT. This makes an
  unauthorized signer deploy loud even though the deploy path itself has no
  second layer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.5  THE STORAGE ADAPTER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

One interface, so the signer can move vendors in an afternoon. Under strict $0
with free tiers that change without notice, portability is an availability
control, not a nicety: a vendor that discontinues its free tier must not be
able to force a rushed migration of the component that holds your keys.

```typescript
// signer/storage.ts — the ONLY storage surface the signer uses.
export interface SignerStore {
  get(key: string): Promise<string | null>;
  /** ttlSeconds is required on every write. Nothing in the signer is stored
   *  forever; unbounded state is how a free tier quota becomes an outage. */
  put(key: string, value: string, ttlSeconds: number): Promise<void>;
  /** Atomic set-if-absent. Used for request dedupe and for rate-limit windows.
   *  MUST be genuinely atomic — a read-then-write implementation is bypassable
   *  by concurrency, which is what an attacker sends. */
  putIfAbsent(key: string, value: string, ttlSeconds: number): Promise<boolean>;
  /** Atomic counter for rate limiting. */
  increment(key: string, ttlSeconds: number): Promise<number>;
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>;
}
```
```typescript
// signer/storage.deno.ts
const kv = await Deno.openKv();

export const store: SignerStore = {
  async get(key) {
    const r = await kv.get<string>(["s", key]);
    return r.value ?? null;
  },
  async put(key, value, ttlSeconds) {
    await kv.set(["s", key], value, { expireIn: ttlSeconds * 1000 });
  },
  async putIfAbsent(key, value, ttlSeconds) {
    // Deno KV atomic with a versionstamp precondition of null == "only if the
    // key does not exist". This is the atomicity the interface requires.
    const res = await kv.atomic()
      .check({ key: ["s", key], versionstamp: null })
      .set(["s", key], value, { expireIn: ttlSeconds * 1000 })
      .commit();
    return res.ok;
  },
  async increment(key, ttlSeconds) {
    for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
      const cur = await kv.get<number>(["s", key]);
      const next = (cur.value ?? 0) + 1;
      const res = await kv.atomic()
        .check(cur)                                   // optimistic concurrency
        .set(["s", key], next, { expireIn: ttlSeconds * 1000 })
        .commit();
      if (res.ok) return next;
    }
    // Contention beyond 5 attempts under a rate limiter means something
    // abnormal. Fail CLOSED: the caller treats a throw as "limit exceeded".
    throw new Error("store_contention");
  },
  async delete(key) { await kv.delete(["s", key]); },
};
```
Adapters for Cloudflare KV, Upstash Redis, or DynamoDB are each about thirty
lines. Write the Cloudflare one at the same time as the Deno one and keep it in
the repo unused — a migration path you have never compiled is not a migration
path.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.6  WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Unchanged from ADDENDUM O, verbatim:
  - The `SigningRequest` protocol and `canonicalize()`      (CTL-101)
  - The policy engine and all its rules P1-P8               (CTL-102)
  - The minimal message parser                              (CTL-103)
  - HALT semantics and triggers                             (CTL-105)
  - KEK rotation                                            (CTL-106)
  - Wallet generation inside the signer                     (CTL-107)
  - The triple-gated local signer                           (CTL-108)
  - The request-signing key as the only host-side secret    (CTL-109)
  - The full TEST-111 policy table and all SUITE 1 tests

Changed only:
  - `env.KV` becomes `store` from 4.5.
  - `wrangler secret put` becomes Deno Deploy environment variables set through
    the dashboard, hardware-key authenticated. The KEK is set once and never
    read back.
  - `wrangler.toml` becomes `deno.json` with no import map.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.7  MIGRATION CHECK BEFORE MAINNET
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [ ] Probe (4.3) run on Deno Deploy; result recorded in the repo.
  [ ] Zero install-time dependencies; DEPENDENCIES.md present; TEST-P01 green.
  [ ] Full SUITE 1 from ADDENDUM O passes against the Deno-hosted signer,
      including every row of the TEST-111 policy table.
  [ ] Manual deploy procedure executed and the /version endpoint verified.
  [ ] HALT tested end-to-end from a phone: set, confirm signing stops within
      one second, clear, confirm recovery.
  [ ] Deno Deploy account: hardware key MFA, no SMS recovery, dedicated email,
      added to the CTL-904 recovery-path inventory.
  [ ] Signing log ships off-platform (1-day vendor retention is not retention).
  [ ] Cloudflare KV adapter written and compiling, as the tested escape hatch.

================================================================================
PART 5 — HTTPS: YES, AND THE PART THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS
================================================================================

Short answer: yes, HTTPS everywhere, no exceptions, and it is already required
by ADDENDUM O (CTL-303, CTL-308). But "do we have HTTPS" is not the question
that determines whether you are safe. Every phishing site has HTTPS. The
padlock means the connection is encrypted to *whoever answered*, not that
whoever answered is you.

The three questions that actually matter:

  1. Is the leg between Cloudflare and your origin also encrypted?
     (This is where people get quietly burned. See 5.1.)
  2. Is the origin's certificate validated, so Cloudflare cannot be tricked
     into connecting to an impostor origin?
  3. Can an attacker reach the origin directly and skip the encrypted path
     entirely?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.1  CTL-310 — THE FLEXIBLE MODE TRAP
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cloudflare has five SSL/TLS encryption modes. Two of them mean the connection
between Cloudflare and your server is plaintext, while the user's browser still
shows a padlock.

  Mode                      Browser→CF   CF→Origin      Origin cert validated
  ------------------------  -----------  -------------  ---------------------
  Off                       plaintext    plaintext      no
  Flexible                  encrypted    PLAINTEXT      no
  Full                      encrypted    encrypted      NO
  Full (Strict)             encrypted    encrypted      yes
  Strict (SSL-Only Pull)    encrypted    encrypted      yes, always HTTPS

  REQUIRED FOR OSIRIS: Full (Strict). Nothing less. Ever.

WHY FLEXIBLE IS DISQUALIFYING HERE
  Flexible is the default a lot of people land on because it "just works"
  without configuring a certificate on the origin. What it means concretely:
  session cookies, trade instructions, and every API response travel in
  cleartext across the public internet between Cloudflare's edge and your
  Oracle instance. Anyone positioned on that path — a compromised transit
  network, another tenant with a network position, an Oracle-side observer —
  reads and can modify everything. The user sees a padlock the entire time.
  For a system that carries session cookies authorizing trades, this is a total
  failure of transport security dressed as success.

WHY FULL IS ALSO NOT ENOUGH
  Full encrypts the origin leg but does not validate the origin certificate.
  Cloudflare will happily connect to anything presenting any certificate,
  including a self-signed one held by an attacker who has managed to get in the
  path or to hijack the origin's address. It stops passive eavesdropping and
  not active interception. For Tier A traffic, validation is the point.

CONFIGURATION
```
Cloudflare dashboard → SSL/TLS → Overview
  Encryption mode: Full (strict)

Cloudflare dashboard → SSL/TLS → Edge Certificates
  Always Use HTTPS:              ON
  Minimum TLS Version:           TLS 1.2   (1.3 preferred; 1.2 for compat)
  Opportunistic Encryption:      ON
  TLS 1.3:                       ON
  Automatic HTTPS Rewrites:      ON
  Certificate Transparency Monitoring: ON

Cloudflare dashboard → SSL/TLS → Origin Server
  Authenticated Origin Pulls (zone-level): ON     ← see 5.3
```
VERIFY, do not trust the dashboard toggle:
```bash
# From outside: the public path must be TLS 1.2+ and present the CF cert.
openssl s_client -connect osiris.trade:443 -tls1_2 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | head -20
# Must FAIL (TLS 1.0/1.1 disabled):
openssl s_client -connect osiris.trade:443 -tls1_1 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -q "no protocols available\|alert" && echo "TLS1.1 correctly refused"

# From the origin's perspective: Caddy must be serving TLS, not plain HTTP.
curl -sk https://127.0.0.1:443 -H "Host: osiris.trade" -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n'
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.2  CTL-311 — THE ORIGIN CERTIFICATE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full (Strict) requires a valid certificate on the origin. Two options; the
first is better for this architecture.

OPTION A — CLOUDFLARE ORIGIN CA CERTIFICATE  (recommended)
  A certificate issued by Cloudflare's private CA, valid up to 15 years, and
  trusted only by Cloudflare. It is not publicly trusted, which is exactly
  right: the origin should only ever be spoken to by Cloudflare.
```
Cloudflare dashboard → SSL/TLS → Origin Server → Create Certificate
  Hostnames: osiris.trade, *.osiris.trade
  Validity:  15 years
  Key type:  ECC (P-256)
  → save the certificate and private key to the origin
```
```caddyfile
osiris.trade {
    tls /etc/caddy/origin-cert.pem /etc/caddy/origin-key.pem {
        client_auth {
            mode                 require_and_verify
            trusted_ca_cert_file /etc/caddy/cloudflare-origin-pull-ca.pem
        }
    }
    # ... headers, rate_limit, reverse_proxy per ADDENDUM O CTL-303/305
}
```
```bash
chown root:caddy /etc/caddy/origin-key.pem
chmod 640 /etc/caddy/origin-key.pem
```
  ADVANTAGES over Let's Encrypt here:
    - No 60-90 day renewal cycle, so no renewal failure mode. A Let's Encrypt
      renewal that fails at 3am on a system with `Full (Strict)` takes the site
      down; a 15-year cert does not.
    - No ACME challenge surface on the origin at all.
    - No public CT log entry pointing at your origin.
    - No Let's Encrypt rate limits to manage.
  DISADVANTAGE: the certificate is worthless if you ever stop using Cloudflare,
  and it cannot be used to serve users directly. Given the design requires
  Cloudflare in front (5.4), that is not a real cost — but write it in the
  runbook so a future migration is not a surprise.

OPTION B — LET'S ENCRYPT VIA DNS-01
  Use if you want the origin to hold a publicly trusted certificate. Caddy
  automates it with the Cloudflare DNS plugin (already in the xcaddy build from
  ADDENDUM O DEF-008). DNS-01 rather than HTTP-01, because HTTP-01 requires the
  origin to be publicly reachable on port 80, which contradicts CTL-302.
  Requires a scoped Cloudflare API token (Zone:DNS:Edit on one zone only) on
  the origin — which is a credential on the box, so Option A is cleaner.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.3  AUTHENTICATED ORIGIN PULLS — THE PART PEOPLE SKIP
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full (Strict) proves to Cloudflare that your origin is your origin. It does
nothing to prove to your origin that the client is Cloudflare.

Without Authenticated Origin Pulls, anyone who discovers your origin IP — via
DNS history, certificate transparency, a leaked email header, a Shodan scan of
the Oracle range — can connect directly, bypassing the WAF, the rate limiting,
the bot protection, and every custom rule. Every edge control becomes optional
from the attacker's point of view.

AOP makes Cloudflare present a client certificate, and Caddy refuses any
connection that does not present it. Combined with the UFW rule accepting
443 only from Cloudflare ranges (CTL-302a), that is two independent mechanisms
— a packet filter and a TLS handshake — with different failure modes. If the
Cloudflare IP list goes stale and UFW starts accepting a new range, AOP still
rejects impostors. If a rule is fumbled during a config change, the other holds.

```bash
# Fetch Cloudflare's origin-pull CA and pin it in the repo.
curl -fsSL https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/static/authenticated_origin_pull_ca.pem \
  -o /etc/caddy/cloudflare-origin-pull-ca.pem
sha256sum /etc/caddy/cloudflare-origin-pull-ca.pem   # record in the repo
chmod 644 /etc/caddy/cloudflare-origin-pull-ca.pem
```
```bash
# TEST-P02 — prove it works. From any non-Cloudflare host:
curl -sv --resolve osiris.trade:443:<ORIGIN_IP> https://osiris.trade/ 2>&1 \
  | grep -qi "alert certificate required\|handshake failure" \
  && echo "PASS: origin refuses non-Cloudflare clients"
```
This test must be run from outside the Oracle VCN, and it must be run again
after any Caddy or Cloudflare TLS change. It is the single highest-value
five-second check in the whole edge configuration.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.4  HSTS — CORRECT, BUT DO IT SLOWLY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Reaffirming ADDENDUM O CTL-308 and DEF-016, because this is the one HTTPS
setting that cannot be undone quickly.

```
Week 1:  Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=300
Week 2:  max-age=86400; includeSubDomains        ← audit every subdomain first
Week 3:  max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
Week 4:  max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload   → submit to
                                                          hstspreload.org
```
Precondition for week 2: every DNS record in the zone resolves to something
serving valid HTTPS. Precondition for week 4: acceptance that no subdomain will
ever need plain HTTP, because removal from the preload list takes months and
never reaches users who do not update their browser.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.5  WHAT HTTPS DOES NOT DO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Worth stating because "we have HTTPS" is often where transport-security
thinking stops:

  - It does not tell the user they are on the real site. A phishing domain has
    a padlock too. That is what CT monitoring, DNSSEC, registry lock, and user
    education about bookmarks are for (CTL-307, ADDENDUM O EP-BONUS).
  - It does not protect against a compromised frontend. If the app host serves
    malicious JavaScript, it serves it over a perfectly valid TLS connection.
    That is what CSP, Trusted Types, and SRI are for.
  - It does not protect against a malicious browser extension, which sits
    inside the TLS boundary by design.
  - It does not authenticate the API caller. That is sessions, passkeys, and
    origin checks.
  - It does not protect data at rest anywhere.

HTTPS is table stakes. It is the floor, correctly configured, and then the
interesting work happens above it.

================================================================================
PART 6 — SHOULD YOU USE CLOUDFLARE, OR IS THERE A BETTER FREE OPTION?
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.1  WHAT YOU ARE ACTUALLY BUYING
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The question is usually asked as "which free host/CDN," but that is not what
this architecture needs from Cloudflare. Under ADDENDUM O ARGUMENT 11 the site
is server-rendered from Caddy on Oracle, so nobody is hosting your frontend but
you. What Cloudflare provides is six distinct things, and four of them are
load-bearing security controls rather than performance features:

  1. DNS with DNSSEC                          (integrity of name resolution)
  2. Reverse proxy that HIDES THE ORIGIN IP    ← load-bearing
  3. WAF custom rules + bot protection + DDoS absorption
  4. Authenticated Origin Pulls                ← load-bearing (5.3)
  5. Cloudflare Tunnel — removes SSH from the internet   ← load-bearing (EP-1)
  6. Cloudflare Access — WebAuthn-gated admin access     ← load-bearing (EP-1)
  Plus: Universal SSL, and R2 for off-box artifacts.

Items 2, 4, 5, and 6 are why the answer is Cloudflare. A pure CDN does not
replace them.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.2  THE ALTERNATIVES, HONESTLY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PROVIDER              WHAT IT DOES WELL           WHY IT DOES NOT FIT HERE
  --------------------  --------------------------  ---------------------------
  Fastly                Excellent CDN, strong       No free tier equivalent to
                        edge compute, good WAF      CF's; no free tunnel/ZTNA;
                                                    generally credit-based
  Bunny.net             Very cheap, fast, clean     Not free; no ZTNA; no tunnel
  Akamai / Imperva      Best-in-class WAF           Enterprise pricing
  AWS CloudFront +      Real WAF, real DDoS         WAF is billed per rule and
  AWS WAF + Shield                                  per request; adds an AWS root
                                                    credential to the threat
                                                    model; Shield Advanced is
                                                    thousands per month
  Google Cloud CDN +    Solid                       Armor is paid; adds a GCP
  Cloud Armor                                       root credential
  Netlify / Vercel      Great for static frontends  They host YOUR site rather
                                                    than proxying YOUR origin.
                                                    No origin-IP hiding for a
                                                    separate backend, no tunnel,
                                                    no ZTNA. Different tool.
  GitHub Pages          Free static hosting         Static only. No API, no
                                                    proxy, no WAF, no headers
                                                    control worth the name
  ngrok                 Tunnels                     Free tier is not suited to
                                                    production admin access
  Tailscale             Genuinely excellent for     See 6.3 — this is the one
                        the SSH/admin path          real alternative worth
                                                    considering

  CONCLUSION: for the specific bundle this design needs — origin hiding,
  origin-pull authentication, a tunnel, and WebAuthn-gated admin access, all at
  $0 — there is no competitor. Cloudflare is not the answer because it is free.
  It is the answer because items 2, 4, 5, and 6 do not exist together anywhere
  else at any price close to zero, and the design depends on them.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.3  THE ONE ALTERNATIVE WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY: TAILSCALE FOR ADMIN ACCESS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

FINDING P-4 is that Cloudflare is a concentration: DNS, edge, WAF, tunnel, and
admin access in one account. Moving the admin path to a different vendor
reduces that concentration the same way moving the signer did.

  Tailscale for SSH instead of Cloudflare Tunnel + Access:
    FOR:      different vendor, so a Cloudflare account compromise no longer
              touches the admin path at all; WireGuard-based; free tier covers
              a solo operator comfortably; SSH still requires the ed25519-sk
              hardware key on top; device-level ACLs.
    AGAINST:  another account and another recovery path to secure (CTL-904);
              a daemon on the host either way; you lose Cloudflare Access's
              browser-based WebAuthn flow and its audit log, and would need to
              replicate that logging.

  RECOMMENDATION: Cloudflare Tunnel + Access is fine for now, because the SSH
  hardware key already makes the Cloudflare account insufficient on its own to
  reach the host (ASSET 4). Revisit at tripwire T-3 (PART 9), where the
  concentration starts to be worth another account. Record the decision either
  way so it is a choice rather than an oversight.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.4  WHAT THE FREE TIER DOES NOT GIVE YOU — AND WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Under decision D-2 (strict $0), these limitations are accepted. Free
compensations follow each.

  LIMIT 1 — ONE RATE LIMITING RULE, IP-ONLY, FIXED 10-SECOND WINDOW
    Pro would give more rules and flexible periods. You have one rule.
    SPEND IT ON: /api/auth/*. Credential stuffing against auth is the one
    attack where an edge block is materially better than an origin block,
    because it never touches your CPU or your database.
    FREE COMPENSATION:
      - WAF custom rules are separate from rate limiting rules and the free
        plan allows several. Use them for shape-based blocking: bad methods,
        missing/bot user agents on /api/*, the Telegram webhook source
        restriction, and a Managed Challenge on /api/auth when threat score is
        elevated.
      - Bot Fight Mode ON.
      - Cache aggressively so static assets never reach the origin.
      - The origin-side tiers (Caddy rate_limit, the Redis limiter, the cost
        budget from ADDENDUM O EP-7 T2-T4) do the heavy lifting. They cost CPU
        but they are correct.
      - "I'm Under Attack" mode is free and is the emergency lever. Put it in
        the runbook (PART 8) so it is used in minute two, not hour two.
    HONEST ASSESSMENT: adequate for launch. If you take a sustained L7 attack,
    $20/month is the answer and pretending otherwise wastes a night.

  LIMIT 2 — NO SLA ON ANY FREE TIER
    Cloudflare free, Oracle Always Free, and Deno Deploy free all have no
    uptime guarantee. Three vendors, three no-SLAs, and the signer's failure
    mode stops trading entirely.
    FREE COMPENSATION: status-page monitoring for all three with alerts; the
    honest availability statement to users; a Cloudflare custom error page so
    an origin outage shows a real message instead of a browser error.

  LIMIT 3 — CLOUDFLARE ACCESS LOG RETENTION IS 24 HOURS ON FREE
    An intrusion discovered on day three has no admin-access logs.
    FREE COMPENSATION: a daily job that pulls the Access log via API and writes
    it to the same immutable off-box store as everything else (CTL-702). This
    is about twenty lines and it converts 24 hours of retention into forever.
    Do the same for the Deno Deploy log (1-day retention, PART 4.2).

  LIMIT 4 — ORACLE IDLE RECLAMATION AND NO SLA
    See PART 7.2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.5  THE DECISION, RECORDED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Edge, DNS, WAF, tunnel, admin access:   Cloudflare free.  No better option
                                          exists at this price, and four of its
                                          features are load-bearing controls.
  Frontend + API hosting:                 Your own origin (Caddy on Oracle),
                                          single origin, per ARGUMENT 11.
  Signer:                                 Deno Deploy. Different vendor. D-1.
  Off-box immutable storage:              Cloudflare R2 or Backblaze B2 with
                                          Object Lock. Prefer B2 for the
                                          backups specifically, so that a
                                          Cloudflare account compromise cannot
                                          reach both your edge and your
                                          backups.
  TLS mode:                               Full (Strict) + Authenticated Origin
                                          Pulls + CF Origin CA certificate.

That last line under "off-box storage" is the independence test applied one
more time: backups stored at the same vendor as the edge share an operator with
the thing most likely to be attacked. Splitting them costs nothing.

================================================================================
PART 7 — WHERE STRICT $0 ACTUALLY HURTS
================================================================================

Decision D-2 is legitimate and workable. It is not free of consequence, and the
consequences should be written down rather than discovered. Two risks from
ADDENDUM O move from "mitigated" to "accepted," and one becomes more important.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.1  RATE LIMITING AT THE EDGE  (RISK-010, now accepted)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
COST OF $0   One rate-limiting rule, IP-only counting, fixed 10-second window.
             A distributed L7 attack from many source IPs is absorbed at the
             origin, on a 4-OCPU shared box, competing with Postgres.
FREE MEASURES  Per 6.4 LIMIT 1: spend the one rule on auth, use WAF shape rules
             for everything else, Bot Fight Mode, aggressive caching, and rely
             on the origin tiers. Under Attack mode in the runbook.
TRIPWIRE     T-2 (PART 9) forces a reconsideration once real balances exist. At
             that point $20/month is not a budget question, it is a rounding
             error against what is at stake.
HONEST LINE  This is an availability risk, not a fund-loss risk. Tier C. The
             right thing to accept when money is tight.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.2  ORACLE IDLE RECLAMATION AND NO SLA  (RISK-011, now accepted)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
COST OF $0   Oracle may reclaim an Always Free compute instance when, over a
             7-day window, the 95th-percentile CPU utilization, network
             utilization, AND memory utilization (on A1 shapes) are ALL below
             20%. There is no SLA and no guaranteed notice.
WHY IT MAY BITE   A pre-launch or low-volume trading bot is plausibly idle by
             that definition. The period of highest reclamation risk is exactly
             the period before you have revenue to pay for an instance.
FREE MEASURES
  - Do not game the metric with artificial load; it wastes the resource and it
    is not the real fix. The real fix is being genuinely ready to rebuild.
  - INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE. Every host configuration in this document lives in
    the repository as scripts. A rebuild is running them in order, not
    remembering what you did in March.
  - Off-box immutable backups with a MEASURED restore time (CTL-406, DRILL-4).
    Know the number. If your RTO is four hours, reclamation is an outage. If it
    is unknown, reclamation is an extinction event.
  - A warm standby costs $0: Google Cloud's Always Free tier includes a small
    e2-micro instance in eligible US regions. It cannot run this workload, and
    that is not the point — it can hold a copy of the rebuild scripts, serve a
    status page, and be the machine you rebuild FROM when the primary is gone.
    Verify current GCP free-tier terms before relying on it.
  - Monitor for Oracle's reclamation notices on the account email, which must
    be an address you actually read (CTL-904's dedicated address).
TRIPWIRE     T-2 forces a paid instance decision.
HONEST LINE  This is the single largest availability risk in the design and it
             is a direct consequence of D-2. It is survivable with a tested
             restore and unsurvivable without one. If you do one thing from
             PART 7, run DRILL-4 and write down the number.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.3  WHAT $0 DOES NOT COMPROMISE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Worth being clear, because the constraint is easy to over-read: nothing in
CHAIN A or CHAIN B is weakened by D-2. The signer, the policy engine, the KEK
separation, RLS, the AAD binding, HALT, the hardware keys, the treasury
multisig, off-box immutable backups, canary wallets, and every detector are all
free or one-time costs. The entire Tier A posture is intact.

D-2 costs you availability and edge-layer DoS resistance. It does not cost you
key security. That is the correct trade to make when money is tight, and it is
worth saying plainly so nobody assumes "free" means "weak."

THE ONE THING THAT IS NOT FREE AND MUST NOT BE CUT
  Two FIDO2 hardware security keys, roughly $50-100 one time. Under D-2 this is
  the only mandatory purchase. Without them, ASSET 6 (the operator's laptop)
  goes from depth 3 to depth 0 and the Red Team's closing worry is unfixed. If
  budget forces a single line item, it is this one, and it is not optional.

================================================================================
PART 8 — ASSUME BREACH: DETECT, CONTAIN, RECOVER
================================================================================

You said hacking is inevitable. Taken seriously, that changes what to optimize.
Once breach is assumed, the metrics that matter are not "how many controls" but
two numbers:

  TTD  time to detect     — from attacker action to you knowing
  TTC  time to contain    — from knowing to the attacker being unable to act

Loss in CHAIN C is roughly linear in (TTD + TTC). Halving them halves the
damage. That is a more useful lever than a twenty-first preventive control.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8.1  CTL-713 — TARGETS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  EVENT CLASS                          TTD TARGET   TTC TARGET   MECHANISM
  -----------------------------------  -----------  -----------  ------------
  Canary wallet signing attempt        < 1s         < 1s         auto-HALT
  Signer decrypt failure / key         < 1s         < 1s         auto-HALT
    mismatch
  Signing velocity above 3x baseline   < 60s        < 60s        auto-HALT
  Policy rejection burst               < 60s        < 60s        auto-HALT
    (undeclared_program_present)
  Unexpected signer deploy             < 24h        < 1s         nightly
                                                                 /version check
                                                                 + auto-HALT
  Unexpected Cloudflare Access login   < 5 min      human        alert both
                                                                 channels
  Audit chain anchor mismatch          < 24h        human        daily verify
  AIDE baseline mutation               < 24h        human        off-box compare
  Decoy email receives mail            < 15 min     human        mail hook
  Unexpected certificate issued        < 15 min     human        crt.sh poll

The auto-HALT rows are the ones that matter, because they do not wait for a
human. FINDING P-6 says everything else has human latency, which at 3am is
hours. The design rule that follows: any detector whose event class implies
irreversible loss must be on the auto-HALT list. If you add a detector and it
is not auto-HALT, be able to say why.

FALSE-POSITIVE COST OF AUTO-HALT: trading stops until a human clears it. That
is annoying and completely survivable. Compare against the alternative and the
choice is obvious. Bias toward halting.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8.2  CTL-714 — THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Print this. Put it somewhere reachable from a phone. The whole point is that it
requires no thinking at 3am and no access to the compromised system.

```
================================================================================
OSIRIS BREACH RUNBOOK — FIRST FIVE MINUTES
================================================================================
Assume you are on a phone. Assume the laptop may be compromised too.
Do these in order. Do not investigate first. Contain first, investigate second.

MINUTE 0 — STOP THE BLEEDING
  [ ] Set HALT on the signer.
      Deno Deploy dashboard → osiris-signer → KV → key "HALT" = "1"
      OR the one-tap HALT endpoint.
      >>> This stops ALL signing globally. Nothing can move. Do it FIRST,
      >>> before you know what happened. It is reversible and it is free.

MINUTE 1 — CLOSE THE DOORS
  [ ] Cloudflare → Security → Settings → "I'm Under Attack" mode ON.
  [ ] Cloudflare → Zero Trust → Access → revoke all active sessions.
  [ ] If you suspect the app host: Cloudflare → DNS → set the record to
      "DNS only" (grey cloud) is WRONG — it exposes the origin. Instead use
      a WAF rule blocking all traffic to /api/*, or pause the tunnel.

MINUTE 2 — PRESERVE EVIDENCE (do not wipe, do not reboot, do not "clean up")
  [ ] Note the exact time and what you saw.
      Oracle Console → Compute → Instance → Create boot volume backup.
      This snapshots the host as-is for later forensics.
  [ ] Do NOT restart the app. Do NOT delete files. Memory and process state
      are evidence and rebooting destroys them.

MINUTE 3 — CHECK WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED
  [ ] Signer log (shipped off-box): any signature issued in the last 24h that
```
