```
      you cannot account for?
  [ ] On-chain: check the hot wallets on an explorer. This is ground truth and
      it does not depend on any of your systems being honest.
  [ ] Audit chain: does today's anchor verify against yesterday's?

MINUTE 4 — TELL PEOPLE
  [ ] Status page / Telegram channel: "Trading is paused while we investigate a
      security event. Funds are not moving. Updates in 30 minutes."
      Say it early, say it plainly, do not speculate about cause.
      Users forgive an outage. They do not forgive finding out from someone
      else.

MINUTE 5 — DECIDE THE BLAST RADIUS
  [ ] If the signer account may be compromised → assume every key is at risk →
      emergency KEK rotation (CTL-106) AND plan wallet migration.
  [ ] If only the app host → keys are safe. Rebuild the host from the scripts,
      restore from backup, rotate the request-signing key, rotate DB and Redis
      credentials, then clear HALT.
  [ ] If unsure → treat as signer-compromised. The expensive assumption is the
      safe one.

DO NOT:
  - Do not clear HALT to "test if it still happens."
  - Do not log in to the compromised host to look around before snapshotting.
  - Do not tell users funds are safe until you have checked on-chain.
  - Do not skip the postmortem. Write it within 72 hours, publish it.
================================================================================
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8.3  RECOVERY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  SCENARIO 1 — APP HOST COMPROMISED, SIGNER INTACT
    Keys are safe. This is the designed-for case.
    1. HALT stays on.
    2. Provision a new instance. Never clean the old one — rebuild.
    3. Run the infrastructure scripts from the repository.
    4. Restore the database from the newest verified backup.
    5. Rotate: request-signing key (update the public key at the signer),
       database password, Redis password, Telegram bot token and webhook
       secret, any upstream API keys.
    6. Revoke all user sessions; bump the auth epoch.
    7. Verify the full test suite green against the new host.
    8. Clear HALT.
    9. Publish a postmortem with dates and what changed.

  SCENARIO 2 — SIGNER COMPROMISED
    Assume every wallet key is exposed. This is the bad day.
    1. HALT stays on. Do not clear it.
    2. Generate a new KEK on a new signer deployment at a new account —
       ideally a third vendor, since two are now suspect.
    3. Every user wallet must be MIGRATED, not rotated: generate new wallets
       inside the new signer and move funds. Re-wrapping an exposed key does
       not help; the plaintext is already out.
    4. Notify every user immediately and directly. Be specific about what was
       exposed and when.
    5. This scenario is why CHAIN A requires two independent vendors to fail.
       If you are here, something in the two-vendor assumption broke, and the
       postmortem's job is to find out which separation was not real.

  SCENARIO 3 — HOST DESTROYED (Oracle reclamation, not an attack)
    1. Provision a new instance, run the scripts, restore, verify, resume.
    2. Target: under two hours. Whatever DRILL-4 measured is the real number.
    3. No key rotation needed — the signer was never involved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8.4  THE DRILL THAT MATTERS MOST
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DRILL-2 from ADDENDUM O, extended: once a quarter, at a random time, set HALT
from your phone without warning and time it. How long from decision to
signing-stopped? How long to notice the UI degraded correctly? How long to
clear it and confirm recovery?

If that number is above sixty seconds, the runbook has a problem — usually a
credential you cannot reach from a phone. Fix that before the day you need it.
This drill takes four minutes and it is the highest-value four minutes in the
quarterly schedule.

================================================================================
PART 9 — CTL-715: BALANCE TRIPWIRES
================================================================================

You said funds under management are unknown but real. Rather than guess, the
system measures itself and forces action at defined thresholds.

IMPLEMENTATION: a daily job computes total user balance across all hot wallets
and writes it to the audit log. When a threshold is first crossed, it posts a
CRITICAL notice listing the required actions and creates a dated obligation.
Crossing a threshold with actions outstanding raises the severity daily until
resolved. The tripwire is not advisory.

```typescript
// src/jobs/tripwire.ts (sketch)
const TRIPWIRES = [
  { id: "T-1", usd:    25_000, actions: [...] },
  { id: "T-2", usd:   100_000, actions: [...] },
  { id: "T-3", usd:   500_000, actions: [...] },
  { id: "T-4", usd: 2_000_000, actions: [...] },
];
// On first crossing: audit log entry, CRITICAL alert to both channels, and an
// open obligation row. Daily escalation while any obligation is open.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T-1 — TOTAL USER BALANCE CROSSES ~$25,000
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You are now holding more than a hobby project's worth of other people's money.
  [ ] Withdrawal allowlist with 24-hour maturity live BEFORE withdrawals are
      enabled at all (CTL-605). Not after.
  [ ] Per-user notional caps enforced at the signer, not just in the app.
  [ ] Monthly restore drill running on a schedule with recorded results.
  [ ] Written, published statement of RISK-002 in plain language: what a
      compromise of the trading host could and could not do to a user.
  [ ] Second hardware key confirmed stored off-site.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T-2 — CROSSES ~$100,000
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The $0 constraint is now costing more than it saves. Revisit D-2.
  [ ] Cloudflare Pro ($20/mo): real rate-limiting rules. RISK-010 closes.
  [ ] Paid compute instance with an SLA. RISK-011 closes.
  [ ] Off-box log retention extended beyond the free tiers' 24 hours.
  [ ] Full ADDENDUM O Gate 2 complete, no outstanding items.
  [ ] Quarterly chaos drills actually happening, with recorded outcomes.
  [ ] A second person who can execute the breach runbook, with their own
      hardware key. FINDING P-5 stops being acceptable around here.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T-3 — CROSSES ~$500,000
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You are a target worth a dedicated attacker's time and budget.
  [ ] Funded external security review of the signer and the policy engine
      specifically. Not a general pentest — a focused review of the code that
      stands between an attacker and the keys. This is where money buys the
      most.
  [ ] Move the admin path off Cloudflare (6.3), reducing FINDING P-4.
  [ ] Managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery, or self-managed PITR with
      a tested drill.
  [ ] Consider splitting the KEK across two vendors with threshold unwrapping.
  [ ] Formal on-call: someone is reachable within fifteen minutes, always.
  [ ] Re-run the LAYER-4 audit and publish the resulting depth table.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T-4 — CROSSES ~$2,000,000
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [ ] The single-operator model (FINDING P-5) is no longer defensible. Two
      humans, separated duties, no individual holding every credential.
  [ ] Hardware security module or equivalent for the KEK.
  [ ] Funded bug bounty with a real triage capacity (ADDENDUM O DEF-059
      becomes affordable and appropriate here, and not before).
  [ ] Legal and regulatory review of custody posture. At this size the question
      stops being purely technical.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
THE POINT OF TRIPWIRES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Security posture should track what is at stake, and the failure mode of every
small project is that it does not — the balance grows quietly, the controls
stay where they were on launch day, and nobody notices the mismatch until it
is expensive. Tripwires make the mismatch impossible to ignore, because the
system itself raises the alarm.

ADDENDUM Q: ALERTING, AUTOMATED MAINTENANCE, AND THE THINGS YOU HAVEN'T ASKED

Document ID:   OSIRIS-SEC-Q

================================================================================
PART 0 — WHAT YOU ASKED FOR, AND THE TWO TRAPS IN IT
================================================================================

You asked for two things and then asked what else you should be thinking about.
Both requests are correct instincts. Both have a trap in them that decides
whether the thing you build actually works.

REQUEST 1 — "Something that tells me when something is compromised, sends me a
Telegram message."

  THE TRAP: an alerting system that runs on the machine being attacked is
  worthless during the attack. An attacker with root does three things in their
  first minute: stop the alerting agent, delete its logs, and — if they are
  good — keep sending you cheerful heartbeats so you believe everything is fine.
  You would be monitoring a system that is lying to you, through a channel the
  attacker controls, and the silence would look identical to safety.

  THE FIX: alerts are classified by the trust level of their SOURCE, and every
  event that could cost you money must have a source that is not the app host.
  PART 1. Plus: silence itself must be an alarm, raised by a service you do not
  operate. PART 2.

REQUEST 2 — "An AI that auto-updates weekly with security updates."

  THE TRAP: an automated pipeline with write access to production IS an attack
  path. It is ADDENDUM P FINDING P-2 with extra steps. If the updater is
  compromised, or an upstream package is poisoned, your automation helpfully
  deploys the attack for you, on a schedule, at 3am, while you sleep. The npm
  registry is the single most common supply-chain vector in this ecosystem, and
  "auto-merge dependency updates" is how a compromised package reaches
  production without a human ever looking at it.

  THE FIX: split by who signs the update and how many people can push it.
  OS packages from a signed distro repo: auto-apply. Application dependencies:
  DETECT and PROPOSE only, never apply. The signer: nothing automatic, ever.
  PART 7.

REQUEST 3 — "What else? Help me think."
  PART 10. The short version, so it is not buried: the highest-value items you
  have not mentioned are (a) your users are a free, massively parallel intrusion
  detection system and you are not using them, (b) you should write the breach
  notification email now, while calm, and (c) an alert path you have never
  fired does not exist.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  CTL-721  Dead man's switch (silence as an alarm)

================================================================================
PART 1 — CTL-720: ALERT SOURCE TRUST LEVELS
================================================================================

This is the organizing idea. It is ADDENDUM P's independence test applied to
detection instead of prevention.

An alert is only as trustworthy as the thing that generated it. Sort every
alert source into three levels:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LEVEL 1 — HIGH TRUST: the signer (Deno Deploy)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Different vendor, different account, different hardware key. An attacker who
  owns the app host cannot suppress these, cannot forge them, and cannot see
  them.
  WHAT IT CAN TELL YOU
    - a wallet key failed to decrypt
    - a derived public key did not match the declared wallet
    - a canary wallet was signed for
    - the policy engine refused a transaction, and exactly why
    - signing velocity crossed a threshold
    - HALT was set, by what, and when
    - an unexpected signer deployment occurred
  WHY IT MATTERS: these are precisely the events that indicate someone is
  trying to move money. The one component that cannot be silenced by the most
  likely compromise is also the one that sees the most important events. That
  is not a coincidence; the architecture was arranged that way.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LEVEL 2 — HIGH TRUST: external observers you do not operate
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Services outside your infrastructure entirely. An attacker inside your
  systems cannot reach them.
  WHAT THEY CAN TELL YOU
    - the site is down or returning the wrong content   (uptime monitor)
    - a heartbeat stopped                               (dead man's switch)
    - a certificate was issued for your domain by anyone (crt.sh / CT monitor)
    - DNS records changed                               (external DNS poll)
    - your domain is approaching expiry                 (registrar + calendar)
    - a decoy email address received mail               (mail provider)
    - the on-chain state of your hot wallets            (a public RPC, queried
                                                         from somewhere else)
  WHY IT MATTERS: level 2 is how you find out that level 3 has gone quiet.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LEVEL 3 — LOW TRUST: the application host
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Useful for operational signal. Untrustworthy during exactly the incident you
  care about, because the attacker is standing on it.
  WHAT IT CAN TELL YOU (and you should still collect it)
    - auth failures, rate limit trips, unusual query patterns
    - job queue depth, error rates, restarts
    - AIDE and auditd findings — but only until the attacker notices them
  HOW TO USE IT: treat level 3 alerts as leads, not as ground truth, and never
  let a level 3 source be the ONLY thing that can report a Tier A event.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  THE RULE (CTL-720)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Every event that could cost money must have a LEVEL 1 or LEVEL 2 source.

    If the only thing that can tell you about an event is the app host, you
    have no detection for that event during a host compromise — which is the
    scenario in which you needed it.

  Apply this as a design check. When you add a detector, write down its level.
  If a Tier A row in the catalog (PART 3) has only level 3 sources, that is a
  finding, not a preference.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1.1  WORKED EXAMPLE OF WHY THIS MATTERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Attacker gets RCE on the app host at 02:14.

  WITHOUT CTL-720 — everything reports from the host:
    02:14  attacker kills the alerting process
    02:14  no alert is sent, and none will be
    02:15  attacker begins forced swaps
    09:30  you wake up, open the app, see something odd
    TTD ≈ 7 hours

  WITH CTL-720:
    02:14  attacker kills the host alerting process
    02:15  attacker's first signing request arrives at the signer
    02:15  policy engine refuses it: undeclared_program_present
           → LEVEL 1 alert fires from Deno Deploy, which the attacker does not
             control → auto-HALT
    02:19  heartbeat to healthchecks.io is missed (grace 5 min)
           → LEVEL 2 alert fires
    TTD ≈ 60 seconds. TTC ≈ 60 seconds, because HALT was automatic.

  Same attacker, same access, same tooling. The difference is entirely where
  the alert came from.

================================================================================
PART 2 — CTL-721: SILENCE IS AN ALARM
================================================================================

The single most common failure of homebrew monitoring: it works perfectly for
eight months, then the process dies, and nobody notices because the absence of
alerts feels like good news. Six weeks later something goes wrong and you learn
the monitor stopped in March.

    You cannot distinguish "nothing is wrong" from "the thing that would tell
    me is dead" unless something external is expecting to hear from you.

THE MECHANISM — a dead man's switch. Your system checks IN on a schedule. If a
check-in does not arrive, an external service pages you.

FREE TOOLING
  healthchecks.io free tier: 20 checks, 100 log entries per check. Supports
  webhook, email, and chat integrations; verify Telegram on their integrations
  page. Self-hostable if you ever want to remove the dependency.
  Alternatives: cron-job.org, UptimeRobot free tier, or a tiny scheduled
  function on any free platform. Verify current terms (rule C-4).

THE CHECKS TO CREATE (five of your twenty)

  CHECK 1  APP HEARTBEAT              period 5 min, grace 5 min
    Sent by the app host. Detects: host down, process dead, network cut,
    attacker killed the agent.
    LIMIT: an attacker who wants to stay quiet will keep this alive. This
    detects availability, not integrity. Do not overtrust it.

  CHECK 2  SIGNER HEARTBEAT           period 1 hour, grace 30 min
    Sent by the signer. Detects: signer down (which means trading is down and
    you should know before a user tells you), or the signer account being
    tampered with.

  CHECK 3  NIGHTLY BACKUP             period 1 day, grace 6 hours
    Pinged only on SUCCESSFUL completion, after the upload and the checksum
    verify. A backup job that fails silently is the default state of the world
    and this is the cheapest possible fix.

  CHECK 4  DAILY AUDIT ANCHOR         period 1 day, grace 6 hours
    Pinged after the audit chain root hash is published off-box and verified.
    Detects: anchoring stopped, chain verification failing, or the job dying.

  CHECK 5  WEEKLY REVIEW COMPLETED    period 7 days, grace 2 days
    Pinged when the weekly maintenance agent (PART 7) finishes. Detects: your
    automation quietly stopped running, which is the thing this whole section
    exists to prevent.

CRITICAL DETAIL — PING ON SUCCESS, NOT ON START
```bash
# WRONG — pings even when the job then fails
curl -fsS -m 10 "$HC_URL" ; run_backup

# RIGHT — only a fully successful run reports success
set -Eeuo pipefail
if run_backup && verify_checksum && upload_offbox; then
    curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 "$HC_URL"
else
    # Report failure explicitly so you get an alert now, not in six hours
    curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 "$HC_URL/fail" -d "$(tail -c 2000 /var/log/osiris/backup.log)"
fi
```
  Sending the tail of the log to the `/fail` endpoint means the alert arrives
  with the reason attached, which is the difference between "backup failed"
  (you have to go look) and "backup failed: no space left on device" (you know
  what to do before you open the laptop).

================================================================================
PART 3 — CTL-722: THE ALERT CATALOG
================================================================================

Every alert that exists, its severity, its source trust level, whether it acts
automatically, and the exact message text. Nothing fires that is not on this
list. Adding a row is a deliberate act, because ADDENDUM O CTL-700 caps you at
about five pages per week and every addition spends that budget.

SEVERITY MEANINGS — these are commitments, not labels:
  CRITICAL  Money may be moving right now. Wakes you. Usually auto-HALTs.
  HIGH      Something is wrong that a human must look at today.
  MEDIUM    Batched into a twice-daily digest.
  LOW       Weekly report only. Never an individual message.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TIER A — CRITICAL. Wakes you at 3am. Most auto-HALT.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  ID     EVENT                          SRC  AUTO-HALT  TTD
  -----  -----------------------------  ---  ---------  --------
  A-01   Canary wallet signing attempt   L1   YES        < 1s
  A-02   Wallet key failed to decrypt    L1   YES        < 1s
  A-03   Derived pubkey != declared      L1   YES        < 1s
         wallet
  A-04   Signing velocity > 3x baseline  L1   YES        < 60s
  A-05   Policy rejection burst          L1   YES        < 60s
         (undeclared_program_present)
  A-06   Unexpected signer deployment    L1   YES        < 24h
  A-07   Bad request signature at the    L1   no         < 60s
         signer
  A-08   HALT set (by anything)          L1   n/a        < 1s
  A-09   Certificate issued for the      L2   no         < 15m
         domain outside your pipeline
  A-10   Decoy email address received    L2   no         < 15m
         mail
  A-11   DNS record changed unexpectedly L2   no         < 5m
  A-12   Hot wallet balance dropped >X%  L2   no         < 5m
         with no matching trade record

  A-12 deserves a note: it is queried from OUTSIDE your infrastructure against
  a public RPC, and cross-checked against your own trade records. It is the
  only alert that would still fire if every single one of your systems were
  compromised and lying, because the chain is ground truth and the attacker
  does not control it. It is the last honest signal you have. Build it.

  MESSAGE FORMAT — Tier A
```
🔴 CRITICAL · A-01 · CANARY WALLET SIGNED

A signing request was made for a canary wallet. No legitimate code path
ever signs for this wallet. Someone is enumerating wallets.

wallet   Ax7f…9Kd2
user     (hashed) 4f2a91c8
session  sess_01J…
time     2026-08-15 02:14:07 UTC
source   signer (deno)
seq      1841

HALT has been set automatically. All signing is stopped.

Runbook: ADDENDUM P PART 8.2. Do not clear HALT to test.
```
  Notes on the format that are deliberate:
  - The event ID is in the subject line so you can search your own history.
  - The one-line explanation says why it matters, because at 3am you will not
    remember what A-01 means.
  - NO CLICKABLE LINKS. Ever. See PART 5.3.
  - The sequence number lets you detect suppression (PART 5.2).
  - It states what already happened automatically, so you do not duplicate it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TIER B — HIGH. Immediate message, but does not auto-act. Look today.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  ID     EVENT                                        SRC
  -----  -------------------------------------------  ---
  B-01   Cloudflare Access authentication you did      L2
         not perform
  B-02   New hardware key enrolled on any account      L2
  B-03   API token created on Cloudflare / Deno /      L2
         Oracle
  B-04   Audit chain anchor mismatch                   L2
  B-05   AIDE baseline mutated                         L2
  B-06   Backup failed, or the nightly check-in        L2
         missed
  B-07   Restore drill failed or was skipped           L2
  B-08   Signer rate limit tripped repeatedly for one  L1
         wallet
  B-09   Withdrawal allowlist entry added              L1
  B-10   Postgres RLS disabled on any table            L3*
         (event trigger)
  B-11   Sequence gap in the alert stream              L2
  B-12   Free tier terms changed on a dependency you   L2
         rely on
  B-13   Domain or certificate expiring in < 30 days   L2
  B-14   Heartbeat missed (any dead man's switch)      L2

  * B-10 is level 3 and that is a known weakness. It is paired with the weekly
    control verification (PART 7), which re-checks RLS from a read-only
    connection, so a suppressed B-10 surfaces within seven days.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TIER C — MEDIUM. Twice-daily digest at 09:00 and 21:00 local.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  C-01  Auth failure rate above baseline
  C-02  Rate limiter fail-open occurred (Redis unavailable)
  C-03  Circuit breaker opened on an upstream provider
  C-04  Job queue depth above threshold
  C-05  Unusual query fingerprint seen in pg_stat_statements
  C-06  Container restarted unexpectedly
  C-07  Telegram webhook received from an unexpected source
  C-08  A user's session showed refresh-token reuse

  DIGEST FORMAT
```
🟡 DIGEST · 2026-08-15 09:00 · 4 events

C-01  auth failures      37 (baseline 12)   ips: 3   window: 12h
C-02  limiter fail-open   1                 redis restart 04:12
C-06  container restart   1                 app, OOM, 04:12
C-08  token reuse         1                 user 4f2a91c8, session revoked

Nothing above requires action. Full detail in the weekly report.
```
  Counts and comparisons to baseline, not one message per event. Four lines,
  not thirty-seven messages. This is what keeps you reading the channel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TIER D — LOW. Weekly report only.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  D-01  Dependency updates available (with CVE context)
  D-02  Control verification results
  D-03  Balance tripwire progress (ADDENDUM P PART 9)
  D-04  Cost and quota usage against free-tier limits
  D-05  Alert budget review: what fired, what was noise

================================================================================
PART 4 — IMPLEMENTATION
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.1  CTL-723: A SEPARATE ALERT BOT AND A SEPARATE CHANNEL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Do NOT send security alerts through the product's Telegram bot. Three reasons,
each sufficient on its own:

  1. The product bot's token lives on the app host. An attacker who takes the
     host can send you fake alerts, fake all-clears, or ten thousand junk
     messages to bury a real one.
  2. Product notifications (trade confirmations, price alerts) will drown
     security alerts in the same conversation.
  3. Rotating the product bot token during an incident would take out your
     alert channel at the moment you need it.

SETUP
```
1. @BotFather → /newbot → "OSIRIS Sentinel" → get ALERT_BOT_TOKEN
   This token is DIFFERENT from the product bot's token.

2. Create a private Telegram channel, "OSIRIS Alerts". You are the only human
   member. Add the Sentinel bot as an administrator.

3. Get the channel id:
   curl "https://api.telegram.org/bot<ALERT_BOT_TOKEN>/getUpdates"
   (post a message in the channel first; the id looks like -1001234567890)

4. Token placement — this is the important part:
   - The SIGNER holds its own copy, set as a Deno Deploy environment variable.
     Level 1 alerts are sent by the signer directly.
   - The app host holds a copy in a Docker secret for level 3 alerts.
   - External monitors (healthchecks.io, CT monitor) are configured with
     their own Telegram integrations and hold their own copies.
   Three independent senders. Killing one does not kill the channel.

5. Mute NOTHING in this channel. If you ever feel the urge to mute it, the
   alert budget is being violated — fix the alerts, do not mute the channel.
```

SECOND CHANNEL — email. Telegram is a single point of failure: account
recovery is SMS-based (which is why ADDENDUM O demoted it as an authenticator),
the app could be down, or you could be locked out. Every CRITICAL and HIGH
alert goes to both. Email goes to the dedicated address from CTL-904, which is
also hardware-key protected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.2  THE ALERT MODULE (shared shape, three senders)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```typescript
// shared/alert.ts — used by the signer and the app, with different transports.

export type Severity = "critical" | "high" | "medium" | "low";
export type SourceLevel = 1 | 2 | 3;

export interface Alert {
  id: string;            // "A-01", "B-04" — from the catalog, no ad-hoc ids
  severity: Severity;
  sourceLevel: SourceLevel;
  title: string;         // short, imperative, no jargon
  why: string;           // one sentence: why this matters at 3am
  fields: Record<string, string>;   // already redacted by the caller
  autoAction?: string;   // "HALT set automatically" or undefined
  seq: number;           // monotonic per sender, for suppression detection
  ts: string;            // ISO 8601 UTC
}

const SEV_ICON: Record<Severity, string> = {
  critical: "🔴", high: "🟠", medium: "🟡", low: "⚪",
};

export function render(a: Alert): string {
  const lines = [
    `${SEV_ICON[a.severity]} ${a.severity.toUpperCase()} · ${a.id} · ${a.title}`,
    "",
    a.why,
    "",
    ...Object.entries(a.fields).map(([k, v]) => `${k.padEnd(9)}${v}`),
    `${"time".padEnd(9)}${a.ts}`,
    `${"source".padEnd(9)}L${a.sourceLevel}`,
    `${"seq".padEnd(9)}${a.seq}`,
  ];
  if (a.autoAction) lines.push("", a.autoAction);
  lines.push("", "Runbook: ADDENDUM P PART 8.2");
  return lines.join("\n");
}

/** Telegram transport. Deliberately dependency-free — it is a fetch call.
 *  MUST NOT throw into the caller: a failed alert must never break the
 *  operation that triggered it, and must never prevent HALT from being set. */
export async function sendTelegram(
  token: string, chatId: string, text: string
): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`https://api.telegram.org/bot${token}/sendMessage`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        chat_id: chatId,
        text,
        // No parse_mode. Alert text may contain attacker-influenced values;
        // Markdown parsing of hostile input is a formatting-injection vector
        // and can make a message unsendable. Plain text always renders.
        disable_web_page_preview: true,
        disable_notification: false,
      }),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000),
    });
    return res.ok;
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}
```

CRITICAL ORDERING RULE, worth stating on its own:
```
  HALT FIRST, ALERT SECOND. Always.

  If the signer detects a canary hit, it sets HALT and THEN sends the alert.
  If Telegram is down, rate limited, or slow, the money is already stopped.
  Never make containment depend on notification succeeding.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.3  SIGNER-SIDE ALERTS (LEVEL 1 — the ones that matter)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```typescript
// signer/alert.ts
import { render, sendTelegram, type Alert } from "./shared/alert.ts";
import { store } from "./storage.ts";

async function nextSeq(): Promise<number> {
  return await store.increment("alert:seq", 60 * 60 * 24 * 90);
}

export async function signerAlert(
  a: Omit<Alert, "seq" | "ts" | "sourceLevel">
): Promise<void> {
  const full: Alert = {
    ...a, sourceLevel: 1, seq: await nextSeq(), ts: new Date().toISOString(),
  };
  const text = render(full);

  // Fire both transports concurrently. allSettled: neither can block the other,
  // and neither can throw into the signing path.
  await Promise.allSettled([
    sendTelegram(Deno.env.get("ALERT_BOT_TOKEN")!, Deno.env.get("ALERT_CHAT_ID")!, text),
    sendEmail(Deno.env.get("ALERT_EMAIL")!, `${full.severity.toUpperCase()} ${full.id}`, text),
    // Durable copy off-platform: Deno Deploy free retains logs for 1 day.
    appendToImmutableLog(full),
  ]);
}

// Wired into the policy engine, at the points already specified in ADDENDUM O:
//   canary hit          -> HALT, then signerAlert A-01
//   decrypt failure     -> HALT, then signerAlert A-02
//   pubkey mismatch     -> HALT, then signerAlert A-03
//   velocity threshold  -> HALT, then signerAlert A-04
//   policy reject burst -> HALT, then signerAlert A-05
//   bad request sig     -> signerAlert A-07  (no HALT: could be a rotation bug)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.4  THE ON-CHAIN WATCHER (LEVEL 2 — the last honest signal)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This runs somewhere that is NOT the app host and NOT the signer. A tiny
scheduled function on any free platform, or the Google Cloud e2-micro standby
from ADDENDUM P PART 7.2. It reads the chain from a public RPC and compares it
to what your system says should have happened.

```typescript
// watcher/balance-check.ts — runs every 5 minutes, off your infrastructure.
/**
 * The only detector that still works when every system you own is compromised
 * and lying to you. The chain does not lie and the attacker does not control
 * the RPC you query from here.
 *
 * It needs exactly two things, both read-only and both harmless if leaked:
 *   - the list of hot wallet addresses (public information anyway)
 *   - a read-only API token for your own /api/expected-balances endpoint
 * It holds NO credential that can change anything, anywhere.
 */
const DROP_THRESHOLD_PCT = 5;

for (const wallet of HOT_WALLETS) {
  const onChain = await getBalanceFromPublicRpc(wallet);
  const previous = await readLast(wallet);
  if (previous && onChain < previous * (1 - DROP_THRESHOLD_PCT / 100)) {
    const expected = await fetchExpectedBalance(wallet);   // read-only
    // A drop your own system cannot explain is the alert. A drop that matches
    // a recorded trade is normal business.
    if (Math.abs(onChain - expected) > tolerance(expected)) {
      await alert({
        id: "A-12", severity: "critical", sourceLevel: 2,
        title: "UNEXPLAINED BALANCE DROP",
        why: "On-chain balance fell and OSIRIS has no matching trade record. " +
             "This is visible from outside your infrastructure, so it holds " +
             "even if your systems are compromised.",
        fields: { wallet, onChain: String(onChain), expected: String(expected),
                  drop: `${pct}%` },
      });
    }
  }
  await writeLast(wallet, onChain);
}
```
If `/api/expected-balances` is unreachable — because the host is down or
compromised — that is itself the alert. Do not fail silently, and do not
default to "assume it's fine."

================================================================================
PART 5 — CTL-724/725: ALERT AUTHENTICITY AND ANTI-SUPPRESSION
================================================================================

An attacker who cannot stop your alerts has two other options: forge them, or
bury them. Both are cheap and both work against naive alerting.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.1  SUPPRESSION DETECTION — SEQUENCE NUMBERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Every sender maintains a monotonic counter and stamps it on every alert. A
consumer-side job checks for gaps.

  seq 1839  →  seq 1840  →  seq 1843
                            ↑ two alerts never arrived

Without this, a suppressed alert is indistinguishable from a quiet hour. With
it, suppression is itself an alert (B-11).

The signer's counter lives in the signer's own storage, so the app host cannot
reset or advance it. Gaps in the level 1 stream are near-certain evidence of
tampering — and note that a *rewind* (a seq lower than one already seen) is
even stronger evidence, because normal operation never produces one.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.2  BURYING — RATE LIMIT YOUR OWN ALERTS, BUT NEVER DROP CRITICALS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
An attacker who can trigger a noisy low-severity alert will trigger ten
thousand of them, pushing the real one off your screen and into Telegram's rate
limiter.

```typescript
// Per-alert-id token bucket. Coalesce, never drop.
const BUCKETS: Record<Severity, { perHour: number }> = {
  critical: { perHour: 60 },   // effectively uncapped; see below
  high:     { perHour: 12 },
  medium:   { perHour: 0  },   // digest only
  low:      { perHour: 0  },   // weekly only
};

// Beyond the budget, alerts of the same id are COALESCED into a single
// message with a count — never silently discarded.
//   "🟠 HIGH · B-08 · 47 occurrences in the last hour (suppressed 46)"

// CRITICAL alerts are never coalesced away entirely. If a critical exceeds its
// budget, that fact is itself escalated: a flood of criticals is an attack on
// the alert channel and warrants HALT on its own.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.3  FORGERY — AND WHY ALERTS CONTAIN NO LINKS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The app host holds an alert bot token, so an attacker on the host can send you
messages in your own alert channel. They will look real, because they are real
— sent by your bot, in your channel.

  DEFENCES
  - Every message states its source level. A "CRITICAL" claiming source L3 for
    an event the catalog says is L1 is a forgery. The catalog is the contract.
  - Level 1 alerts are sent by the signer, whose token the app host does not
    have. An attacker on the host cannot produce a convincing A-01 through
    A-08.
  - NO CLICKABLE LINKS IN ANY ALERT. Ever. You navigate manually to
    dashboards you already have bookmarked. This makes "🔴 CRITICAL: click here
    to review" a tell rather than a trap, and it removes the possibility of an
    alert-channel phishing attack against the one person who can HALT the
    system.
  - No `parse_mode`. Plain text only, so attacker-influenced field values
    cannot inject formatting or hidden links.
  - An "all clear" is never sent by automation. Only you decide the incident is
    over. If a message says "resolved, no action needed" and you did not write
    it, that is an attack.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.4  CTL-725: THE MONTHLY SYNTHETIC ALERT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    An alert path you have never fired does not exist.

Once a month, automatically, fire one synthetic alert down every path:

```typescript
// src/jobs/alert-selftest.ts — first of the month, 10:00 local
await selfTest([
  { source: "signer",   channel: "telegram" },
  { source: "signer",   channel: "email"    },
  { source: "app",      channel: "telegram" },
  { source: "app",      channel: "email"    },
  { source: "external", channel: "telegram" },  // healthchecks.io test ping
]);
// Message: "⚪ SELFTEST · monthly alert path verification · seq NNNN
//           If you are reading this, this path works. No action needed."
```
And — this is the part that makes it a control rather than a ritual — the
self-test job asserts that it can OBSERVE its own message arriving where that
is possible, and pages if a path fails. A self-test that only sends is testing
the sender, not the path.

Add to the quarterly drills: delete the alert bot token from the app host and
confirm that level 1 alerts still arrive. That proves the independence you have
been claiming.

================================================================================
PART 6 — THE ZERO-DOLLAR AUTHENTICATOR STRATEGY
================================================================================

You said you do not want to buy hardware keys and you want this completely
free. Fair — and I was wrong to call them the one mandatory purchase without
first checking what free options exist. There is a genuinely good free
substitute, and it is one you already own.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.1  YOUR PHONE IS ALREADY A HARDWARE SECURITY KEY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A passkey stored in your phone's secure enclave (Face ID / Touch ID on iPhone,
fingerprint or StrongBox on Android) is WebAuthn — the same protocol a YubiKey
speaks. It is phishing-resistant, the private key is generated and held in
dedicated security hardware, and using it requires your biometric.

Cloudflare supports this explicitly. Their documentation describes a security
key as using "a built-in authenticator (Apple Touch ID, Android fingerprint, or
Windows Hello) or an external hardware key" — the built-in option is a
first-class citizen, not a fallback.

So the plan changes from "buy two YubiKeys" to "register two platform
authenticators you already own," and most of the security is preserved.

WHAT TO REGISTER, PER ACCOUNT — always at least two, on two different devices:
```
  Authenticator 1:  your phone         (Face ID / fingerprint)
  Authenticator 2:  your laptop        (Touch ID / Windows Hello)
  Authenticator 3:  printed backup codes, stored physically, in a second
                    location
```
Two devices means losing one is not a lockout. That is the failure mode that
actually bites people, and it is free to prevent.

ACCOUNT BY ACCOUNT
```
  Cloudflare       WebAuthn built-in authenticator. Confirmed supported.
                   → disable email-TOTP fallback (see 6.3)
  GitHub           Passkeys supported. Covers Deno Deploy if you sign in with
                   GitHub.
  Google / Apple   Passkeys supported. These matter more than you think — see
                   6.2.
  Oracle Cloud     Check the MFA options in your tenancy. Prefer FIDO/passkey;
                   if only TOTP is offered, use a TOTP app, never SMS.
  Registrar        Prefer a registrar that supports WebAuthn. If yours does
                   not, that is a reason to move — transferring a domain is
                   cheap and the registrar is ASSET 8.
  Password manager Bitwarden free tier supports 2FA; use the strongest method
                   it offers on your plan.
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.2  WHAT YOU ACTUALLY GIVE UP — HONESTLY, IN THREE ITEMS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I am not going to tell you this is identical to a hardware key. It is not.
Here is the exact difference, so you can decide with real information.

  LOSS 1 — THE PHONE HAS AN OPERATING SYSTEM. A YUBIKEY DOES NOT.
    A security key has no network stack, no apps, no browser, and no way to be
    remotely compromised. Your phone runs a general-purpose OS with a browser
    and third-party apps. A sufficiently capable attacker with a phone exploit
    could potentially use the passkey.
    HOW BIG IS THIS REALLY: small for most attackers. Platform passkeys live in
    the secure enclave and require a biometric per use, so this needs a serious
    exploit chain, not a malicious app from a sketchy store. It is a real
    difference and it is not the most likely path against you.
    FREE MITIGATION: if you have an old phone in a drawer, factory reset it, no
    SIM, WiFi only, no apps beyond what you need, and use it ONLY as your
    authenticator device. That is functionally very close to a hardware token,
    and it costs nothing.

  LOSS 2 — SYNCED PASSKEYS MEAN YOUR APPLE/GOOGLE ACCOUNT IS NOW A CROWN JEWEL.
    iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager sync passkeys across your
    devices. That is excellent for not getting locked out and it means the
    passkey is no longer confined to one piece of hardware. A hardware key's
    private key can never leave the token; a synced passkey exists in your
    platform account.
    CONSEQUENCE: whoever owns your Apple ID or Google account can potentially
    reach your Cloudflare passkey. Your platform account joins the asset list.
    FREE MITIGATION: protect the Apple/Google account with its own passkey,
    remove SMS recovery from it, turn on the strongest account protection the
    platform offers (Apple's Advanced Data Protection, Google's Advanced
    Protection Program — both free), and treat that account with the same
    seriousness as the Cloudflare one. Where a platform offers device-bound
    (non-synced) passkeys, prefer them for the signer account specifically.

  LOSS 3 — NO `ed25519-sk` FOR SSH. THIS IS THE REAL ONE.
    ADDENDUM O specified an SSH key bound to a FIDO2 token with
    `verify-required`, so that a compromised laptop yields nothing without a
    physical touch. Without a token, the SSH key is a file protected by a
    passphrase — and a passphrase typed on a keylogged laptop is not a secret.
    WHAT SAVES YOU ANYWAY: Cloudflare Access sits in front of sshd and requires
    your phone passkey. So a compromised laptop alone is still not enough — the
    attacker needs your laptop AND your phone. That is two devices, and it is
    still meaningfully better than a single factor.
    NET EFFECT: ASSET 6 (laptop compromise) moves from "attacker gets nothing"
    to "attacker needs your phone as well." Depth drops from 3 to 2 on the
    admin path. It does NOT drop on the key-custody path — the signer is still
    at a separate vendor behind a separate passkey, and user private keys are
    exactly as safe as they were.

  THE HONEST SUMMARY: you keep roughly 80% of the value for $0. The 20% you
  lose is concentrated in the admin path, not in key custody. Given the
  architecture already assumes the app host will fall, that is a defensible
  trade. Revisit at tripwire T-1 (ADDENDUM P PART 9) — a basic FIDO2 key is
  around $25-30, not the $50-100 I quoted for a pair, and at $25k of user funds
  it stops being a real decision.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.3  THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: KILL THE WEAK FALLBACKS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    A strong factor with a weak fallback is a weak factor. The attacker
    simply uses the fallback.

This is worth more than the choice between a phone and a YubiKey, and it is
completely free. Registering a passkey on Cloudflare accomplishes nothing if
the account will also accept an emailed code, because now the account is only
as strong as your email.

  DO THIS ON EVERY ACCOUNT:
  [ ] Remove SMS as a 2FA method. Everywhere. No exceptions.
  [ ] Remove your phone number from account recovery. Everywhere.
  [ ] Cloudflare: after registering WebAuthn, review whether email-TOTP is
      still enabled as an alternative and disable it if the option exists. If
      it cannot be disabled, understand that your Cloudflare account is only as
      strong as your email account, and protect the email account accordingly.
  [ ] The email account behind all of this: its own passkey, no SMS recovery,
      used for nothing else, and its recovery address is a second such account.
  [ ] Print every set of backup codes. Store them physically, in a location
      that is not your desk. Delete the digital copies.
  [ ] Registrar: registry lock ON. This blocks transfers even if someone gets
      into the account, and it is usually free.

  THE RECOVERY-PATH INVENTORY (ADDENDUM O CTL-904) is now more important than
  it was, not less. Write down every account, its 2FA method, and every way it
  can be recovered. Then look at the weakest line. That line is your actual
  security level.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.4  THE PHONE AS YOUR ADMIN DEVICE — A FREE UPGRADE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

There is a free move here that genuinely improves on the hardware-key plan, and
it comes from noticing what the phone is good at.

Your laptop runs `npm install`, opens repositories, browses the web, and reads
email. It is the machine most likely to be compromised. Your phone does none of
those things with the same exposure and has aggressive app sandboxing.

So: do the highest-privilege actions from the phone, not the laptop.

  DO FROM THE PHONE
    - Set HALT (Deno Deploy dashboard, or the one-tap endpoint)
    - Cloudflare dashboard: Under Attack mode, WAF changes, Access policies
    - Review alerts and the weekly report
    - Approve anything in the breach runbook (ADDENDUM P PART 8.2 is written
      for a phone deliberately)
  DO FROM THE LAPTOP
    - Write code, run tests, open PRs
    - SSH for operational work
  NEVER
    - Store production credentials on the laptop
    - Run `npm install` on a machine holding admin sessions

This means that in the most likely compromise — a malicious dependency or a
bad link on your dev laptop — the attacker does not get your emergency controls
and cannot stop you from halting them. That is a real property, and it is free.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.5  THE ONE COST THAT CANNOT BE ZERO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The domain. Roughly $10-15 a year. Free subdomain providers are unreliable, get
blocklisted, and — for something handling money — signal exactly the wrong thing
to a user deciding whether to trust you. This is not in the same category as a
$50 purchase you can defer; it is the cost of being a real site, and there is no
architecture that removes it.

Everything else in ADDENDUM O and ADDENDUM P is genuinely free with the
substitutions above. Revised total: about $12 a year, plus per-trade Solana
fees and Helius Sender tips.

================================================================================
PART 7 — CTL-730: AUTOMATED MAINTENANCE, AND WHAT IT MAY NOT TOUCH
================================================================================

You want an AI that keeps things patched weekly. Good instinct — unpatched
CVEs are a real way to get owned, and keeping up manually is tedious enough
that nobody actually does it.

But an automated pipeline with write access to production is itself an attack
path. It is ADDENDUM P FINDING P-2 restated: whatever can deploy can deploy an
attack. So the question is not "should it be automatic" but "automatic for
what, and who signed it."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.1  THE SPLIT — SORTED BY WHO CAN PUSH AN UPDATE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    AUTO-APPLY when the update is signed by a distribution with a small,
    accountable set of maintainers and a review process.

    PROPOSE ONLY when any one of thousands of people can publish a new version
    directly to a registry.

    NEVER AUTOMATE anything touching the component with no second layer.

  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WHAT                     │ POLICY      │ WHY                               │
  ├──────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ubuntu security updates  │ AUTO-APPLY  │ Signed distro repo, small         │
  │ (unattended-upgrades)    │             │ maintainer set, security-only     │
  │                          │             │ pocket. Risk of NOT patching      │
  │                          │             │ clearly exceeds risk of patching. │
  ├──────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Docker base image        │ PROPOSE     │ Digest-pinned. A new digest is a  │
  │ digests                  │             │ diff a human should see.          │
  ├──────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │ npm dependencies         │ PROPOSE     │ Anyone can publish. This is the   │
  │                          │ ONLY        │ single most common supply-chain   │
  │                          │             │ vector in this ecosystem.         │
  │                          │             │ Auto-merge here is how a          │
  │                          │             │ compromised package reaches       │
  │                          │             │ production unread.                │
  ├──────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │ THE SIGNER               │ NEVER       │ Zero dependencies (ADDENDUM P     │
  │ (code, deps, deploy)     │             │ CTL-110). Manual, hardware-       │
  │                          │             │ authenticated deploy only         │
  │                          │             │ (CTL-112). No exceptions, not     │
  │                          │             │ even for "just a patch version."  │
  ├──────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Database migrations      │ NEVER       │ Run deliberately, with a backup   │
  │                          │             │ taken first.                      │
  ├──────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Cloudflare / firewall /  │ NEVER       │ A misapplied rule is an outage or │
  │ Access config            │             │ an opening. Human, from the phone.│
  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.2  THE AUTO-APPLY HALF: OS PATCHING
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Already CTL-208 in ADDENDUM O; here is the configuration that makes it real
rather than installed.
```
# /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades
Unattended-Upgrade::Allowed-Origins {
    "${distro_id}:${distro_codename}-security";
    "${distro_id}ESMApps:${distro_codename}-apps-security";
    "${distro_id}ESM:${distro_codename}-infra-security";
};
// Security pocket ONLY. Do not auto-apply feature updates.
Unattended-Upgrade::Remove-Unused-Kernel-Packages "true";
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true";
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-Time "04:30";
Unattended-Upgrade::Mail "alerts@yourdomain";
Unattended-Upgrade::MailReport "on-change";
```
```
# /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades
APT::Periodic::Update-Package-Lists "1";
APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1";
```
REBOOTS ARE NOT OPTIONAL HERE. Livepatch on arm64 landed with Ubuntu 26.04 and
is not available for a 22.04 arm64 host, so kernel CVEs require an actual
reboot. Automatic-Reboot at 04:30 is the mechanism. Verify it happens:
```bash
# Weekly check, reported in the weekly report (D-02)
[ -f /var/run/reboot-required ] && echo "REBOOT PENDING SINCE $(stat -c %y /var/run/reboot-required)"
uptime -p    # an uptime of 200 days on this stack is a finding, not a badge
```
The containers must come back cleanly after an unattended reboot. Test that
deliberately once — a reboot policy you have never exercised is a scheduled
outage.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.3  THE PROPOSE-ONLY HALF: DEPENDENCIES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```
  Renovate or Dependabot, configured to open PRs and NEVER auto-merge.
  Both are free on GitHub. Verify current terms (rule C-4).
```
```jsonc
// renovate.json
{
  "extends": ["config:recommended"],
  "automerge": false,               // the whole point
  "rangeStrategy": "pin",           // exact versions, matches ADDENDUM O
  "prConcurrentLimit": 5,           // do not drown yourself
  "schedule": ["before 6am on monday"],
  "vulnerabilityAlerts": {
    "labels": ["security"],
    "schedule": ["at any time"]     // security PRs are not batched
  },
  "packageRules": [
    {
      "matchPaths": ["signer/**"],
      "enabled": false              // the signer has no dependencies at all
    },
    {
      "matchDatasources": ["docker"],
      "pinDigests": true
    }
  ]
}
```
THE HUMAN STEP, and why it is not ceremony: before merging a dependency PR,
look at the diff for the specific things that indicate a compromise rather than
a fix — a new `postinstall` script, a new network call, a new dependency added
in a patch release, a maintainer change, a version published after a long gap
of inactivity. Most of the time this takes ninety seconds. The one time it does
not is the time it matters.

CI must run the full ADDENDUM O verification suite on every dependency PR. A
dependency change that breaks TEST-401, TEST-402, or any SUITE 1 test does not
get merged regardless of what it claims to fix.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.4  CTL-731: THE WEEKLY REVIEW AGENT — AND ITS CREDENTIAL MODEL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    THE RULE: the agent holds NO credential that can change anything.

Read-only, everywhere, with one exception: it may open a pull request. That is
the entire scope of its write access, and a PR is a proposal a human merges.

```
  MAY HAVE                                   MUST NOT HAVE
  ---------------------------------------    -------------------------------
  Read-only Postgres role (osiris_ro)        Any write DB credential
  Read-only Cloudflare API token             Cloudflare edit permissions
    (Analytics:Read, Logs:Read only)
  Read-only Oracle metrics access            SSH access to the host
  GitHub token scoped to open PRs            Push-to-main, deploy, or release
  Public internet (OSV.dev, crt.sh,          The signer account. At all.
    vendor status and pricing pages)         Ever. Not read-only either.
  The alert channel (write)                  The KEK, the request-signing key,
                                             any Docker secret
```
If the agent is compromised, the worst outcome is a misleading report and a bad
PR that a human declines. That is the correct blast radius for automation.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES, weekly:

  1. CVE SWEEP — the part a human genuinely cannot keep up with.
     OSV.dev has a free API with no key and, per their documentation, no rate
     limits. Batch-query every pinned dependency.
```bash
# Extract the exact pinned versions and ask OSV about all of them at once.
jq -r '.packages | to_entries[] | select(.key != "") |
       {package:{name:(.key|sub("^node_modules/";"")), ecosystem:"npm"},
        version:.value.version}' package-lock.json \
  | jq -s '{queries: .}' \
  | curl -s -X POST -d @- https://api.osv.dev/v1/querybatch \
  | jq '.results[] | select(.vulns != null)'
```
     Then the judgement part, which is where an LLM earns its place: for each
     finding, is the vulnerable code path actually reachable in this
     application? A prototype-pollution CVE in a package used only at build
     time is not the same as an RCE in the JSON parser on the webhook path.
     Rank by real exposure, not by CVSS score. Most weeks the honest answer is
     "none of these matter," and saying so clearly is valuable.

  2. CONTROL VERIFICATION — is the security posture still what we think?
```
     [ ] RLS enabled AND forced on every user-scoped table (read-only query)
     [ ] osiris_app still has rolbypassrls = false, rolsuper = false
     [ ] CSP header present on a live request, no unsafe-inline, nonce differs
         between two requests
     [ ] Cloudflare SSL mode is Full (Strict) — via API, not the dashboard
     [ ] Authenticated Origin Pulls still refuses a direct origin connection
     [ ] fail2ban active with the expected jails
     [ ] auditd reports enabled 2
     [ ] Signer /version matches the last recorded deploy commit and hash
     [ ] Every dead man's switch pinged on schedule this week
     [ ] Last backup succeeded; last restore drill passed and when
     [ ] Audit chain verifies from the last anchor
     [ ] No new Cloudflare API tokens, Access policies, or enrolled
         authenticators
```
     This catches the quiet regression — the control that got turned off during
     debugging three weeks ago and never turned back on. That is a far more
     common cause of breach than a zero-day.

  3. DRIFT DETECTION (CTL-733) — the risk that is specific to running on free
     tiers.
```
     [ ] Deno Deploy free tier terms and quotas: unchanged?
     [ ] Cloudflare free plan limits: unchanged?
     [ ] Oracle Always Free terms: unchanged? Any reclamation warning?
     [ ] Backblaze B2 / R2 free tier: unchanged?
     [ ] Current usage against each quota, with a projection
     [ ] Anything approaching 70% of a free limit → flag now, not at 100%
     [ ] Every perishable claim in ADDENDUM O APPENDIX A and ADDENDUM P
         APPENDIX: still accurate?
```
     Under a strict-$0 architecture this is not housekeeping. A free tier
     changing under you is a real availability and security event, and it
     arrives without a notification you will notice.

  4. EXPIRY WATCH — boring, and the cause of a surprising number of outages.
```
     [ ] Domain expiry               (alert at 90, 60, 30, 14, 7 days)
     [ ] Auto-renew actually enabled AND the card on file is valid
     [ ] TLS certificates            (edge, origin, origin-pull CA)
     [ ] Any pinned SPKI approaching rotation
     [ ] Telegram bot token age vs the 90-day rotation policy
     [ ] Node.js / Postgres / Redis version approaching end of life
```
     Losing the domain to an expired card is a total, self-inflicted outage
     with a phishing opportunity attached, and it happens to real companies
     every year.

  5. THE ALERT BUDGET REVIEW (ADDENDUM O CTL-700).
     What fired this week, how many times, and did any of it lead to an action?
     Any alert that fired more than twice without producing an action gets
     retuned or deleted. This is what stops the channel from becoming noise you
     mute — which is the failure mode that makes the entire alerting system
     worthless.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.5  WHERE THE AGENT RUNS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```
  OPTION A  A scheduled Claude session (this is set up for you — see the note
            at the end of this document). Best at the judgement parts: CVE
            triage, free-tier terms changes, reading advisories, writing the
            report in plain language. It has no access to your infrastructure,
            which is exactly the credential model above taken to its limit.

  OPTION B  A GitHub Actions scheduled workflow with read-only secrets. Best at
            the mechanical parts: OSV queries, control verification against
            live endpoints, expiry checks. Free minutes on public repos; 2,000
            minutes/month on private (verify current terms).

  RECOMMENDED: both. B produces a machine-readable facts file every Monday and
  posts it; A reads those facts, applies judgement, and writes the report.
  Machines for the checking, model for the interpretation.

  NEVER: an agent with SSH access, write DB access, deploy rights, or any
  signer credential. If a proposal ever begins "give the agent access so it can
  fix things automatically," that is the proposal to decline.
```

================================================================================
PART 8 — CTL-732: THE WEEKLY REPORT
================================================================================

One message, Monday morning, that you actually read. If it is longer than a
screen you will stop reading it by week six, so the format is constrained on
purpose.

```
📋 OSIRIS WEEKLY · 2026-08-10 to 2026-08-16 · week 33

  All controls verified. No action required this week.
```
